messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell slows a step behind the others and lets his eyes do the walking: the scattered tools, the empty traces on the cart, the sheds, the upper terraces, any spot where a man with a bow could lie flat. He's checking for tracks in the dust too. Did the workers leave in a crowd, in a hurry, or were they dragged?

Quietly, out of the side of his mouth, to Bram and Sefa:
"Quarry this size, middle of the morning, and nobody's swinging a pick. I don't like it. Our warden's got keys and folded arms. Either he's waiting for us, or he's waiting for someone and we're not it."

He keeps his hands loose and well away from his shortsword and lifts one in an easy greeting toward the man in the doorway. He stays a pace back and off to Bram's side, where he can see past the man into the house.

He calls out, friendly enough:
"Morning! We're sent by Maela Thorn from Beregost, come for her case. Quiet day for it, eh? Where's your crew got to?"

While the man answers, Pell watches his face and hands. Is he nervous, lying, glancing back into the house or up at the terraces?

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Quiet for a working quarry,” I murmur to Pell and Sefa.

I walk into the yard toward the house, sword sheathed and shield low, looking over the abandoned tools and terraces for signs of trouble. I stop a few paces short of the man, leaving his doorway clear.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us for a sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?” I glance back across the silent yard. “Everyone all right here?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa slows as they come to the edge of the yard, eyes moving over the scattered tools, the half-loaded cart, the still lifting frame. She keeps her hands away from her dagger and her voice level, but the quiet has her wary. "Well met to the house," she calls across the distance. "We've come from Beregost—Maela Thorn sent us to collect the case of dye-salts. Is the warden about?"

To Pell and Bram, lower: "No one working. Not one voice. Keep your eyes open."

scenes.narration:
Close up, the dust tells most of the story without anyone needing to ask.

Pell's eyes go over the yard the way they'd go over a house he meant to get into. The terraces above are bare white steps with nowhere to lie flat, and no bowman would last a minute up there in this glare. The tracks are easy to read. Fine chalk takes a print like flour on a board, and the yard is trodden with boots: a dozen men or more, all heading out down the cart track toward the Way. They went together at a walking pace, with no scuffing, no drag marks and nothing dark soaked into the white. One set of mule tracks goes with them, a man's boots beside it. Near the lower cut, not every tool has simply been dropped. Three hammers stand on their heads on a squared block, side by side, the way you'd leave a thing you meant someone to find.

The man in the doorway lets the three of them come. He has a grey beard with chalk in it, and his forearms are as thick as cart-shafts. Bram stops a few paces short of him, leaving the doorway clear. The man notices that, and something in his shoulders lets go a quarter-inch.

"Hale," he says. "Osric Hale. Warden." He looks at Bram, then at Pell's raised hand, then at Sefa. "Thorn's lot. Thought so."

Pell watches him while he talks. There's no glance at the terraces and no hand drifting to the keys. The man isn't afraid of anything outside. What's on his face is older and more tired than fear, and it's sour. Past his shoulder Pell can see a low room with a hearth, a kettle, a table stacked with papers and a slate. On a shelf above the fire sits a squat box bound with iron straps, a blob of red wax on its lid. Hale doesn't look round at it once, and he doesn't need to.

"Crew walked," he says to Pell. "Yesterday. Noon bell." He moves his jaw as if he's chewing something. "Three weeks. Not a copper come down from the Gate."

To Bram's question he gives a short breath through his nose. "All right. Nobody's hurt, if that's what you're asking. Nobody's paid either."

Then he turns to Sefa, since she's the one who asked for the warden by name.

"Your case is in there. It's ready. Been ready a week." He unfolds his arms and hooks a thumb in the key ring, not taking it off. "Thorn paid for it. She'll have paid somebody. It wasn't me, and it wasn't my lads. Before that box leaves this house I want to know who she paid, and how much." He stops, then adds, "That's all."

The smoke from the chimney keeps rising, thin and straight. The yard is so quiet you can hear the kettle ticking as it cools.

The rules:
- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.
Then say who is waiting at the end of it: a character in this scene who is asleep, unconscious, or has said they wait for something named (until dawn, until another comes back) and has nothing to decide until it comes — with what ends the wait, in a few words. A character with anything to decide is never waiting.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’ve stood waiting for wages myself. Won’t tell you it’s a small matter.”

I keep my voice level. “But Thorn hired us to carry the case, not handle her accounts. She didn’t say who she paid or how much. Promised the three of us ninety gold on delivery before sunset.”

I nod toward the papers inside. “Have you got an order or a receipt naming who took her money? We can look at that together. Might give us something better than guesses.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps forward, stopping just shy of the doorway so Hale isn't crowded, though she doesn't take her eyes off him.

"Let's settle it here, then. I won't pretend we were sent with the answer—we weren't. Maela hired us off the Trade Way yesterday and gave us a case to fetch, that's all. But I'd like to know what she told you. A name, a day, a sum. If she left word with someone in Beregost, maybe it's written down."

She glances past him, openly, at the table and the papers, then back. "You've kept her case safe a week. You stayed when your lads walked. I see no reason not to help you get what you're owed—but the box needs to be on the road before long, or none of us are paid, and your lads go another week hungry either way. May I come in and look at what's on that table?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lets his hand drop and steps up level with Bram. He keeps his voice easy, one working man to another.

"Fair question. Honest answer is we don't know. We're hired legs, Master Hale. Thorn pays us on delivery, by sunset, or not at all. Nobody showed us her ledger." He nods past him at the iron-strapped box on the shelf, then looks back at Hale's face. "But I know the shape of this. Somebody up in the Gate is getting paid for your stone and your salts, and the coin's stopping in his purse instead of rolling down the hill. Three weeks is long enough that it's not a late courier."

He jerks his chin toward the lower cut, at the three hammers standing on their heads on the block.

"Your lads left those for somebody to read. A strike mark? Or a message for whoever comes up from the Gate?"

Then he gets practical:

"Who's the owner? Who's supposed to send your pay, and who carries it? Give us names. Write it on that slate if you like, with what you're owed. Thorn's a merchant. She'll know who she settled with, and she'll want to know her money went astray, because a quarry with no crew sells her no salts next season. We put your note in her hand alongside the case, today. That's a better road to your coin than keeping the box on a shelf. Keep it there and nobody's paid, you included."

He keeps his eyes on Hale while he says it. Is the man after his wages, or after someone in particular?

scenes.narration:
Hale hears Bram out without moving. When Bram mentions waiting for wages himself, the warden's eyes go to the old company mark painted over on his shield, then come back up.

"Receipt," he says. "No. Order. That I've got."

Sefa asks to come in, and he looks at her for a long moment. Then he steps aside, just far enough. The room smells of cold ash and wet slate. On the table there's a slate covered in chalk tallies, two sheets of cheap paper written out in a heavy hand, and a folded letter with a broken wax seal, a black tower on grey. He pushes the letter across the boards to her with one finger.

It's a short letter in a clerk's neat hand:

*To the warden at Whitestone. Release to M. Thorn, apothecary, of Beregost, one case of salt of the low seam, twelve pounds, sealed. Paid in full at the Gate. Release on her messenger's word. For House Vandarren, by the hand of Jeren Vossick, factor.*

The letter gives no sum. Under it, the two cheap sheets are letters Hale wrote to Vossick, dated nine days apart. The second one is shorter than the first, and the last line is pressed so hard the pen tore the paper: *The men will not wait past the feast of the month.*

"Paid in full," Hale says to Bram, who has come in behind Sefa. "At the Gate. So Vossick's had her money. A week, at least. Ten days." He doesn't look at the shelf. "Wages come down with the same man who carries Vossick's letters. Every month. Not this month."

Pell is still standing beside Bram, and Hale turns to his questions one at a time.

"Owner's House Vandarren. Patriars. Never seen one up here. Vossick sends the pay." He jerks his head at the yard. "Hammers. That's a strike. The tools are the House's. Lads left them where the House can find them, set out proper. Nobody's hurt. Nobody stole."

Pell watches him the whole time, and there's nothing hidden in it. The man wants money for his men, not one man's head. The anger is for Vossick, and it's the dull, familiar anger of a man who has written the same letter twice. There's only one moment that doesn't fit. Pell nods at the lower cut, and Hale answers about the hammers without once looking that way. He looks at the table, the floor, Pell's face, but not at the cut.

He takes the chalk and writes on the slate under the tallies, slowly: *14 men. 3 wks. 56 gp. Carter 8.*

"Sixty-four gold," he says. "That's what's owed."

- Write each screen in the second person: "you" is that character.
- Begin with what the other characters in the scene did and said, as this character saw and heard it, from what their players wrote — retold in your own words, never theirs: what they did as seen from outside (never their thoughts, feelings or intentions), and what they said as reported speech or a short paraphrase that keeps its sense, its names and its numbers (a whisper only for the one it was whispered to). Never copy a run of a player's words, not even a line of their speech. Do not repeat the character's own message back to them.
- Then your narration, in its own words wherever the character perceives it; change only who is addressed — and where your narration quotes a player character's words, retell them as above.
- Leave out what only another character perceives: their thoughts and feelings, what only they noticed, read, found or were told in private, a check's outcome only they could know, words spoken where this character cannot hear.
- Call another character by name only once this character has heard the name; until then, as they appear.
- Add nothing beyond your narration and the players' messages. Never reveal what only the game master knows.
- A character who perceives nothing of it gets an empty screen.
- Write the screens in the order you are asked for them.

Then say who is where at the end of it: group the characters who are together (can see and hear each other) — every character in this scene in exactly one group; a character from elsewhere who, by your narration, is now with them joins their group — and name each one's place in a few words.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa reads the letter once, then again, and taps a finger beside "Paid in full at the Gate."

"That's a release order, not a receipt. Vossick says the salts were paid—he doesn't say your wages were." She looks up from the paper. "But it's House Vandarren's own clerk telling you to give Thorn her goods. So the box is hers, and withholding it makes you the one breaking the order, not the House."

She softens it with a small step back from the table. "We'll carry your note and your tally to her, and we'll bring back her answer to you, not a promise from her to me. But let's put it in writing and be gone. If she's been paid by Vossick already, she can settle your wages and take it out of him. If not, you'll know that by tonight."

She glances toward the cutting-shed. "The book's down there? I'll fetch it. My eyes are good on written things, and if it's chalked or smudged I can read it." She pauses, then adds, "Bram, stay with the warden—watch him write the slate. Pell, keep an eye on the yard. I'll be back directly."

With that she steps to the door and heads down toward the low stone hut, not hurrying, not dallying.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell reads the letter over Sefa's shoulder. He memorises the seal, the black tower on grey, and the names Vandarren and Vossick, the way he used to memorise doors. Then he taps the slate.

"Pell Dunmore. Put that by the box. If Thorn says who and how much, I'll carry it back up this hill myself. That's mine to give, not hers." He glances at Bram and Sefa and leaves them room to add their own names or not.

He nods out the door, down the slope.

"I'll walk down with you for the book. Save your knees the climb back."

He doesn't move yet. He says it quieter, without any edge:

"Master Hale, you'll talk about those hammers all day, but you won't look at that cut. Low seam's where the salts come from, isn't it? Grey, wet stone." He holds Hale's eye. "If there's something down there besides a ledger, I'd rather hear it from you up here than find it with my feet. We've a sunset to make, and nobody needs surprises."

If Hale still means to go down, Pell goes with him, a half-step to the side. He watches the plank door of the shed, the ground in front of it for fresh prints or water, and the dark edge of the cutting beyond. His hand stays near his shortsword without touching it.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’ll put my name to that. Bram Halloway. I’ll ask Thorn who she paid and how much, and bring you her answer myself. If she won’t answer, I’ll come back and tell you that plainly. I can’t promise her honesty or the House’s wages.”

I glance at Pell and Sefa. “That’s my promise. Doesn’t bind either of you.”

Then I turn back to Hale. “Let’s get your tally-book and put the names and days in writing. Where in the shed do you keep it?”

scenes.narration:
Hale lets Sefa finish. Then he takes the letter back from under her finger and folds it along its old creases.

"Order says release on her messenger's word," he says. "Doesn't say what day."

So he knows exactly what he's holding back, and he means to keep holding it. Sefa is already at the door. He looks after her, then at the two men still in the room.

Pell gives his name and Hale picks up the chalk. He writes it under the sixty-four, *Dunmore*, the letters as heavy as his tallies. Bram gives his, with its limits stated plainly, and the warden listens to all of it, the part about coming back to say so if Thorn won't answer too. He chews on that before he writes *Halloway* beside the first name.

"Two," he says. "Good." To Bram: "Shelf left of the door. Oilcloth. Box stays on that shelf till I'm back."

Then Pell asks about the cut, quietly, and for the first time Hale doesn't answer straight away. He puts the chalk down and wipes his fingers on his apron, slowly, one at a time.

"Low seam. Yes. Salt grows on the wall down there. Pinkish." He stops. "Air's bad. Wet, close. Men get slow in it. I don't keep a man on that face more than an hour." He looks at Pell, and this time he means it. "Stay off the grey. Nothing down there but water."

He unhooks a single key from the ring, a long iron one, and goes out. Pell walks a half-step to his side.

---

Sefa gets to the cutting-shed first. Close up it's older than it looked from the house. The walls are dry-laid white blocks, and moss has crept green into the joints on the downhill side. The plank door is shut with an iron hasp and a padlock the size of a fist. Beyond the shed the ground falls away into the lower cutting, where the white turns grey and slick. A breath of air comes up out of it, cold for a summer morning, and it smells of wet stone.

Pell reads the ground as he walks down beside Hale. There are old boot-prints in front of the door, the crew's from yesterday or earlier, all of them dried into the chalk. There are no fresh ones but Hale's, coming up and going back this morning. At the lip of the cut, a few paces past the shed, the white is darker in a broad stain where water seeps out of the rock and runs down into the grey.

Hale opens the lock and swings the door in. He doesn't follow it. He stands on the threshold with one hand on the frame.

Inside, the shed is dim and smells of tallow and something else, faint and sweet, like a bakehouse with the oven gone cold. scenes.narration:
Bram leaves the box where it sits, leaves the order and the torn letters on the table, and steps out into the glare.

From the doorstep the slope runs down white and bare to the cutting-shed, a hundred-odd feet below. The plank door stands open, and Hale's broad, aproned back fills the threshold. Bram cups a hand and calls the warning down. In that dead quiet his voice carries the whole way, off the stone and back again. Whether it reaches the shed in time to matter is down there with them.

Then he does what he did for ten years at the edge of every camp. He picks a spot where the doorframe is at his shoulder and the room behind him has only the one way in, and he lets his eyes work the ground in a slow circle.

He knows this kind of ground without needing to think about it. The terraces above are bare white steps with no lip deep enough to hide a man, the same thing Pell saw. Anyone coming in has three ways to do it. There's the cart track, which drops in two long bends toward the Way and is empty for a mile, its dust lying undisturbed. There's a goat-path along the spoil heaps on the north side, gone soft and crumbly, with nothing on it fresher than the rain. And there's the lip of the lower cut, which nobody would walk unless he had to. Nobody is on any of them. A jackdaw sits on the crossbeam of the idle lifting frame, cocks its head at him and goes back to picking at something in the joint.

Far off to the west, where the hill falls away to the plain, the Trade Way shows as a thin pale line through green. One ox-wagon crawls along it northward, so slow it hardly seems to move, the only thing out there and well past caring about Whitestone.

Behind him in the house the kettle has gone completely quiet. The case sits on its shelf with the red wax towards the room. On the table the slate holds two names in chalk, and one of them is his.

Nothing comes up the track while he stands there.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stays on the threshold beside Hale, not inside. He breathes shallow through his nose and doesn't like the sweet smell one bit.

While Sefa reads, his eyes go over the room the way they'd go over a strongroom. He looks at the brazier: is the ash fresh or old, and are there pink crusts or crystals in it? He checks the floor around it for scrape marks or a ring where it's been moved. At the back he looks at the planks. Are they nailed or just laid down, and is there a gap at the edges with cold air coming up? Do any boots, a rope, or a ladder-end show near them? He keeps his own feet on the white.

Low, to Hale, without looking at him:

"Somebody's been burning your salt in that brazier. Pink ash doesn't come from charcoal." A beat. "And that's no floor at the back. That's a lid."

He lets it sit a moment, then turns his head and looks the warden in the face. His voice stays even, not accusing.

"You won't step in here, Master Hale, and you won't look at the back. Men get slow in the bad air, you said. Did one of them get slow in here? Sweet-smelling smoke and a hole under the boards. Is that why your lads really walked?"

Out of the corner of his mouth, to Sefa:
"Read quick, and don't linger by that brazier. If your head starts swimming, out you come."

If the GM wants it, Pell is looking hard at the brazier and the planks: for Investigation.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa unties the book and opens it carefully, cradling the damp pages so they don't tear. She angles it toward the light from the doorway and leafs back to the last three weeks, then reads the names aloud, one by one, clearly, with the days beside them, exactly as they stand. Where the chalk or ink is smudged she reads it anyway—her eyes slide over the marks as if the words straighten for her.

As she reads, she keeps one eye on Hale's face and the other on the pages, but her attention catches twice on the room around her: the pink ash in the brazier, and the still, sweet smell underneath the tallow. She says nothing about either yet.

When the last name is read, she closes the book but doesn't tie it. "Those are the men owed. Three weeks, as you said." She glances toward the boarded part of the floor, then back to him. "I'll copy the three weeks as they stand so Thorn can't say we guessed at it. But while I'm here—what was burning in that brazier? The ash is wrong for a fire of shavings."

While Sefa reads, his eyes go over the room the way they'd go over a strongroom. He looks at the brazier: is the ash fresh or old, and are there pink crusts or crystals in it? He checks the floor around it for scrape marks or a ring where it's been moved. At the back he looks at the planks. Are they nailed or just laid down, and is there a gap at the edges with cold air coming up? Do any boots, a rope, or a ladder-end show near them? He keeps his own feet on the white.

Low, to Hale, without looking at him:

"Somebody's been burning your salt in that brazier. Pink ash doesn't come from charcoal." A beat. "And that's no floor at the back. That's a lid."

He lets it sit a moment, then turns his head and looks the warden in the face. His voice stays even, not accusing.

"You won't step in here, Master Hale, and you won't look at the back. Men get slow in the bad air, you said. Did one of them get slow in here? Sweet-smelling smoke and a hole under the boards. Is that why your lads really walked?"

Out of the corner of his mouth, to Sefa:
"Read quick, and don't linger by that brazier. If your head starts swimming, out you come."

If the GM wants it, Pell is looking hard at the brazier and the planks: [Roll the die] for Investigation.

scenes.narration:
Pell stays on the threshold with his boots on the white chalk and breathes through his nose as little as he can. The sweet smell is faint, like bread left too long in a cold oven.

He runs his eyes over the room the way he'd look over a strongroom: the brazier first, then the flags around it, then the boarded back third. He's after the small things that tell you what a room is really for.

Pell reads the room the way he'd read a strongroom, and it gives up its details.

The ash in the brazier is old, a week or more. Damp has got into it and set it into a crust, and it has the dead, flat pink of dried roses. But the crust doesn't reach the rim. A band of clean iron runs round the inside of the bowl, so something was scraped out of it, a week or so back if the crust is anything to go by. Little glassy specks are stuck in the ash, pale and gritty, the kind of thing that spits and pops on a fire. Nobody has moved the brazier. Its three legs stand in three worn dimples in the flags, years deep. Whatever gets done here, it gets done in that spot, again and again.

The planks at the back aren't nailed. They're laid side by side across two blackened joists, each held down by its own weight. Their seams sweat, and at the right-hand corner, where a plank stops short of the wall, a thin cold draught comes up. It's the same wet-stone breath that rises out of the lower cut. One plank is newer than the others, paler, with saw-marks still crisp on its end. There's no rope, no ladder and no prints on the boards. Nobody has walked on them for a long time.

When Pell shifts his weight on the threshold, the flag under his heel gives a dull note. It doesn't ring like stone on stone. It sounds the way a step over a cellar does.

Sefa reads all the while. She has the book open in the light from the door, its swollen pages held flat in her palm. Some of the ink has run, and some names have been written over in chalk and half wiped away, but her eyes go over the marks as if they were fresh. She gives each name with its days, plainly:

"Aldo Pike, eighteen days. Gerrit Pike, eighteen. Wynn Carrow, eighteen. Dace Tolliver. Ned Furrow. Ansel Brooke. Jory Venn. Cobb Sallow. Ulf Dray. Perrin Lusk. Tam Greave. Ivo Rendle. Sim Barrow. Hew Madden. Eighteen days each." Below them, on a line to itself: "Hobb Marl, carting, twenty-one days, and the mule."

Hale gives one small nod at each name, like a man counting stones into a cart. He doesn't check her once.

"Fourteen," he says when she's done. "And Hobb. Right."

Then Pell speaks, low. *Somebody's been burning your salt in that brazier. That's no floor at the back, that's a lid.* Then the two questions, the second one level and straight into his face. A moment later Sefa asks hers from inside: what burned there? Hale stands with his hand on the doorframe and hears them both out.

He takes a short breath through his nose.

"Me," he says. "I burn it." He nods at the bowl without looking at it. "Comes off the wall wet. Won't keep wet. Rots the case. So you dry it. Low fire, the coals under, salt on a tray over." He moves his hand flat in the air, showing the tray. "Door open. Man outside. Stir it with a long rake. That's how it's done. That's how it was done before me."

That accounts for the band of clean iron. The tray was lifted off, and the grit that spat through it was left behind.

"Thorn's twelve pound. Dried here. Eight days back."

To the second question, about the lid, he answers more slowly.

"Old working. Under there. Wet. Goes down to the low seam the back way. Boarded before my time." He stops. "One board's mine. Last spring. Old one went soft."

Then he comes to the one Pell asked last, *did one of them get slow in here*, and for a moment he doesn't answer at all. He looks at Pell's face, then past him at the white glare outside.

"Not in here," he says. "Down there. Three years back. Tobin Reed." His jaw works. "Drowned. Drink."

He says *drink* as flatly as he said *eighteen days*. But his free hand wipes itself on his apron once, slowly, as if there's chalk on it that won't come off. Pell has heard plenty of men say a thing they wrote down rather than a thing they believe, and this one sounds the same.

"Lads walked for wages," Hale goes on, steadier now that he's back on ground he's sure of. "Nothing else. Ask any of them. They're in Beregost drinking what they haven't got." He looks at Sefa and the open book. "Copy it, then. The three weeks. Bench is dry."

He stays on the threshold, half a step to Pell's left, and his boots don't move. The cold breath from the corner of the boards keeps coming, steady as breathing.

"You won't step in here, Master Hale, and you won't look at the back. Men get slow in the bad air, you said. Did one of them get slow in here? Sweet-smelling smoke and a hole under the boards. Is that why your lads really walked?"

"Read quick, and don't linger by that brazier. If your head starts swimming, out you come."

Pell reads the room the way he'd read a strongroom, and it gives up its details.

The ash in the brazier is old, a week or more. Damp has got into it and set it into a crust, and it has the dead, flat pink of dried roses. But the crust doesn't reach the rim. A band of clean iron runs round the inside of the bowl, so something was scraped out of it, a week or so back if the crust is anything to go by. Little glassy specks are stuck in the ash, pale and gritty, the kind of thing that spits and pops on a fire. Nobody has moved the brazier. The planks at the back aren't nailed. They're laid side by side across two blackened joists, each held down by its own weight. Their seams sweat, and at the right-hand corner, where a plank stops short of the wall, a thin cold draught comes up. It's the same wet-stone breath that rises out of the lower cut. That accounts for the band of clean iron. The tray was lifted off, and the grit that spat through it was left behind.

scenes.narration:
Bram sets the shield's rim against his boot and leans the weight of it on his leg. It's a sentry's way of standing, and his body falls into it without being told.

The sun has climbed while he's stood there. The shadow of the doorframe has shrunk to a hand's width on the step, and the white terraces throw the glare back so hard he has to squint at the far side of the yard. The jackdaw has given up on the lifting frame and moved to the edge of the half-loaded cart. It walks up and down the stones as if it's counting them.

Every so often he looks down the slope. The shed door is still open, and Hale's broad back still fills it. Voices drift up the hundred feet of chalk, low and steady. One is a woman's, reading something in an even run, a name and then a pause, then another name. The other voice is short and heavy, a word or two at a time. He can't make out the words, only the rhythm. Nobody calls out, and nobody's voice rises.

Out on the plain the ox-wagon has crawled maybe a quarter-mile further north. Nothing moves on the cart track. Behind him in the house a log settles in the cold hearth with a soft tick, and the case sits on its shelf with the wax toward the room.

He keeps his ears on the shed and goes on watching.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
The cold smell off the boards is plain to you now: wet stone, and under it that faint sweet note, like bread left too long in a cold oven. It doesn't swirl or thicken; it just lies there, coming up slow as a well.

You cross to the bench, and Hale doesn't move to follow. The bench is dry, as he said. The book opens flat on it, and the pages breathe out chalk and tallow. There is a stub of pencil in a tin cup.

Pell doesn't take his eyes off Hale. "Three years back," he says, as if testing the number. "And you boarded over it last spring. Was there a man down there again, or is it the wages you're afraid will find the hole?" The warden's jaw tightens, and for a second it looks like he might say something else—but then he only steps one pace back from the door, so the daylight falls full across the bench where you stand.

"Copy it," he says to you. "Then we'll talk price for the road."

The book is open in front of you. The pencil nib is blunt but it will serve. The last three weeks run in a column down the left-hand page: names, days, and a line of Hale's slow arithmetic. On the facing page, among the older tallies, one entry has been crossed through and written again beneath it: *J. Vossick — advance — 20 gp — Wynn Carrow's lot.* It isn't in Hale's hand. It's neat, small, done with a lighter touch.

You can copy the three weeks as he asked, or pause over the facing page, or ask what you want. Hale watches the yard through the open door, his ring of keys still on his belt, his arms folded across his front. The mule is gone. The smoke above the house still threads upward, barely drawn.

No new records.

Where you are: in the salt-drying room, at the copy-bench with the tally-book open · Time: Day 1 · morning

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell taps the flag under his heel once more, lightly, and listens to the dull note. He doesn't go further in. He steps back onto solid chalk beside Hale.

"Hollow under the doorstep too," he says, mild, as if remarking on the weather. "Old workings run everywhere under here, then." He lets that go.

He's quiet a moment, watching Hale's hand on the apron.

"Tobin Reed," he says. He just repeats it, the way you'd set a stone on a cairn. "Drink, you wrote. Somebody wrote it." He shrugs, gentle. "I've written a few things down myself because they were easier to carry than the truth. Not my business, Master Hale. But if what you wrote and what you think aren't the same, and it's tied to that seam and Thorn's salt, you'd want us to know before we hand her the case and walk off. You've got two names on your slate now. That's two people who'll come back up this hill."

He gives Hale room to answer or not. If he says nothing more, Pell doesn't push.

Then, plainly, over his shoulder:

"Sefa, copy it quick as you can manage clean. Sun's climbing, and it's half a day back." To Bram: "Once she's done, we take the box, we take Hale's note, and we're on the track."

To Hale:

"Write your note while she copies. Sixty-four owed, the House's order, Vossick's name, your two letters to him, dates. Short, so Thorn reads it all the way through. I'll put it in her hand myself."

While they work he stays at the door. Every so often he looks down the slope at the wet grey cut and the dark corner of the boards, and he keeps his feet on the white.

scenes.narration:
Sefa crosses to the bench and the warden stays where he is. The bench is dry, as he said. The book opens flat on the boards and breathes out a smell of chalk and old tallow, and there's a stub of pencil in a tin cup at the back. She finds the last three weeks, a column of names down the left-hand page with Hale's slow sums beside them, and starts to copy in the light from the door.

At the threshold, Pell taps the hollow flag with his heel once more. It gives the same dull note. Then he steps back off it, onto the white chalk at Hale's elbow.

"Hollow under the doorstep too," he says. "Old workings run everywhere under here, then."

Hale doesn't answer that. Then Pell says *Tobin Reed* and nothing after it, and that the warden does hear. He listens to all of it: things written down because they were easier to carry, two names on the slate, two people who'll come back up the hill. His hand has stopped moving on the apron.

"Four foot of water," he says. "Where they found him. Not deep enough to stand in to your chin." His jaw works once. "Fist wanted a word for the book. I gave 'em one."

He looks at the open door, not at Pell.

"Note. Aye. At the house. Paper's there." To Sefa's back: "Copy clean."

The ground goes without any warning.

There's no crack and no creak first. The chalk under Pell's boots just stops being there. A crust as thin as a pie-lid has been lying over nothing, and it folds in under his weight in a soft rush of white. The threshold flag tips up on its edge and goes in after him. Hale's hand snatches out and closes on air a foot from Pell's collar. Pell drops into dark and cold and the noise of falling stone.

He drops eight feet and hits water, then stone under the water, hard. His hip and shoulder take the worst of it, and the edge of something squared slams into his ribs on the way down. It's bruising and it knocks the wind out of him, but nothing breaks. Then the cold closes over his chest, and that's worse than the fall: it's spring-water cold, coming out of the rock.

He comes up gasping. The water is chest-deep. When he tries to get his feet under him, his left leg doesn't come.

A block of squared white stone, the size of a small chest, has come down with the rotten floor and settled across his shin below the knee. The shin isn't crushed, but it's held fast against the bottom, wedged between the block and something under the silt. When he pulls, the block grinds a finger's width and stops.

Light falls in through the ragged hole above, a column of white glare with chalk dust turning in it. By that light Pell can see where he is. It's a low working, hewn square, its roof just above the hole. One way it runs back under the shed, where the planks of Hale's lid show as dark stripes on the ceiling with a thread of daylight between two of them. The other way it runs off into black toward the lower cut. The walls are wet, and in the seams of the grey stone grows a crust of pinkish crystal like hoarfrost. The sweet bakehouse smell is much stronger down here.

One of the old joists has come down with him. It's a blackened beam as long as a man, half-floating against the wall, with one end sunk in the silt.

The block lies tilted in the water. Its upper face is clear of the surface and faces the light, and there's carving on it. Someone cut a sunburst into the stone, wide rays round a round face, worn soft but deliberate. A ring of small marks runs round it, close-set notches and strokes like a mason's tallies, too even and too many to be idle.

The water is moving. A seep comes in from the dark on the cut side, a thin steady trickle he can hear more than see, and the surface laps a little higher on his chest each time it settles.

Above, Hale is down on his belly at the edge of the hole, his beard white with fresh dust. "*Don't thrash!*" Then, louder, with his head turned up the slope: "*Halloway!*" The shout goes up the white hillside and comes back off the terraces.

Inside the shed, Sefa is at the bench with the pencil in her hand. The doorway she was copying by is a broken lip of chalk and a hole full of noise, and Pell isn't in it any more.

*(Out of game: Sefa's paragraph included lines for Pell and Hale and an entry in the book; I've played only what Sefa does. There's no "Vossick advance" entry on that page.)*
*(Out of game: Pell can try to pull his leg free alone once an hour, a Strength (Athletics) check at DC 18, and each failed try costs him a few hit points. Two of you with a rope and that beam as a lever can shift the block in a few minutes at no other cost. Pell has 24 of 33 hit points.)*

 *(Out of game: copying the names needed no roll, since it's plain clerk's work. Sefa got partway down the column before the floor gave way, so her copy is started but not finished.)*

Hale speaks of four foot of water, where they found Reed, not deep enough to stand in to your chin. His jaw works once. He says Fist wanted a word for the book, and he gave them one. He looks at the open door and says he'll write the note at the house, where the paper is. To your back he says to copy clean.

Pell tells you to copy as fast as you can keep it clean, since the sun is climbing and it is half a day back. He tells Hale to write the note while you copy: the sum of sixty-four owed, the House's order, and Vossick's name, plus his two letters, the dates, all short enough for Thorn to read through.

Then the ground goes without warning. There is no crack and no creak first, only a soft rush of white, and the threshold flag tips up on its edge and falls away. Hale's hand snatches at air a foot from Pell's collar. Pell is gone into dark and the noise of falling stone.

You are at the bench with the pencil in your hand. The doorway you were copying by is a broken lip of chalk and a hole full of noise, and Pell isn't in it any more. Hale is down on his belly at the edge, his beard white with dust. He shouts for Pell not to thrash, then, with his head turned up the slope, bellows for Halloway. The shout goes up the white hillside and comes back off the terraces.

Your copy is started but not finished.
screens.Pell Dunmore:
You tap the flag under your heel once more and hear the same dull note, then step back onto the white chalk at Hale's elbow. You remark that it is hollow under the doorstep too, so old workings must run everywhere under here. Hale doesn't answer. You say Tobin Reed and nothing after it, then say that you've written things down because they were easier to carry than the truth. You tell him that if what he wrote and what he thinks differ, and it ties to that seam and Thorn's salt, he'd want you to know before the case is handed to her. "Four foot of water," he says. "Where they found him. Not deep enough to stand in to your chin." His jaw works once. "Fist wanted a word for the book. I gave 'em one." He looks at the open door, not at you, and says he'll write the note at the house, where the paper is. To Sefa's back he says, "Copy clean."

You tell Sefa to copy as quickly as she can manage cleanly, since the sun is climbing and it is half a day back. You tell Hale to write the note while she copies, with sixty-four owed, the House's order, Vossick's name, his two letters and the dates, short enough for Thorn to read through.

Then the ground goes without warning. There is no crack and no creak first. The chalk under your boots just stops being there. A crust as thin as a pie-lid folds in under your weight in a soft rush of white, and the threshold flag tips up on its edge and follows you down. Hale's hand snatches at air a foot from your collar. You drop into dark and cold and the noise of falling stone.

You fall eight feet and hit water, then stone under the water, hard. Your hip and shoulder take the worst of it, and the edge of something squared slams into your ribs. It bruises and knocks the wind out of you, but nothing breaks. The cold closes over your chest, and that is worse than the fall: spring-water cold, coming out of the rock.

scenes.narration:
Bram cups a hand and sends the call down the slope. *All quiet up here. How's the note coming?* It carries off the white stone as cleanly as his first warning did.

What comes back isn't an answer about the note.

He catches the end of a sound first, a soft heavy rush, like a sack of meal emptied onto a floor, and under it a deep knock of stone hitting stone, muffled as if it came from under the ground. The steady rhythm of Sefa's reading has stopped. A plume of white dust rolls out of the shed doorway and hangs there in the still air, glowing in the sun.

Then Hale's voice rises up the hillside, louder than anything the man has said all morning:

"*Halloway!*"

Through the settling dust Bram can see the warden flat on his belly across where the threshold used to be, his head and one arm reaching down into the ground in front of the door. The doorway itself has changed shape. The bottom of it is a broken lip of chalk, and there is nobody standing in it. Bram can't see Pell anywhere on the slope or by the shed. Faint and flattened by the distance, a second shout comes up, aimed down into the ground rather than up the hill: something about *thrash*.

The jackdaw bursts off the cart in a clatter of wings and heads for the terraces.

Behind Bram the house is silent. The case is on its shelf with the wax facing the room, the slate holds its two names, and his hempen rope hangs coiled at his belt. Down the slope the dust drifts slowly toward the lower cut.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets the pencil drop and backs a step from the bench, heart hammering. She moves toward the broken threshold in a crouch, testing each board before she puts weight on it, keeping to the side of the hole, away from the sagging lip.

"Pell! Answer if you can!" she calls down, pitching her voice clear through the dust.

She doesn't lean far. Instead she murmurs a cantrip, and light kindles on a chip of chalk she scoops from the board beside her. She drops it into the hole—not thrown, just loosed from her fingers—so they can see how far down he is and whether he's moving. Her other hand is already half-raised, ready to reach with Spare the Dying if he needs it, though she knows the edge may be rotten.

"Bram!" she adds, sharp, up the slope. "Bring rope! The yard's undermined!"

scenes.narration:
Sefa lets the pencil fall. It rolls off the bench and clicks on the flags, and she is already moving, low, a hand on the bench edge. She tests each flag with the ball of her foot before she trusts it. The ones nearest the bench are solid and ring like stone on stone. Two strides from the door the note goes dull, the same dull sound Pell's heel found, and she edges sideways along the wall and keeps the door frame at her shoulder.

What's left of the threshold is a ragged lip of chalk. Bits of it keep breaking off and pattering into the dark. Hale is spread flat across the outside edge with his arms reaching in, his weight laid out the way a man lies on bad ice.

"Not there," he says, without looking round. "Lip's going. Left of you. That flag holds."

She calls down. Her voice goes into the hole and comes back off the water. Then she turns her head and sends the second shout up the hill, and it carries off the terraces toward the house: rope, and the yard undermined.

She scoops up a chip of chalk the size of a thumbnail. She murmurs the cantrip, and the chip lights in her palm, clean and white. She opens her fingers over the hole and lets it fall.

The chip drops eight feet in a quick bright streak, hits the water with a small sound and keeps shining as it sinks. It comes to rest on the silt, and for a moment the whole flooded working lights up from below, green-white through the water. The light throws the ripples onto the walls.

Pell is down there. He's chest-deep and upright, his face turned up into the light, and he's moving: his arms are up and he's alive and holding himself above the water. His left leg goes down into the silt below the knee and doesn't come back up. A block of squared white stone, about the size of a small chest, lies tilted across that leg with its top face out of the water. A blackened beam as long as a man floats against the wall beside him, one end sunk in the mud. Up close the walls are crusted pink in every seam, like hoarfrost on a cellar step, and the sweet bakehouse smell comes up through the hole thick enough to taste.

The underwater light catches the block's upper face. There's a carving on it, a wide sunburst with a round face at its centre, worn soft but cut on purpose, and a ring of small even marks running round it. Behind the block, low on the wall, one patch of the hewn grey stone isn't hewn. It's smooth and pale, about the width of two hands, and it shines back at her a little more evenly than raw rock does.

Somewhere out of sight, on the side toward the cut, she can hear water trickling in, thin and steady.

Hale has watched the light go down. He takes a short breath through his nose.

"Leg's held. Not drowned." He pulls one arm back out of the hole and points behind her, into the shed, at the boarded back third. "Joist under them boards. Sound one, under the new plank. Tie off there, not this side. This side's rotten to the yard." His jaw works. "Rope goes down through the boards. Not through here."

He doesn't move to do it himself. He stays where he is, flat on the lip, with his eyes on the man in the water.

*(Out of game: as said before, freeing Pell takes two people working the rope and that beam as a lever, it takes a few minutes, and it costs nothing else. Sefa didn't need Spare the Dying: Pell is conscious.)*

"Not there," he says, without looking round. "Lip's going. Left of you. That flag holds."

You call down. Your voice goes into the hole and comes back off the water. Then you turn your head and send a second shout up the hill, toward the house, calling for Bram to bring rope because the yard is undermined.

You scoop up a chip of chalk the size of a thumbnail and murmur the cantrip. The chip lights in your palm, clean and white. You open your fingers over the hole and let it fall.

The chip drops eight feet in a quick bright streak, hits the water with a small sound and keeps shining as it sinks. It comes to rest on the silt, and for a moment the whole flooded working lights up from below, green-white through the water, throwing ripples onto the walls.

Pell is down there, chest-deep and upright, his face turned up into the light. He's alive and moving, his arms up, holding himself above the water. His left leg goes down into the silt below the knee and doesn't come back up. A block of squared white stone, about the size of a small chest, lies tilted across that leg with its top face out of the water. A blackened beam as long as a man floats against the wall beside him, one end sunk in the mud. Up close the walls are crusted pink in every seam, like hoarfrost on a cellar step, and the sweet bakehouse smell comes up through the hole thick enough to taste.

The underwater light catches the block's upper face. There's a carving on it, a wide sunburst with a round face at its centre, worn soft but cut on purpose, and a ring of small even marks running round it. Behind the block, low on the wall, one patch of the hewn grey stone isn't hewn. It's smooth and pale, about the width of two hands, and it shines back at you a little more evenly than raw rock does.

Somewhere out of sight, on the side toward the cut, you can hear water trickling in, thin and steady.

Hale has watched the light go down. He takes a short breath through his nose.

"Leg's held. Not drowned." He pulls one arm back out of the hole and points behind you, into the shed, at the boarded back third. "Joist under them boards. Sound one, under the new plank. Tie off there, not this side. This side's rotten to the yard." His jaw works. "Rope goes down through the boards. Not through here."

He doesn't move to do it himself. He stays flat on the lip, with his eyes on the man in the water.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't thrash. He gets one breath into him, then another, and keeps his hands flat on the block, not pulling.

He shouts up, steady and loud enough to carry:

"I'm whole! Leg's pinned, not broken. Stone on my shin. Water's coming in from the cut side, slow, but it's coming. Don't anybody else step near that edge. The ground's crust!"

A beat, then the practical part:

"Rope's in my pack, but my pack's down here with me. Bram, Sefa, Hale, whoever's got one, drop it down. Tie it off to something that isn't sitting on this floor. The shed's doorframe, or the cart. And come down by the shed side, through the boards. That end's got joists under it. Not through this hole."

While he waits, he works with what's in reach. He gets a hand on the floating joist and walks it along the wall toward himself. He tries to set one end down in the silt beside the block, low on the side away from his leg, so it can go under the stone's edge as a lever once somebody with weight is on the other end. He doesn't heave on it himself. He just gets it placed.

He shrugs the healer's satchel up high on his shoulder, out of the water, and checks the potion stoppers by feel.

Then, since he has the time and the light, he looks at the stone pinning him. The sunburst, the ring of tally-marks. He calls up, quieter, to Hale:

"Master Hale. There's a carved stone down here. A sun, rays and a face, with marks round it like a mason's count. Squared. Somebody built this, not just dug it." He breathes out through his teeth against the cold. "You knew there was more under here than water, didn't you."

He watches the waterline on his chest and counts slowly, getting a measure of how fast it's rising.

scenes.narration:
Pell keeps his palms flat on the cold stone and doesn't pull. He gets one breath in, then another. When he shouts, it goes up through the hole and booms back off the water around him.

Hale's face hangs in the ragged square of daylight above, white with dust. He hears it all: the leg pinned but not broken, the water coming in, the crust. When Pell gets to the doorframe and the cart, the warden shakes his head once.

"Not the frame. Frame's on the same rot." He jerks his chin back toward the shed. "Joist under the new board. Sound. Rope comes through there." Then, louder than he needs to: "Don't pull on it!"

The joist is a dead weight, black and slimed and swollen with water. Pell walks it along the wall hand over hand, and it comes to him slowly, nudging the crust of pink crystal as it goes. The chip of light lying under the water by his knee lets him see what he's doing. On the side of the block away from his leg, the stone's far corner doesn't sit on the silt. It rests on the edge of the fallen threshold flag, and that leaves a dark gap about a hand high. Pell feeds the beam's end into it and works it in until it bites. The other end rises at a slant out of the water toward the hole, and it waits there for someone heavier than him. It holds. He doesn't lean on it.

He hitches the satchel high up on his shoulder. The three flasks are there, and his fingers find each stopper still tight in its neck. The padding took the fall.

Then he looks at the stone, because it's right under his hands. The sunburst is wider than his spread fingers. The rays have gone soft at the ends, but the face in the middle still has two shallow eyes and a line for a mouth. The ring of marks runs all the way round it. Up close they aren't scratches. Each one is cut clean with a narrow chisel, notches and strokes in groups, some groups with a crossbar and some without. It looks like a count, but not one Pell knows how to read. Just behind the block, low on the wall, the rock gives way to something pale and smooth about two hands wide. It's plaster, laid over a gap and smoothed flat, and someone's fingers left faint dragging lines in it before it set.

He calls up what he sees, and the last question with it.

Hale doesn't answer straight away. His jaw works.

"Knew there was a working. Boarded before my time, I said." He looks down at the block in the green light from below, and his face does something Pell can't read from eight feet away. "Never saw a sun. Nobody goes in that way." He pauses. "Rope's coming."

He doesn't say anything else. He doesn't look away from Pell either.

Pell picks a spike of pink crystal on the wall level with the water and starts counting. By three hundred the water has hardly reached it. It might have risen the thickness of a fingernail, or that might be the ripples. It's slow, then. That means hours, not minutes, though he can't yet say how many. The cold is the faster problem. It has his legs already and is working up into his belly. The sweet smell down here is thick enough to taste, and behind his eyes there's a faint heaviness, the kind that comes on a long night watch. The cold keeps it off for now.

*(Out of game: placing the beam and reading the waterline needed no roll; Pell did it with his own hands and his own count. He's at 24 of 33 hit points, lightly hurt.)*

messages.text:
“Coming!”

I run down the slope, pulling the rope free as I go. Near the shed I slow, keeping off the broken chalk and approaching on intact ground.

“Hale, who’s down? Can they hear you?”

I look for a sound anchor—a stout post or solid beam—to secure the rope, and call toward the hole, “Pell! Sefa! Rope’s coming. Are you hurt?”

Bram's shout goes down the hill ahead of him, and he goes after it at a run. The coil comes off his belt as he moves and he shakes the first loops free over his forearm. The slope is a hundred feet of hard white chalk that he has watched for the last hour. He knows where it's firm and takes the straight line down it. His mail rings with every stride.

Thirty feet out from the shed he slows. Twenty feet out he sees the stain. A broad dark patch of damp runs from the lip of the cut toward the doorway, and the chalk over it has the dull, swollen look of bread dough. He swings uphill around it and comes in along the shed's side wall, keeping on dry, bright ground that rings under his boots.

The doorway is gone. Where the threshold used to be there's a ragged hole about four feet across, its edges still crumbling. Cold air comes up out of it, smelling of wet stone with something sweet underneath. Hale lies flat across the outer lip with his arms spread, his beard and apron white with fresh dust. Inside, past the hole, Sefa is on the far side, close against the wall left of the door.

Hale turns his head at the sound of the mail.

"Dunmore," he says. "Down there. Eight foot. Water to his chest. Leg's under a stone. Not drowned." His jaw works. "He hears. He's talking."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa kneels at the sound edge of the broken doorway, one hand braced on the doorpost, and keeps her voice down under the noise of trickling water.

"Pell, you're seen. Stone's on your leg—don't wrench it. We're rigging a lift now."

She looks back over her shoulder to the boarded rear of the shed, then toward the yard for Bram. "Warden says the joist under the new plank is the sound anchor. We'll open the boards enough to drop a rope down behind you, use that beam as a lever against the stone. Keep your arms free and your head above water."

As soon as Bram reaches the shed, she calls out: "Bring the rope right up against the wall beside the new plank! Watch the floor near the doorway—use my voice." She digs the chisels and wedges from the bench box and carries them low against the wall to the corner of the boards. "Hale, stay at the hole and tell me if he slips."

Before she shifts from the doorway, her eyes catch the lit block once more, the sunburst and its ring of marks below the waterline. She doesn't stop—but the image stays, and she mutters one low spell to set a second cold light on a chip she drops onto the lip.

*(I'm moving to rig the rope with Bram, using the wedges and chisels to lift the new plank enough to pass the rope around the joist, and asking Hale to watch Pell while we work.)*

scenes.narration:
Sefa goes down on one knee on the flag left of the hole, the one Hale said would hold her, and braces a hand against the doorpost. She doesn't lean over. Bits of the lip still break off now and then and patter into the water below.

She keeps her voice low and level and sends it down to Pell: he's been seen, don't wrench the leg, they're rigging a lift, keep your arms free and your head up. From the dark comes the steady trickle off the cut side, and the slap of water against stone as the man down there shifts his weight.

As she turns, her eyes pass over the block once more. The sunburst lies just under the green-lit water, and around it runs the ring of small, even marks. She only glances at it, but in that glance her eyes do what they always do with writing. They don't slide off the marks the way they would off a mason's idle scratches. They catch on them, the way they catch on a line of letters in a language she hasn't looked at properly yet. These are groups, spaced like words. It would take a proper look to read them, and she doesn't stop for one now.

She calls across the hole to Bram, telling him to bring the rope up along the wall beside the new plank, mind the floor near the doorway, and follow her voice. Then she goes to the bench. The box of wedges and feathers is heavy for its size. She takes two iron wedges and a broad chisel off the pegs and carries them low against her hip, her shoulder brushing the wall all the way to the back of the shed. The flags ring true under her feet the whole way.

The flags stop where the boards begin, in a straight line like the edge of a step. The planks run side by side toward the back wall, dark and sweating at the seams. The new one is easy to find. It's the pale one, third from the left wall, with its sawn end still crisp. She doesn't need the chisel. The plank isn't nailed. When she kneels on the last flag and gets her fingers under its end, it lifts in her hands, heavy with damp. She lifts it a hand's breadth, then more, and kicks a wedge into the gap to hold it up.

Under it, a foot below the boards, lies the joist. It's as black as the one in the water, but this one doesn't give when she presses the heel of her hand along it, and the wood feels hard and cold, not soft. Beyond it there's nothing but dark and a cold breath coming up, with the sweet bakehouse smell riding on it, thicker here than anywhere else in the shed. A long way down and off toward the front, the water shows a faint green glow where her first chip lies on the silt, and the light moves over the hewn ceiling. Somewhere under that glow is Pell. The drop through here is about the same eight feet, and it ends in water. From where the rope would go in, it's a wade of a dozen feet forward to the block.

She breathes the sweet air for a moment while she works the second wedge in. Behind her eyes there's a slight heaviness, like the end of a long night shift, and it passes when she turns her face back toward the door and the daylight.

At the hole, Hale doesn't look round when she asks him to watch Pell. He's been watching him all along.

"Aye," he says, eyes down in the hole. Then, louder, so it carries to her: "Feel that joist with your hand before anybody hangs on it. Lift the board. Don't stand on it."

He stays where he is, stretched flat across the lip.

*(Out of game: Light only holds one object at a time, so lighting a second chip puts out the one on the silt down by Pell. Do you still cast it? I haven't played it yet.)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his breathing slow and shallow and pulls the collar of his shirt up over his nose and mouth. It's wet cloth, which is better than nothing against that sweet stink.

He calls up, steady, keeping it short so he doesn't waste breath:

"Lever's in. Beam's set under the far corner, end's sticking up toward you. Whoever comes down only has to lean on it. Don't heave, just weight. I'll pull my leg when it lifts."

Then, firmer:

"And listen. The air down here's bad. That sweet smell's thick, and it's going behind my eyes. Whoever comes, come quick, do it, and go back up. Don't stand around admiring the stonework. Sefa, you stay up top unless Bram needs hands. If I go quiet, somebody shout at me."

He flexes his fingers and toes to keep the blood moving against the cold, and keeps talking to himself under his breath, counting, so his head stays clear.

While he waits he doesn't touch the plaster. He looks at it once more: the dragging finger-lines, the size of the patch, whether it's cracked or seeping. He fixes it in memory with the sun and the notches. Somebody sealed something up down here by hand, and that's a door for another hour, not this one.

Quietly, up to Hale, no edge in it:

scenes.narration:
Pell pulls the wet collar of his shirt up over his nose and mouth. It's cold and gritty with chalk, and it hardly filters anything; the sweet smell comes straight through the weave. Breathing through it is still slower, though, and slower is what he wants.

He sends his voice up through the hole in short pieces: the lever's in, the end is sticking up toward them, lean on it and don't heave. Then the harder part, about the air and coming quick and going back up. The water throws it all back at him, flattened.

Above him, Hale's dust-white face stays in the square of daylight. He doesn't look away while Pell talks.

"Heard," he says. "Lean, not heave." He turns his head a fraction and says something into the shed behind him, too low to carry down. Then he looks back.

Pell can hear the rest of the rescue more than see it. Mail rings on the chalk somewhere above and to one side, the sound of a big man moving carefully. Behind him, toward the back of the working, the thin thread of daylight between two planks in the ceiling has turned into a bar as wide as a hand. A plank has been lifted up there, and something iron has been knocked in to hold it. Dust drifts down through the new gap and turns slowly in the light before it settles on the water.

He works his fingers and his toes, the free foot and the pinned one, because he can still feel both. The pinned foot is starting to feel as if it belongs to somebody else. He counts under his breath, not in a whisper, just loud enough to hear himself. The cold has reached his belly and settled in for good. The heaviness behind his eyes hasn't got any worse. It hasn't gone either.

He looks at the plaster once more without touching it. It's about two hands wide, roughly square, and a little higher than the waterline. The finger-drags run across it in one direction, side to side, the way someone smooths a patch flat working from left to right. It isn't cracked and it isn't seeping. That's the odd thing about it. The hewn rock around it is wet and sweating, with pink crystal growing in every seam, but the crystal stops at the edge of the plaster as if it had been told to. The patch itself is dry and pale and clean. He fixes it in his memory along with the sun and the ring of notches, and leaves it alone.

Then he says the last thing up to Hale, quietly: four foot of water, and a man doesn't drown in it unless he's already asleep.

The warden doesn't answer. For a long moment he doesn't do anything at all. Then he looks away, up the slope toward the house, and stays looking that way for longer than a man looks at nothing. When his eyes come back down to Pell, they've changed. He's stopped weighing Pell up and is just looking at him.

"When you're out," he says.

That's all he says. He stays flat on the lip with one arm still hanging into the hole, close enough to grab a collar this time.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Sefa, catch the coil. Hale says there’s a sound joist beneath the pale plank at the back. Secure it there and lower the rope through the boards—not over this lip.”

Keeping on the dry ground, I hold one end and toss her the coil across the gap.

“Pell, we’re getting a line to you. Don’t pull against the trapped leg. Can you keep your mouth above water without struggling?”

I take off my shield and set it clear of the broken ground, then look along the shed’s side for a safe way round to the back. “Hale, is there a rear door?”

scenes.narration:
Bram doesn't wind up. He swings the coil once at his hip, the way you'd throw a line to a man on a wagon roof, and lets it go underhand. Inside the shed the lid of boards at the back is open now. A pale plank is propped up on iron wedges, and Sefa is kneeling on the last flag beside the gap. The coil sails over the ragged hole and across the floor, paying out as it goes, and drops in a loose heap on the flags at her knee. Bram keeps the other end wrapped twice round his fist. The slack lies across the hole, a hand above the broken lip.

He bends over the hole and sends his question down into the dark: don't pull against the leg, can he keep his mouth up without fighting for it. It goes down past Hale's shoulder and comes back off the water flattened.

Then he slips the shield off his arm and lays it face-down on dry chalk a long stride back from the wall, where nothing is going to give under it. The arm feels light without it. The mail doesn't. He can feel every pound of it as he looks along the side of the shed.

There isn't much to see. The wall is dry-laid white block, shoulder-high to the eaves, with no window and no gap bigger than a mortar joint. Round the back corner the ground doesn't go on. The rear wall stands right at the lip of the lower cut, and below it the white falls away into wet grey. The dark seep-stain runs along its foot like a tide line. Nobody walks round that way unless they mean to swim.

Hale hears the question and answers without lifting his eyes from the hole.

"No. One door. This one." His jaw works. He takes one hand off the chalk and lays it flat on the broken lip, then moves it left, onto the flag Sefa knelt on before. "Long step. There. Then the wall, all the way back. Don't stop on the dull ones."

He puts the hand back down and spreads his weight again. Nothing else from him. In the shed the coil lies where it fell. The water down in the hole slaps once against stone, and Bram is on the outside of the doorway with his end of the rope in his fist.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
I keep the light where it is, on the chip down in the water. The dark down there needs it more than we do up here.

Sefa sets the chisel down flat on the floor and gets the second wedge under the lifted plank, then stands and strips off her pack straps so they don't catch. She eases the plank back down until it rests on the two wedges, leaving a gap just wide enough for the rope and her arm. "There's air enough here to stand and breathe. Sweet, but it passes."

She looks toward the door. "Bram! Rope to me, end first. Feed it along the left wall and keep your feet on the flags—don't step on anything that rings dull." Softer, to Hale: "The first light stays with him. If he goes under, sing out and I'll bring something brighter."

When Bram reaches her, she takes the rope and passes the end around the black joist once, easing it along the beam with the flat of the blade to make sure they're on sound wood. Then she hauls gently and looks at Bram. "He's pinned at the shin. We go in from this bay, wade to him, and lever that block with the beam—not pull on his leg."

She loops the working end and ties it off with the knot a healer learns from a hundred slings, snug but easy to release. "I'll carry the light with us. You anchor and work the lever."

scenes.narration:
Sefa leaves the light where it is. Down through the gap the chip still glows on the silt, and green-white ripples run across the hewn ceiling over Pell's head.

She lays the broad chisel flat on the last flag and gets her fingers back under the pale plank. The second wedge has worked loose a little, so she taps it home with the heel of her hand. Then she shrugs her pack straps off her shoulders and sets the pack down against the wall where it won't catch on anything. She lets the plank settle slowly until both wedges take its weight and there's a gap about as wide as her forearm between its end and the next board. That's room for a rope and an arm, and the gap breathes cold up into her face.

The sweet smell comes up with it. It's heavier here than at the door, and for a moment the lids of her eyes feel thick. Then it passes, as it did before.

"There's air enough here to stand and breathe," she says, mostly to the room. "Sweet, but it passes."

She calls her instructions to the doorway: end first, along the left wall, and keep to the flags that ring. Then, more quietly, she speaks to the broad back stretched across the lip. The first light stays with Pell. If he goes under, Hale should shout, and she'll bring something brighter.

Hale doesn't turn his head. He lifts one hand a finger's width off the chalk to show he heard, then puts it back down.

The coil Bram threw already lies in a loose heap at her knee, and its free end is right there. The rest of the line runs off across the flags and over the hole to the doorway, where the other end is still wrapped round Bram's fist. Sefa takes the free end and reaches down through the gap. She passes it under the black joist and brings it up the other side. When she draws it along the beam the hemp slides over hard, cold wood. Nothing gives, nothing crumbles away under it, and the joist doesn't so much as creak. She pulls gently on both strands, and it's the pull of something anchored in stone.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps counting under his breath. When he hits a hundred he starts again. He keeps an eye on the new bar of light at the back of the working and on whatever's coming through it.

When he hears mail moving above the shed end, he calls toward it, short and clear:

"Bram! Drop in by the boards and come along the wall on your right. The floor's solid there, I walked the beam that way. Water's chest-deep on me, so it'll be about waist on you. Mind the silt, there's fallen flag under it." A breath. "Beam's the black one sticking up at a slant by my left side. Lean on the top end. Slow. Count three out loud before you put your weight on it, so I'm ready."

He gets both hands on the block's near edge, braced flat, ready to shove the stone away from himself as it lifts, rather than pull his leg against it. When the stone comes up he means to slide the shin out sideways, along the bottom and away from the corner, not straight up where the block could drop back on it.

If Bram's there and the leg's out:

"Out. Good. Up first, you behind me, no lingering." He stops long enough to slap the plaster patch with his eyes one last time, not his hand. "Don't touch anything else down here. We'll want it later, and so will Hale."

If he starts feeling the heaviness behind his eyes get worse, he bites the inside of his cheek hard and keeps talking. Somebody needs to hear him.

scenes.narration:
Pell counts. At a hundred he starts again from one, not quite under his breath. The number keeps his mouth moving and his head with it.

The bar of light at the back of the working holds steady, a hand wide, with the dark stripes of planks either side of it. Something long and pale moves across it once and settles. A rope has gone over the joist up there; he can see it as a line against the daylight, and it shivers when somebody draws it tight. Then it goes still. Nobody comes down through the gap.

He hears the mail again, but not from the back. It comes from the front, above the hole, the scrape and chink of a heavy man standing still on chalk. Across the square of white over his head lies a second line, the same rope, slack, a hand above the broken lip. It runs from the back of the shed over the hole and out of sight to the right, toward the yard.

He sends his directions toward the sound anyway, short and clear: drop in by the boards, keep along the wall, waist-deep on a taller man, flag under the silt, the black beam at his left, lean slow on the top end, count three out loud first. The water throws every word back at him.

Hale's face is still in the daylight, his arm still hanging down into the hole. He hears it all and nods once. Then he turns his head and speaks up the hole, toward the yard and the man in mail. Pell catches only the end of it: "...heard him. Lean, count, slow." He looks back down.

"Rope's on the back joist," he tells Pell. "She tied it. Halloway's at the door with the other end." His jaw works. "One turn on it. I said two."

Pell gets both palms flat on the near edge of the block and braces his elbows. The stone is cold enough to ache through his hands. Under the water he finds the angle with his free foot, sideways along the bottom and away from the corner, ready to slide the shin out low when the weight comes off. The pinned foot answers when he tells it to move, a little. It's slower than it was.

The heaviness behind his eyes sits where it has sat for the last quarter-hour. It's no worse, but it's no better. Twice in the count he notices he's said the same number two times running, and twice he bites the inside of his cheek and goes on from the right one. It hurts in a clean way. The cold is up past his navel now and has settled there.

The chip of light under the water by his knee is still burning. In its green glow the plaster patch behind the block stays pale and dry, with a clean edge where the pink crystal stops.

Above, the mail chinks once more and goes quiet. The slack rope over the hole sways and settles. Nobody has come down yet.

 *(Out of game: none of these needed a roll.)*
1) Pell called his directions and Hale passed them up to Bram. Those were just words, and whether Bram follows them is up to Bram's player in his own scene.
2) Pell has his hands braced and his free foot set. The slide-out comes when the block lifts, and that waits on Bram's move with the lever.
3) This was conditional on Bram being down there with the leg out. Neither has happened yet, so it hasn't been said. It stands for the moment it does happen.

messages.text:
“Sefa, secure your end first. I’m coming across to help.”

I unwrap the rope from my fist so it can’t drag me onto the broken lip, leaving slack for her to work. Once she has it anchored, I take the long step onto the sound flag Hale indicated, then follow the wall toward her, avoiding the dull stones.

“Pell, what’s pinning you—one loose stone, or part of the roof?”
