scenes.narration:
Bram unwinds the two turns of hemp from his fist and lets the end drop. Across the hole the line goes slack. It sags until it nearly touches the broken lip, then lies still, and nothing is pulling it toward the edge now. At the far end, in the dim back of the shed, he can see where it goes down through a gap under the pale plank, which is propped on its iron wedges. The rope is already tied off to something below. Sefa's end was made fast before he called.

Then the long step.

He judges it the way he'd judge a wagon-bed from the ground: four feet of ragged hole, and on the far side a flag with a darker seam along its edge. He sets his rear foot on the bright chalk by the doorpost and keeps one hand flat on the wall stones. He doesn't jump. He reaches, the way you step over a ditch with a pack on, and brings his weight down onto the flag all at once.

The flag grates. It's a short, gritty sound, stone settling on stone, and it drops perhaps the thickness of a fingernail under his boot. A trickle of chalk runs off the hole's edge beside it and patters into the water. Then the flag stops moving. It holds him, mail and all.

Hale is still flat on the outer lip and watches it the whole way. He lets his breath out through his teeth.

"Holds," he says. "Don't stand there admiring it."

For the moment he's over the hole, Bram can see down into it. It's eight feet of green-white light coming up off the silt, with ripples crawling over a hewn ceiling. A man's head and shoulders stand up out of the water, and beside them a squared block lies tilted with its top face out. A black beam rises from under its far corner at a slant toward him, like a pump-handle waiting for a hand. The smell coming up is sweet and thick, like a cold bakehouse.

Then he's past it. He puts his shoulder to the wall and follows it toward the back. He tests each flag with his heel before he trusts it. Every one along the wall rings clean and hard, the way the ground did all morning. The brazier goes by on his right with its crust of rose-coloured ash. Ahead, the flags stop in a straight edge and the dark sweating boards begin. Beside the edge, Sefa's pack leans against the wall and the pale plank sits up on its wedges. A cold breath comes out of the gap and smells of wet stone and something sweeter.

His question goes down ahead of him, through the hole behind him and the gap in front: *one loose stone, or part of the roof?*

Hale answers first. That one he can answer from what he's seen.

"Block. One. Size of a meal-chest." He jerks his chin at the ceiling of the shed and the dark boards. "Roof's sound. That's the old floor come down. Doorstep with it." His jaw works once. "He'll tell you the rest."

Bram is at the back of the shed now, at the edge of the boards. The rope runs down through the gap at his feet into the dark.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't argue with Hale. She tugs the tail of the knot, loosens it, and passes the rope around the joist a second time, the coils snug side by side against the old black wood. When she leans back on it, it holds like it's bolted to the floor.

"Two turns. Done." She says it over her shoulder, half to Hale, half to herself, and tests the line once more with her full weight before she straightens.

She picks the broad chisel up off the flag and hooks a thumb toward the gap. "If this rope walks, say so." Then she pitches her voice down into the hole. "Pell! Line's anchored. Keep your arms clear of the stone. Don't try to move it by yourself—we're coming in by the back boards and we'll lever it off you."

To Bram at the door, without turning: "Two ropes if you've got the length—one for us, one to make a sling for the beam. If not, I'll go down first and we'll work the lever from the lip. Keep clear of the bad flags."

She stays by the joist, hands on the rope, waiting on Bram's end.

scenes.narration:
Sefa doesn't argue. She pulls the tail and the hospice knot falls open in her hand, the way it was made to. She takes the wet hemp round the black joist a second time and lays the two turns side by side against the old wood, then ties off again. When she sits back on the line with her full weight, it doesn't creep. It doesn't shift at all. It holds as if the joist were part of the hill.

"Two turns. Done."

Across the shed, Hale has turned his head to watch, flat on his belly at the lip. He looks at the knot for about as long as he looked at it the first time.

"Aye," he says. "That's a lift."

Then he looks back into the hole.

Sefa picks the broad chisel up off the flag. When she tells him to say so if the rope walks, he lifts two fingers off the chalk without looking round. She leans over the gap and sends her voice down to Pell: the line's anchored, keep his arms clear of the stone, don't try it alone, they're coming in by the back boards. The cold air from below takes her words and throws them back off the water. Down past the joist the green light lies steady on the silt, and the seep goes on trickling in from the cut side, thin and patient. For a breath her eyelids feel heavy again, then she lifts her face out of the draught and it passes.

She turns toward the door to call about two ropes and the lip, and Hale answers before anyone else can.

"One rope. That one." He jerks his chin at her line without lifting his chest off the chalk. "Beam's set already. He said. Lean on the top end. No sling wanted." He works his jaw once. "Not from this lip. Lip won't take a woman kneeling, never mind working a beam. Both of you go down by the boards, or it doesn't shift."

Then he points at the long slack of hemp lying across the hole, its loose end trailing out over the broken edge toward the yard.

"And haul that in. It's lying on rot. Somebody'll put a foot on it."

The rope runs from her two turns on the joist, across the flags and over the hole, and lies loose on the far lip. The gap under the pale plank breathes up cold and sweet at her knees.

*(Out of game: in his own scene this round, Bram has already crossed the shed and is standing at the back edge of the boards beside you, so your call toward the door reaches him there. What he does about it comes in his own scene.)*

 *(Out of game: none of these four needed a roll, because tying off a rope she has already tested, putting her weight on it and calling out are all certain. The narration covers each one: the two turns hold her full weight, her words to Pell go down the gap, and her call reaches Bram beside her. Hale answered it, and Bram's own answer comes in his scene.)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell stops counting long enough to shout up, sharp and clear, so the men at the top have one plan between them:

"Hale's right. Two turns on that joist, not one! Bram, put the second turn on before anybody trusts it."

A breath through the wet collar, then the rest in short pieces:

"Throw me the slack end, the one over the hole. Drop it straight down to my hands."

When it comes he doesn't tie it to the stone. He takes a quick bowline round his own chest, under the arms, high and snug, and pulls it hard to check it holds. Then he calls up:

"Rope's on me, not the block. If I go quiet, you haul me straight up whether the leg's free or not. Better a skinned shin than a Tobin Reed."

Then, toward the back gap and the mail:

"Bram, come down the back way now, on the rope, quick. Three steps along the right wall, lean on the black beam, count three out loud, I slide out, you go straight back up. Half a minute in this air, no more. Sefa, Hale, keep the line over the hole taut on me while he does it."

He sets his palms flat on the block's edge again, free foot braced sideways along the bottom, and starts the count over from one. He says each number out loud now, plainly, so those above can hear that he's still there.

scenes.narration:
Pell's shout goes up through the hole and booms back off the water around him. His breath shows faintly in the green light from the chip on the silt.

Hale is still in the square of daylight above, flat across the outer lip. He waits for the end of it.

"Two on it now," he says. "She did it. I watched."

The loose end of the rope lies trailing over the broken edge beside the warden's shoulder. He gathers it in without lifting his chest off the chalk, a few hand-lengths at a time, until he has the end. He doesn't throw it. He reaches his arm down into the hole as far as it goes and lets it fall straight. The wet hemp drops onto the water a hand's width from Pell's fingers and lies there in a loose coil.

Pell gets it in one hand, and he doesn't need to look at what he's doing. The rope goes round his chest under the arms, high and snug, and he ties a bowline in the cold with numb fingers. It's slower than it would be on a dry roof, but it's right. He hauls on it and the loop bites and holds. The line now runs up from his chest, over the inner edge of the hole, and away across the shed floor toward the back. Where it crosses the lip, a little chalk breaks off and patters into the water beside him.

Hale watches the crumbs fall.

"Rope's on the bad edge. Haul you up through here, the lip comes down with you." He doesn't take his eyes off it. "Slow, if it comes to that. Not straight. That's all."

He lays one forearm flat on the chalk beside the rope, close enough to grab, and stays there.

At the back of the working the bar of daylight between the lifted plank and the next board has a shadow across it now, something broad standing above the gap. Somebody up there is talking, low, but Pell can't make out the words through the boards. Nobody has come down yet.

Pell puts his palms flat on the near edge of the block again. The stone is just as cold as before. He sets his free foot sideways along the bottom, away from the corner, ready to slide out when the weight lifts. He starts the count again from one and says every number out loud, plainly, so it carries.

*One. Two. Three.*

His voice comes back off the wet walls. The cold has reached his belly and stays there. The heaviness behind his eyes hasn't moved either, no better and no worse. At *eleven* he catches himself about to say *eleven* again, and says *twelve*.

*(Out of game: tying the bowline needed no roll; it's Pell's own rope work.)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa pulls the slack back hand over hand, coiling it on the flag beside her, never stepping toward the broken lip. When the rope lies clean, she slips the broad chisel into her belt and turns to Bram at the back edge of the boards.

"We go down through here, one behind the other. You first—you carry the weight on the lever. I'll tail the rope from up top and follow you down." She plants a boot against the last sound flag. "When you reach the water, keep near the wall. The mud's soft where his leg's down. We wade to him, tip that beam up under the block, and lift."

She calls to Hale: "Sing out if the light below goes out. We'll have the rope." Then she braces her heels and feeds the line through her hands, ready to check Bram's descent, her own breathing steady now despite the sweet air pulling at the back of her head.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I kneel on the sound flags beside the gap, spreading my weight, and look down to see where the rope reaches Pell and whether I can reach the raised end of the black beam.

“Pell, I saw a beam under that block. Is it set to lever the stone off your leg?”

To Sefa I say, “If we can lift it, he’ll need to pull clear before we lower it. Keep the rope steady—don’t haul him against the stone.”

I check what the beam rests on and where it would move before putting any force on it.

scenes.narration:
Sefa takes the slack in hand over hand and lays the coils on the sound flag beside her, keeping her feet back from the broken lip. The first arm-lengths come in light and wet, dragging a little chalk across the floor. Then the rope stops coming. Something heavy is holding it down in the hole, though it isn't fighting her. She keeps a gentle pull on it and the line lies snug along the flags, rises over the inner edge of the hole and goes straight down into the green light.

Hale is still flat on the outer lip and doesn't look round.

"That's on him now," he says. "Round his chest. He tied it." His jaw works once. "Keep it like that. Snug, not hauled."

So the coil beside her is short. Most of Bram's fifty feet runs from the joist under her knee, across the shed and down to Pell, and none of it hangs through the gap at the back.

She slips the broad chisel through her belt and talks Bram through it: he goes first because he's the weight, she follows, they keep to the wall where the mud is soft, then the beam and the lift. She turns her head toward the door to ask Hale to sing out if the light below goes out.

"Light's steady," Hale says. "I'll say."

She sets her heels against the last sound flag with the line running through her hands. The draught from the gap brushes her face, and the heaviness behind her eyes comes and goes with it.

---

Bram kneels at the edge of the boards with his knees on two flags and one hand flat on a third to spread his weight. The flags take it without a sound. He puts his face to the gap under the pale plank.

The first thing he sees is how narrow it is. Sefa eased the plank down onto its wedges, and the opening at its end is about as wide as his forearm. A rope and an arm fit through it. A man in chain mail won't fit until that plank comes off, and maybe the one next to it as well. The planks are wide and not nailed. They're only heavy.

He looks down past the black joist with Sefa's two turns of hemp on it. Eight feet below is water, dark at first and then paler where the light comes through. Pell had it at his chest, so on Bram it should come about to the waist. The working runs forward from under his knees, hewn square with a low roof, for a dozen feet to where the green glow lies on the silt under the hole at the door. Pell is in that glow with his head and shoulders out of the water. A rope comes down over the lip of the hole to his chest, the same line Sefa is holding up here.

The beam is to the left of Pell as Bram looks at it. The black joist comes up out of the water at a slant, its top end a little above the surface and leaning toward the hole. Bram used to lever loaded wagons out of the ruts below Nashkel, and he reads the rig without trying. The low end is pushed into a dark gap a hand high under the block's far corner. That corner sits on the edge of the fallen threshold flag, and the flag is the only thing for the beam to pivot on. The bite is shallow. A straight push down on the top end will lift that corner. A push off to one side could twist the beam out of the gap. When the weight comes off the beam, the block will come down exactly where it is now.

He sends his question down the gap to Pell: is the beam set to lever the stone? Then he tells Sefa: Pell pulls clear before anything is lowered, keep the rope steady, don't haul him against the stone.

Hale answers from the front, since he's had it from Pell twice already.

"Set. Far corner. Lean on the top end. Slow." He looks down at the rope crossing the lip by his elbow. "She's not hauling. I'm watching it."

Bram kneels where he is, with the sweet cold breath of the working coming up into his face. For a moment his eyelids feel heavy, as they do on the last hour of a night watch. It passes. Nobody has come down into the water yet.

*(Out of game: Hale dropped the rope's end to Pell in Pell's own scene and Pell tied it round his chest, so it can't be fed down through the gap. Bram can still hang from the joist and drop into the water.)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps the count going between sentences, so the numbers never stop for long.

"Fourteen. Heard you, Hale. Fifteen." He turns his head toward the bar of light at the back. "Then nobody hauls me through the hole. If it comes to that, drag me toward the back gap, along the water, under the good joist. Sixteen. Bram! Talk to me, man. You coming down, or is something stopping you?"

He waits a beat, listening hard to the low voices behind the boards, trying to catch even one word.

"Seventeen. If the gap's too narrow for a man in mail, take the mail off, or send the beam-weight some other way. Shove a pole down through the boards onto the end of my lever. Anything heavy on it will do. Eighteen."

He shifts his hands a finger's width on the block to keep them from going dead, and checks that the bowline hasn't slipped.

Quieter, to Hale, still counting:

"Nineteen. You're doing fine up there. Keep the arm where it is. Twenty."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Bad air’s reaching up here. Sefa, stay above with the line. One of us down there is enough.”

I help lift the loose plank clear, and the next if needed, keeping my weight on the sound flags. Then I lower myself from the sound joist and drop the remaining distance into the water, bending my knees.

I wade toward Pell along the wall, careful not to knock the lever sideways.

“Ready to pull clear, Pell. I’ll lift slowly. Tell me when your leg’s free.”

Once he’s ready, I press straight down on the beam’s raised end, steadily, keeping its shallow bite aligned beneath the block. I hold the pressure while he works his leg out.

scenes.narration:
Bram looks at the gap and then at the man beside him, and says it once: the bad air is reaching up this far, so Sefa stays above with the line, and one of them down there is enough.

He doesn't wait for anyone to agree. He gets his fingers under the end of the pale plank, and the wedges drop out and ring on the joist below. The plank is waterlogged and heavy, about what a wet door weighs, and he walks it back hand over hand and lays it flat across the solid flags. The board beside it is darker and older. It comes up with a wet sucking noise, slime trailing from its underside, and he lays it on top of the first. The gap is as wide as a man's shoulders now. The cold, sweet breath of the working comes straight up into his face.

When he looks round, Sefa has already turned away. She lays the broad chisel down flat on the last flag and picks her pack up off the wall. Along the left wall the flags ring under her steps, past the brazier and the bench, where the tally-book still lies open beside the fallen pencil. She takes the long step over the corner of the hole onto the flag that holds and goes out through the broken doorway into the glare. The light swallows her and she's gone. Hale, flat on the outer lip, turns his head to watch her go by. Then he looks back down into the hole and says nothing.

The rope stays where she left it. It's two turns round the black joist and the knot, tied off and snug, and nobody has to hold it.

Bram sits on the edge of the flags with his legs down in the gap, takes hold of the joist with both hands and lowers himself. The mail drags at his shoulders the whole way and his arms take every pound of it. He hangs at full stretch with his boots about two feet above the black water, then lets go and bends his knees as he lands.

The cold hits him harder than the drop does. The water closes round his waist and comes straight in through the rings and the padding underneath, spring-cold and sharp enough to stop his breath. His boots sink into the silt up to the ankle. Something hard lies under it, a fallen flag or a loose stone, and he finds it with his heel before he trusts his weight to it.

The working is low enough that he has to stoop. Bands of daylight fall through the planks overhead. Ahead, a dozen feet off, the green glow comes up from the silt under the front hole. He can see a head and shoulders above the water there, the tilted block, and the black beam slanting up past the block's far side toward the square of white sky.

He goes along the wall the way he'd go along a riverbank with a horse, slowly, testing every step, his left hand flat on the wet stone. Pink crystal crusts every seam under his palm and crunches as he goes. The sweet smell is thick enough down here to taste. Halfway along, his eyelids get heavy the way they do in the last hour before dawn on a night watch. He knows that feeling and how to deal with it. He breathes through his teeth and keeps moving.

He comes in on the beam from the side away from its bite, keeping his hip and his mail clear of it. The top end is right under the hole, and Hale's dust-white face is a yard above it.

"Straight down," the warden says. "Not toward me. It twists, it's out."

Bram tells Pell to get ready to pull clear, says he'll lift slowly, and asks Pell to tell him when the leg is free. Then he sets both hands on the slimed black wood, one above the other like a man on a pump-handle, plants his heels in the silt and leans.

He doesn't heave. He puts his shoulders over his hands and lets his weight go down into the beam a little at a time, and the mail adds its own weight. For a moment nothing happens except the wood creaking and the water slapping against his ribs. Then the beam goes down a finger's width under his hands, and then a hand's width. On the far side of the block the corner riding on the fallen flag comes up out of its bed with a gritty grind of stone, and a cloud of silt rolls up through the green light. The whole block tilts back off whatever it was lying on. It rises the height of a fist and stops there, held up by the lever and the man on the end of it.

Bram holds it there with his arms locked and the beam steady and straight. Every muscle in his back is talking to him. Above him Hale has his arm all the way down into the hole beside the rope, his fingers spread a foot above the water.

"Holding," Hale says, down to the water. "Now."

*(Out of game: the block is up and Bram is holding it. Pell's slide-out happens in his own scene.)*

messages.text:
Pell keeps counting, but he tightens it up and gives one plan.

"Twenty-one. Right. Then the weight goes on from your side, Hale." He tips his head at the beam, which slants up toward the lip. "How far's the top end from your hand? If you can reach it, put your forearm on it and lean. Don't heave. Your chest stays on the chalk. Twenty-two."

Louder, toward the back gap:

"Bram! Forget the boards. Come round to the hole, to Hale's side. Stand on the *outer* edge, where he's lying. That's the ground that's held two men all morning. Reach down and lean on the beam's top end with him. Two of you, slow, count three. Sefa keeps the rope snug on me. Twenty-three."

He sets his palms on the block again and gets his free foot braced sideways along the bottom.

"If nobody can reach it, drop something heavy onto it. A sledge from the bench, a wedge-box, the cart's chock. Tie it on a line and lower it onto the top end. Twenty-four. Whatever you pick, call it before you do it. I want your three."

He breathes through the wet collar, keeps his eyes on the beam end where it rises out of the water, and waits for someone up top to start counting.

"Twenty-five."

scenes.narration:
"Twenty-one."

Pell gets the plan out in short pieces between the numbers. He wants Hale's forearm on the top end of the beam and his chest kept flat on the chalk. He wants Bram round at the outer edge, two men leaning slow on a count of three, and something heavy lowered on a line if nobody can reach. Hale listens with his head turned down toward him. The warden opens his mouth to answer.

From the back of the working comes a splash, deep and heavy, the sound of a big man landing in water. The bar of daylight at the back has gone twice as wide, and in it a dark shape is getting up out of the water. Then Pell hears mail moving through water, a slow wade, with the crunch of pink crystal under a palm on the wall. Each step comes after a pause while the man tests the silt.

"He's down," Hale says. "Back way. In the iron." He looks along the working, then at Pell again. "Your count'll do."

"Twenty-four," says Pell. His voice is a little higher than he meant it to be.

Bram comes into the green light from the side away from the bite. He's stooped under the low roof, his breath short from the cold, and water runs off the rings at his shoulders. He doesn't look at the carving or the walls. He looks at the black beam, then at Pell, and tells him he's ready, he'll lift slowly, and Pell should say when the leg is free. Above them Hale tells him straight down, not toward him, because if it twists it comes out. Bram sets his hands on the slimed wood like a man taking hold of a pump-handle, and leans.

Pell feels it before he hears it. The pressure on his shin doesn't let go at once. It eases off, like a hand slowly opening. The beam creaks. On the far side of the block the corner grinds up off the fallen flag, and a brown cloud of silt rolls up through the green light around his legs. The block tilts back on its bed and stops a fist's height off the bottom. Bram holds it there with his arms locked. Nothing is pinning Pell's shin now except the silt and his own numbness.

"Holding," Hale says, his arm all the way down the hole. "Now."

Pell does what he set up three times over. He pushes against the block's near edge with both palms to keep his body away from it. He doesn't lift the leg into the gap. He drags it out sideways along the bottom, low through the silt, away from the corner. The heel catches on something under the mud, and he turns the foot and pulls again. The leg comes free.

It doesn't feel like his for the first breath. Then the blood comes back into it, a hot crawling ache from knee to ankle that makes his eyes water. The shin is bruised and swollen tight under the wet hose, but when he puts his weight on it, the bone holds. He stands on two feet in water up to his chest, with the rope snug under his arms, a yard clear of the stone.

"Out. Good." Then, to Bram's face a yard off: "Up first, you behind me, no lingering." His eyes go once to the pale plaster behind the block and stay off it. "Don't touch anything else down here. We'll want it later, and so will Hale."

The beam is still taking Bram's weight, and the block hangs on it, tilted. Over Pell's head, in the square of white sky, Hale lets out a long breath through his teeth. He doesn't pull his arm back out of the hole.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell gets his breath through his teeth while the ache settles in his shin. He keeps one hand on the wall and doesn't shift his weight onto the bad leg more than he must.

"Ease it down, Bram. Slow, straight down like he said. Let it settle where it was. Don't drop it." He waits until the block is back on its bed and the silt starts to clear, so nobody's leaving a loaded lever behind them.

Then he calls up to the lip:

"Hale, I'm not coming up through your hole. You were right about that edge. Let the line go slack, I'm slipping it." He works the bowline loose with numb fingers and lets the end drop on the water. "I'm going out the back way, on the good joist, same as Bram came."

He looks round once in the green light for his pack. If it's floating or lying within arm's reach he hooks it up by a strap and slings it over the satchel. If it isn't, he leaves it. He isn't going groping in the silt in this air.

To Bram, low and plain:

"You lead. I'll be right on your heels with a hand on your belt. If I stop talking, keep walking and pull." He fixes the place in his memory once more: the sun, the ring of notches, the dry plaster. Then he turns his back on it.

He wades after Bram along the right-hand wall, testing each step on the silt. He keeps the swollen leg behind and the good one leading, and he counts out loud again, from one. At the back gap he takes the rope over the joist, lets Bram go up first, and follows. His arms do most of the work, and he hauls himself up quick and light the way he would a drainpipe.

As soon as he's out on the boards in the daylight he rolls onto the solid planks, away from the gap. He pulls the wet collar off his face and takes three long breaths of clean air.

"Sefa," he says, still flat on his back, "tell me if my eyes look right. And somebody get that door open wide."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Steady, Pell. Stone’s up.”

I keep my weight straight over the lever, holding it down without shifting sideways. I watch Pell through the silt-clouded water.

“Hale, help him up as soon as he’s clear. Pell—tell me when you’re out from under it. I won’t lower till you say.”

scenes.narration:
Pell lets his breath out through his teeth and keeps one hand flat on the wet wall. He holds the swollen leg just off the bottom and puts as little weight on it as he can. The ache has settled into a steady, hot throb from knee to ankle.

His voice carries off the water to the man on the beam: ease it down, slow, straight down the way Hale said, let it settle where it was and don't drop it.

Bram's answer crosses his on the way. Steady, stone's up, and he won't lower it until Pell says. Bram stays where he is with his arms locked and his shoulders over the slimed black wood. The block hangs a fist's height off its bed, held up on the lever, and he doesn't let it move by so much as a finger's width. Through the brown silt still drifting in the green light he watches Pell's face. Pell's word reaches him. The beam is still under his hands, and the block is still up.

So Pell waits, as he said he would. He uses the time for the rope.

"Slack," he calls up. "Slipping it."

Hale is still flat across the outer lip. He hooks two fingers under the hemp where it crosses the edge and lifts it clear of the rotten chalk, and a little slack slides down to the water. Pell works the bowline with fingers that have mostly stopped answering. The knot fights him for a moment, swollen with wet, and then it gives. He lets the loop fall, and the end lies on the water beside him in a slow coil, still tied off up above.

He looks round once for his pack and finds he never lost it. The straps are still over his shoulders under the satchel. The fall and the water haven't shifted them. It's soaked through and heavy as a stone, and it's his.

Then Bram's request comes up to the lip: help him up as soon as he's clear.

Hale looks down at the two of them for a long moment. He takes a short breath through his nose.

"Not through here," he says.

He draws his arm back out of the hole for the first time since Pell went in. He gets his knees under him, then his feet, slowly, testing the outer chalk with his weight before he stands. He looks into the shed. Then he takes the long step over the corner of the hole onto the flag that holds. It grates under him the way it grated under Bram, and he puts his shoulder to the wall.

He goes along the wall toward the back, heel first on each flag. As he passes the brazier he keeps his eyes on the boards ahead and not on the bowl. At the edge of the boards he goes down on one knee beside the lifted planks and the gap Bram opened. He spreads one big hand on the flag and reaches the other down past the black joist, toward the water, toward the way out.

"Here," he says, down into the working. "I'll take him here."

Down in the green light the silt is starting to settle. The block hangs where Bram holds it, its carved face tilted toward the hole above, the sunburst and its ring of notches just under the surface. Behind it the plaster patch stays dry and pale. The seep goes on trickling in from the cut side. The cold has Pell to the belly, and the heaviness behind his eyes still hasn't moved.

*(Out of game: Pell's word to lower has reached Bram. Lowering the block is Bram's player's move, so it's still up, and Pell is waiting by it as he said. The wade out and the climb come after that.)*

messages.text:
“Lowering.”

With Pell clear, I ease the beam upward slowly, keeping it aligned until the block settles fully onto its bed. Only then do I let go.

“Leave anything heavy if you need to. Let’s get out of this air.”

I offer Pell my shoulder on his injured side and help him along the wall toward the rear gap, testing my footing as we go. Beneath Hale’s hand, I brace myself to help Pell up onto the sound floor.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell nods up at Hale's hand by the back gap. "Coming to you, Master Hale."

Then, to Bram, plain and steady:

"Right, I'm clear. Ease it down now, Bram, slow and straight. Let it settle." He watches the block go back onto its bed and waits until the silt stops rolling. "Good. Leave the beam where it lies. Now out, you and me. No more standing in this air."

He goes first along the right-hand wall since Hale's waiting there, keeping a hand on the wet stone and the good leg leading. He stays clear of the pink crust where he can and counts out loud from one so Bram knows where he is.

"One. Two. Bram, you're right behind me. If I stop counting, push me along. Three."

At the back gap he reaches up and takes Hale's wrist, not his fingers. With his other hand on the joist he lets the warden take some weight while he hauls himself up. He goes up quick and light with his arms doing the work and keeps the swollen shin off the edge. Once he's up he rolls clear of the gap onto the sound flags by the wall and lies there a moment on his back. He drags the wet collar off his face and breathes the cold, clean air three times, slow.

"Thanks." To Hale, quietly, still flat on the floor: "That's twice today you've been where I needed a hand."

Then, louder, toward the door:

"Sefa, prop that door wide and get Bram's arm when he comes up. And when you've a moment, look at my eyes and tell me if they're right. My head's been thick since I went in."

He keeps watching the gap until Bram's head and shoulders come through it.

scenes.narration:
"Lowering."

Bram lets the beam rise under his hands the way he leaned it down, a little at a time, keeping it straight. The block comes down off its fist of air. Its far corner finds the edge of the fallen flag with a soft grinding of stone and sinks back into the bed it came out of. One more cloud of silt rolls up brown through the green light and starts to drift. Bram holds the beam until it's carrying nothing, then takes his hands off. The black wood stays where it is, slanting up toward the square of sky. Pell's word to ease it down reaches him just as the stone settles, so the two of them are already doing the same thing.

The carved face ends up where it was before, tilted toward the hole and just under the surface. The plaster behind it is still dry.

"Leave anything heavy if you need to," Bram says. "Let's get out of this air."

He comes round onto Pell's bad side with his shoulder down and ready. Pell is already moving, one hand flat on the wet stone and the good leg leading, counting out loud. *One. Two.* Bram keeps a half-step behind him and just to his left, close enough to catch a sleeve. The silt sucks at their boots. Pink crust crunches wherever a palm touches the wall, and Pell keeps his hand off it where he can. Mail chinks behind him, steady. *Three. Four.* Nobody stops counting.

The bars of daylight between the planks get wider overhead. Then the gap is above them, a man's width of white, with the black joist across it, Bram's hemp in two turns round the joist, and Hale's big hand reaching down past it.

"Coming to you, Master Hale."

Pell reaches past the fingers and takes the wrist, and Hale's hand shuts on his wrist in turn like a vice. Below him Bram plants himself in the silt, gets a shoulder under Pell's good thigh and lifts. With the warden pulling from above and the fighter pushing from below, Pell barely has to do the work himself. Still, he does it the way he'd go up a drainpipe, arms doing it all, quick and light. He keeps the swollen shin up off the edge of the boards. He comes over the edge, rolls clear of the gap onto the sound flags by the wall and lies on his back.

He drags the wet collar down off his face. The shed air smells of tallow and cold ash, and after the working it tastes like a mountain. He takes one slow breath, then a second and a third. The thickness behind his eyes doesn't go all at once. It thins like fog going off a field, and by the third breath the roof beams over him have stopped looking far away.

"Thanks." Then, quietly, still flat on the floor: "That's twice today you've been where I needed a hand."

Hale is still on one knee by the gap and doesn't look round.

"Once," he says. "First time I missed."

Pell calls toward the door for Sefa: prop it wide, get Bram's arm, look at his eyes. His voice goes out over the hole and into the glare. Nobody answers from the yard. A jackdaw calls somewhere up on the terraces, and that's all.

Hale lets it hang for a moment.

"She's gone," he says. "Took her pack. Walked out while Halloway was going down." He looks at the door, then back at the gap. "Didn't say."

Then he turns his head and looks at Pell properly for the first time since the floor went. He takes Pell's jaw in his chalky fingers and tips his face toward the daylight from the door, the way you'd turn a stone to look at its grain, and stares into one eye and then the other.

"Seen men come up off that face," he says, and lets go. "You're slow. Not gone. Clean air does it. An hour." He leans back over the gap, and the same hand goes down past the joist toward the water again. "Halloway."

Below, Bram stands waist-deep under the gap, his breath smoking a little in the cold and water running off his rings. Above him the rope is tied off and taut, the joist is sound, and the warden's hand is waiting a yard over his head. Behind him the green light still lies on the silt. The seep keeps trickling in from the cut side.

*(Out of game: Bram's own climb out is his player's next move, so he's still at the foot of the gap.)*

The carved face ends up where it was before, tilted toward the hole and just under the surface. The plaster behind it is still dry.

"Leave anything heavy if you need to," Bram says. "Let's get out of this air."

He comes round onto Pell's bad side with his shoulder down and ready. Pell is already moving, one hand flat on the wet stone and the good leg leading, counting out loud. *One. Two.* Bram keeps a half-step behind him and just to his left, close enough to catch a sleeve. The silt sucks at their boots. Pink crust crunches wherever a palm touches the wall, and Pell keeps his hand off it where he can. Mail chinks behind him, steady. *Three. Four.* Nobody stops counting.

The bars of daylight between the planks get wider overhead. Then the gap is above them, a man's width of white, with the black joist across it, Bram's hemp in two turns round the joist, and Hale's big hand reaching down past it.

"Coming to you, Master Hale."

Pell reaches past the fingers and takes the wrist, and Hale's hand shuts on his wrist in turn like a vice. Below him Bram plants himself in the silt, gets a shoulder under Pell's good thigh and lifts. With the warden pulling from above and the fighter pushing from below, Pell barely has to do the work himself. Still, he does it the way he'd go up a drainpipe, arms doing it all, quick and light. He keeps the swollen shin up off the edge of the boards. He comes over the edge, rolls clear of the gap onto the sound flags by the wall and lies on his back.

He drags the wet collar down off his face. The shed air smells of tallow and cold ash, and after the working it tastes like a mountain. He takes one slow breath, then a second and a third. The thickness behind his eyes doesn't go all at once. It thins like fog going off a field, and by the third breath the roof beams over him have stopped looking far away.

"Thanks." Then, quietly, still flat on the floor: "That's twice today you've been where I needed a hand."

Hale is still on one knee by the gap and doesn't look round.

"Once," he says. "First time I missed."

Pell calls toward the door for Sefa: prop it wide, get Bram's arm, look at his eyes. His voice goes out over the hole and into the glare. Nobody answers from the yard. A jackdaw calls somewhere up on the terraces, and that's all.

Hale lets it hang for a moment.

"She's gone," he says. "Took her pack. Walked out while Halloway was going down." He looks at the door, then back at the gap. "Didn't say."

Then he turns his head and looks at Pell properly for the first time since the floor went. He takes Pell's jaw in his chalky fingers and tips his face toward the daylight from the door, the way you'd turn a stone to look at its grain, and stares into one eye and then the other.

"Seen men come up off that face," he says, and lets go. "You're slow. Not gone. Clean air does it. An hour." He leans back over the gap, and the same hand goes down past the joist toward the water again. "Halloway."

Below, Bram stands waist-deep under the gap, his breath smoking a little in the cold and water running off his rings. Above him the rope is tied off and taut, the joist is sound, and the warden's hand is waiting a yard over his head. Behind him the green light still lies on the silt. The seep keeps trickling in from the cut side.

*(Out of game: Bram's own climb out is his player's next move, so he's still at the foot of the gap.)*

messages.text:
I take hold of the secured rope and use it to climb within reach of Hale’s wrist, bracing a boot against the wall where I can find sound purchase.

“Mind your footing. I’m heavier than he is.”

With Hale’s help, I haul myself over the joist onto the sound flags and crawl clear of the opening. I sit back against the wall for a few breaths.

“Thank you.” I look toward Pell. “How’s the leg? Can you put any weight on it?”

scenes.narration:
Bram takes the rope in both hands above Sefa's two turns. The wet hemp creaks against the joist but doesn't creep. He walks his boots up the wall below the gap, and the first place he tries is soft, a slab of grey crusted with pink that crunches and slides under his toe. A hand's width higher he finds bare hewn stone that holds. He goes up hand over hand with the mail dragging at his shoulders and water pouring off the rings and back into the dark.

He tells Hale to mind his footing, since he's heavier than Pell.

"I know what you weigh," Hale says. "Watched you step."

The warden is already braced for it. He has dropped from one knee onto both, spread them wide on the sound flags and set his free hand flat on the floor behind him. When Bram's wrist comes up level with the boards, Hale's hand closes on it the way it closed on Pell's. He doesn't pull at once. He waits until Bram's other hand is over the joist, then leans back, and his shoulders take the weight. For a moment the two of them hold there with the joist between them. Then Bram gets an elbow onto the flags, then a knee. He comes up out of the cold in a long scrape of iron on stone, crawls clear of the gap and sits back against the wall. The working's cold has gone right through the padding, and water pools round him on the flags.

The shed air smells of tallow, ash and chalk dust after the working. It's still faintly sweet, but it's nothing to what's down there. The heaviness behind his eyes thins in a few breaths, the same as when he walks away from a fire on the last hour of a night watch.

He thanks Hale.

Hale doesn't answer it. He gets up off his knees, one at a time, and wipes his palms down his apron. He looks down the gap once more, at the green glow on the silt and the slack end of rope lying on the water, and then he doesn't look at it again.

Bram puts his question across the floor to Pell, about the leg and whether he can put weight on it. The answer will come from Pell.

Hale has turned to the room. He looks at the hole where the doorstep was, the brazier, the open tally-book on the bench and the pencil on the flags, and his jaw works once.

"Not here," he says. "House. There's a fire laid. You're both wet through." He nods at the broken doorway. "Same step out. Left flag. Wall."

He doesn't go yet. He stands by the back wall, between the two of them and the gap, with his arms hanging at his sides and chalk and water to the elbows. He waits for them to be ready.

 *(Out of game: none of the four needed a roll, and all four happen in the scene above. Bram climbs the tied-off rope with Hale hauling from above, crawls clear, sits against the wall and thanks him.)*

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lies still a breath longer while that sinks in. Then he rolls onto his good side and gets an elbow under him.

"Gone," he says, flat. "Right."

He doesn't waste words on it yet. He shifts over beside Hale at the gap, sets his knee on the sound flag and reaches down with him. He takes Bram's other wrist so the fighter has two hands to come up on.

"Up you come, Bram. Hale's got one side, I've got the other. On three. One, two, *three*."

Once Bram is out and clear of the gap, Pell sits back on his heels, breathing. His eyes go straight to the bench. Is the tally-book still there, and Sefa's copy, if she ever made it? He looks without touching, then up at Hale.

"The book's where she left it?" A nod at the bench. Then, quieter, the question that matters: "Master Hale. The box. You said it stays on its shelf till you're back. Is your house locked?"

He gets to his feet slowly, testing the swollen shin. It holds, so he picks up the oilcloth book (or what's left on the bench) and tucks it under his arm, out of the wet.

"I'm not saying she's done anything but walk off. People do. Maybe the hole scared her, maybe she had her own reasons." He looks at Bram, level. "But we go up to the house now, the three of us, and see that box with our own eyes before anybody thinks about anything else. Then I'll dry off by Hale's fire for the hour he says I need, he writes his note, and we decide whether we can still make sunset."

He starts for the door, keeping close to the wall, heel first on each flag the way Hale walked. He stays well clear of the hole. At the threshold he stops and looks down the cart track toward the Way, and up the slope toward the house. Is there any sign of Sefa, dust on the track, a figure on the road?

"Lead on, Master Hale. It's your house."

scenes.narration:
Pell has his knee on the sound flag beside Hale and one arm already going down past the joist when the climb ends without him. The warden leans back and the iron comes up over the edge in a long scrape of rings on stone. Pell's hand closes on nothing but cold air coming out of the gap. He takes it back and sits on his heels, breathing.

*(Out of game: Bram's climb was played in his own scene, and he was already over the joist by the time Pell reached it.)*

His eyes go to the bench. The tally-book is where Sefa left it, lying open and flat, with the damp pages fanned in the light from the broken doorway. The pencil is on the flags below the bench where it rolled. There's no loose sheet anywhere on the boards and no copy half-done. Whatever she wrote went out the door in her pack.

"Where she left it," Hale says, following his look. "Not touched."

Then Pell asks about the house.

Hale looks at him a moment before answering.

"Open. Halloway came down for you. I didn't lock it." He wipes his palms down his apron again, though they're as clean as chalk and water will let them be. "Box was on the shelf when I came down. That's what I know."

Pell gets up the way a man gets up off a roof he's not sure of, putting the good leg under him first and then the bad one. The shin throbs hot under the wet hose, tight as a drumskin, but when he puts his weight on it, it takes it. He crosses to the bench along the wall, heel first. He closes the book on its swollen pages, ties the twine and tucks the oilcloth bundle under his arm against his ribs, on the side away from the wet.

Hale watches him take it and doesn't object.

"Bring it. Names are in it."

Pell says his piece about Sefa: people do walk off, maybe the hole scared her, maybe she had her own reasons. Then he says they'll see the box, dry out, write the note, and decide on sunset. Hale hears it without a word of his own. When Pell gets to *the three of us*, the warden's eyes go once to the open doorway she walked out of. That's all the answer he gives it.

Pell goes to the door along the wall the way Hale came in. He passes the brazier and its rose-coloured crust without looking into the bowl. He takes the long step over the corner of the hole onto the left flag, which grates under him and holds, and steps out into the glare.

After the working the sun is like a slap. He stops on the dry chalk by Bram's shield and looks.

Up the slope, the house door stands open the way Bram left it, a dark square under the slate roof with the thin grey thread still rising from the chimney. Then he looks down the cart track toward the Way. The first long bend is empty. On the second, a good half-mile off and small as a thumbnail, a single figure is walking west with a pack on its back and a pale smudge of dust at its heels. It walks at a steady pace, not hurrying, and doesn't look back. As he watches, it goes round the shoulder of the hill and the track is empty again.

Hale comes out behind him by the same step. He stands on the white beside Pell and looks where Pell is looking, at the empty bend, for about as long as it takes to say a name. He doesn't say one.

"House," he says, and goes up the slope ahead of him.

It's a hundred feet of hard chalk, and the shin complains about every one of them. The jackdaw is back on the lifting frame. Hale reaches the door first and stops on the step to let Pell see past him without being told to.

The room is as they left it: cold ash and wet slate, the kettle on the hearth, the letters and the order on the table, the slate with its sixty-four and two names under it. On the shelf above the fire the squat iron-strapped box sits with its red wax toward the room. The seal is whole, and there's no new scrape in the dust of the shelf around it.

Hale looks at it for a moment, then goes past it to the hearth. He kneels and starts breaking kindling over the laid fire with his big hands.

"Sit," he says, without turning round. "Near it. Boots off."

Nothing else is waiting on you up here for the moment. The fire, the note and the warden's talk come when you want them.

<<<
Pell Dunmore: Pell lies still a breath longer while that sinks in. Then he rolls onto his good side and gets an elbow under him.

"Gone," he says, flat. "Right."

He doesn't waste words on it yet. He shifts over beside Hale at the gap, sets his knee on the sound flag and reaches down with him. He takes Bram's other wrist so the fighter has two hands to come up on.

"Up you come, Bram. Hale's got one side, I've got the other. On three. One, two, *three*."

Once Bram is out and clear of the gap, Pell sits back on his heels, breathing. His eyes go straight to the bench. Is the tally-book still there, and Sefa's copy, if she ever made it? He looks without touching, then up at Hale.

"The book's where she left it?" A nod at the bench. Then, quieter, the question that matters: "Master Hale. The box. You said it stays on its shelf till you're back. Is your house locked?"

He gets to his feet slowly, testing the swollen shin. It holds, so he picks up the oilcloth book (or what's left on the bench) and tucks it under his arm, out of the wet.

"I'm not saying she's done anything but walk off. People do. Maybe the hole scared her, maybe she had her own reasons." He looks at Bram, level. "But we go up to the house now, the three of us, and see that box with our own eyes before anybody thinks about anything else. Then I'll dry off by Hale's fire for the hour he says I need, he writes his note, and we decide whether we can still make sunset."

He starts for the door, keeping close to the wall, heel first on each flag the way Hale walked. He stays well clear of the hole. At the threshold he stops and looks down the cart track toward the Way, and up the slope toward the house. Is there any sign of Sefa, dust on the track, a figure on the road?

"Lead on, Master Hale. It's your house."
>>>

<<<
Pell has his knee on the sound flag beside Hale and one arm already going down past the joist when the climb ends without him. The warden leans back and the iron comes up over the edge in a long scrape of rings on stone. Pell's hand closes on nothing but cold air coming out of the gap. He takes it back and sits on his heels, breathing.

*(Out of game: Bram's climb was played in his own scene, and he was already over the joist by the time Pell reached it.)*

His eyes go to the bench. The tally-book is where Sefa left it, lying open and flat, with the damp pages fanned in the light from the broken doorway. The pencil is on the flags below the bench where it rolled. There's no loose sheet anywhere on the boards and no copy half-done. Whatever she wrote went out the door in her pack.

"Where she left it," Hale says, following his look. "Not touched."

Then Pell asks about the house.

Hale looks at him a moment before answering.

"Open. Halloway came down for you. I didn't lock it." He wipes his palms down his apron again, though they're as clean as chalk and water will let them be. "Box was on the shelf when I came down. That's what I know."

Pell gets up the way a man gets up off a roof he's not sure of, putting the good leg under him first and then the bad one. The shin throbs hot under the wet hose, tight as a drumskin, but when he puts his weight on it, it takes it. He crosses to the bench along the wall, heel first. He closes the book on its swollen pages, ties the twine and tucks the oilcloth bundle under his arm against his ribs, on the side away from the wet.

Hale watches him take it and doesn't object.

"Bring it. Names are in it."

Pell says his piece about Sefa: people do walk off, maybe the hole scared her, maybe she had her own reasons. Then he says they'll see the box, dry out, write the note, and decide on sunset. Hale hears it without a word of his own. When Pell gets to *the three of us*, the warden's eyes go once to the open doorway she walked out of. That's all the answer he gives it.

Pell goes to the door along the wall the way Hale came in. He passes the brazier and its rose-coloured crust without looking into the bowl. He takes the long step over the corner of the hole onto the left flag, which grates under him and holds, and steps out into the glare.

After the working the sun is like a slap. He stops on the dry chalk by Bram's shield and looks.

Up the slope, the house door stands open the way Bram left it, a dark square under the slate roof with the thin grey thread still rising from the chimney. Then he looks down the cart track toward the Way. The first long bend is empty. On the second, a good half-mile off and small as a thumbnail, a single figure is walking west with a pack on its back and a pale smudge of dust at its heels. It walks at a steady pace, not hurrying, and doesn't look back. As he watches, it goes round the shoulder of the hill and the track is empty again.

Hale comes out behind him by the same step. He stands on the white beside Pell and looks where Pell is looking, at the empty bend, for about as long as it takes to say a name. He doesn't say one.

"House," he says, and goes up the slope ahead of him.

It's a hundred feet of hard chalk, and the shin complains about every one of them. The jackdaw is back on the lifting frame. Hale reaches the door first and stops on the step to let Pell see past him without being told to.

The room is as they left it: cold ash and wet slate, the kettle on the hearth, the letters and the order on the table, the slate with its sixty-four and two names under it. On the shelf above the fire the squat iron-strapped box sits with its red wax toward the room. The seal is whole, and there's no new scrape in the dust of the shelf around it.

Hale looks at it for a moment, then goes past it to the hearth. He kneels and starts breaking kindling over the laid fire with his big hands.

"Sit," he says, without turning round. "Near it. Boots off."

Nothing else is waiting on you up here for the moment. The fire, the note and the warden's talk come when you want them.

messages.text:
“Aye. House.”

I get to my feet and offer Pell an arm. “Lean on me along the wall. At the gap we’ll go one at a time—don’t want both our weight on that flag.”

I take the tally-book and pencil from the bench as we pass, then follow Hale’s safe route out. Once we’re on firm ground, I retrieve my shield and help Pell up toward the house.

scenes.narration:
Bram gets to his feet against the wall. The wet padding drags at his shoulders, and water runs out of the rings and pools on the flags. He turns with his arm out for Pell.

There's nobody there to take it. The shed has emptied while he caught his breath. The bench is bare, and the tally-book is gone from where it lay. Only the pencil is left, down on the flags where it rolled. From outside, up the slope, comes the sound of the warden's boots on chalk, fading.

*(Out of game: in his own scene Pell has already taken the book and gone up to the house with Hale, so Bram's arm finds nobody to lean on it.)*

He picks up the pencil and puts it in his belt pouch. Behind him the gap at the back of the boards still breathes up cold and sweet. His hempen rope is tied off round the joist in Sefa's two turns, and its end lies somewhere down on the water. The green light still sits on the silt. He leaves the rope where it is.

He goes along the wall the way Hale showed him, heel first. Every flag rings clean. He passes the brazier with its crust of rose-coloured ash, then the bench. At the hole he puts one hand flat on the doorpost and takes the long step onto the left flag. It grates under his weight, the same short gritty settling as before, and then holds. One more stride puts him out onto bright, hard chalk.

His shield is where he left it, face-down a stride from the wall. He picks it up and the strap goes back over his forearm, and the arm stops feeling light.

The climb back is the same hundred feet of white he ran down an hour ago, and it's slower now, in soaked mail, with the cold still deep in him. The sun on his back helps a little. The jackdaw has gone back to the lifting frame. Thin grey smoke is rising from the house chimney again, thicker now, with the smell of fresh kindling in it.

The door stands open. Inside, Hale is on his knees at the hearth, feeding split wood to a small fire that has just caught. He looks round at the ring of mail on the step, takes Bram in from boots to collar, and has another short breath through his nose.

"Mail off," he says. "Hang it by the fire. Rings'll rust by noon." He turns back to the flames. "Stool by the wall."

The case is on its shelf above him, red wax toward the room, and the slate on the table still has its two names.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell lowers himself onto the stool nearest the hearth, good leg first, and sets the oilcloth bundle on the table beside the slate. He works his boots off. They come away with a wet suck, and he tips a cupful of grey water out of each onto the flags, then stands them on their heels toward the fire. He peels the hose down off the swollen shin to see it in the light, bruised purple from knee to ankle and tight, and leaves it bare to the warmth.

Before he settles he looks up at the shelf. He doesn't touch the box. He just looks at the red wax from where he sits: whether the impression in it is the black tower, the same as on Vossick's letter, and whether the iron straps sit clean in their old marks.

"Whole," he says, mostly to himself. "Good."

He holds his hands out to the new fire while Hale gets it going and lets the heat climb into his fingers. Then, quietly, without looking away from the flames:

"I said we'd talk when I was out. I'm out."

He gives Hale a moment.

"I'll tell you what I saw, and you tell me where I'm wrong. Your salt grows on a wall where the air puts a man to sleep standing. You dry it here, door open, man outside, long rake. That's not habit, that's a rule somebody learned the hard way. Tobin Reed went to sleep in four foot of water, and the Fist got 'drink' for their book because 'the seam did it' would've shut the House's best earner." He turns his head and looks at Hale, level, no edge in it. "And under your shed there's a carved sun, a ring of count-marks, and a patch of plaster the salt won't grow on. Somebody sealed something up down there on purpose. Before your time, you said. I believe you. But you knew it was more than water, or you'd have walked on those boards."

He leans back a little, rubbing warmth into his calf above the bruise.

"I'm not the Fist, and I'm not the House. I just want to know what I'm carrying down the hill in that box, and whether anyone who breathes it dried is going to sleep the way Tobin did." A beat. "Thorn's buyer has a coach for the Gate tonight. I'd like to know who's on the other end of that."

Then, practical again, he nods at the table:

"Write while you talk, if you can do both. Sixty-four owed, the order, Vossick, your two letters and the days. The book's there for the names." He taps the oilcloth. "I'll want the hour by the fire anyway. Bram'll want it too, by the look of him."

He glances at Bram, then, drier: "And Sefa took her copy of your three weeks with her, and nothing else, it seems. So whoever she's walking to, she's carrying your lads' names. Worth remembering."

scenes.narration:
Pell sits down on the stool nearest the hearth, good leg first, and puts the oilcloth bundle on the table beside the slate. The boots come off with a wet suck. Each one gives up a cupful of grey water onto the flags, and he stands them on their heels facing the fire. He peels the hose down off the shin. In the firelight the bruise runs purple from knee to ankle, the skin tight and shiny over the swelling, but there's no break in it. He leaves it bare to the heat.

He looks up at the shelf without getting up. It's a habit and needs no effort: the red wax, the straps, the dust. The straps sit in their old marks, each one in a pale line where the iron has lain a week without moving. The wax is whole, but the stamp in it isn't the black tower. It's a plain ring with a W inside it, pressed a little off-centre by a heavy thumb.

"Whole," he says. "Good."

Hale sees where he's looking. "Quarry's mark. Mine." He snaps another stick across his knee. "House never sent a seal up here."

Then the fire catches properly and the warden sits back on his heels. Pell says his piece to the flames: he's out, so now they talk. Hale doesn't stop him. He listens to all of it, the wall that sleeps a man standing, the rake that's a rule and not a habit, *drink* for the Fist's book, the sun and the count-marks and the plaster the salt won't grow on. When Pell gets to the boards, the warden's jaw works once, slowly.

Then he gets up, goes to the table and pulls a sheet of paper off the pile. He uncorks a pot of ink and sits down across from Pell with the pen. He doesn't write yet.

"Tobin didn't drink," he says. "Not a drop. Chapel man. His mother's." He looks at the nib. "Found him on his face. Hands open. No mark on him. Water to here." He lays the edge of his hand flat against his own ribs. "Lamp still on the ledge. Gone out."

He dips the pen.

"House didn't ask. Fist wanted a word. I gave 'em the one that closes a book." He starts writing, slowly and hard, the way he chalks. "You're not wrong. That's all I'll say on it."

The pen scratches for a while. He takes the names off the tally-book with Pell's help, the book open between them on the boards, and copies each one with its days. He doesn't hurry and he doesn't look up.

"The rake," he says to the paper. "Abel Garrow's. Warden before me. Twenty years. He had it off the one before him." The pen stops. "Same with the boards. *Don't lift the lid.* Said it the day he gave me the keys. Said it the day he died." He goes back to the names. "Never said why. I never asked. You don't, with Abel."

Pell asks about the box itself, whether dried salt in a case will put anyone to sleep, and Hale shakes his head before he has finished.

"Cold. Dry. Shut. Nothing. I've carried it on my back to the Way." He blots a line with the side of his fist. "Heat it, it smokes. Smoke does what the face does. Worse. Quicker." He taps the table once with the end of the pen. "Door open. Man outside. That's why."

Then comes the coach, and the buyer on the other end of it.

"Thorn's buyer's Thorn's business. Never heard a name." The pen moves again. Then it stops, and he looks at the wall for a moment as though he's counting something written there. "Used to be one case every two, three years. Dyer in the Gate. Small." He moves his jaw. "Thorn started last spring. Every two months since. Twelve pound a time." He dips again. "House likes her. Pays at the Gate."

He says it flatly, like a figure on the slate, and goes back to writing.

To Pell's dry remark about Sefa and the names she carried off, he gives a short shake of the head without lifting the pen. "Names don't pay anybody."

*(Out of game: Bram's arrival belongs to his own scene, so Pell's remark about him lands on Hale for now.)*

It takes him a long while. Pell's fingers warm up at the fire, the steam rises off his breeches, and the hose dries stiff on the stool. When Hale finally sets the pen down, the sheet is covered edge to edge in that heavy, upright hand:

*To M. Thorn, apothecary, Beregost. From O. Hale, warden at Whitestone.
Crew unpaid three weeks. Fourteen men eighteen days. Carter Hobb Marl twenty-one days and the mule. 56 gp and 8 gp. 64 gp owed.*
Under that are all fifteen names, each with its days.
*House Vandarren's order says your case was paid in full at the Gate, to J. Vossick, factor. I wrote him twice, nine days apart. No answer.
Who took your money, and how much. Send it by Dunmore or Halloway.
O. Hale.*

He reads it through once with his lips moving, then sands it from a pinch of chalk dust off his own sleeve, blows it clean and folds it in three. He doesn't hand it over. He lays it on the table on top of the closed tally-book, between himself and Pell.

"Note's done." He looks up at the shelf, then at Pell's bare shin. "Box goes with it when you go. Not before your eyes clear." He leans back. "Half a day to Beregost. Leave by noon, you've the time."

opening.narration:
The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind them, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life — a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.
