screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10
Skills: Athletics +6; Perception +4; Survival +4; Intimidation +3; Tools: land vehicles +3
Saves: Strength saving throw +6 (proficient); Constitution saving throw +5 (proficient); Dexterity saving throw +1; Intelligence saving throw +0; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +0
Attacks: Longsword +6 to hit, 1d8+3 slashing (1d10+3 two-handed); Javelin +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 30/120; Extra Attack: two attacks with the Attack action
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Extra Attack: attacks twice when taking the Attack action; Fighting style, Protection: with a shield, a reaction imposes disadvantage on an attack against a creature within 5 feet of him; Second Wind: a bonus action, regains 1d10+5 hit points; once per short rest; Action Surge: one additional action on his turn; once per short rest; Improved Critical (Champion): a weapon attack crits on 19 or 20; Healer's kit: stabilises a dying creature without a check (ten uses)
Limits: No magic at all; Heavy armour: disadvantage on Stealth; Second Wind and Action Surge return only after a short rest
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Second wind 1/1; Action surge 1/1; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 23 gp; 14 sp; 30 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Chain Mail; Main hand: Longsword; Off hand: Shield
Pack: Bedroll and Hardtack; Healer's Kit; Hempen Rope (50 feet); Javelin ×4; Tinderbox; Torch ×3

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Behind you, Pell murmured to you and Sefa that a quarry this size should not be silent at mid-morning, and that the warden is either waiting for you or for someone else. He stayed a pace back, off to your side, hands well away from his shortsword, and called a friendly greeting, saying Maela Thorn of Beregost had sent you for her case and asking where the crew had got to. Sefa, at the yard's edge, greeted the house, asked whether the warden was about, and told you both in a low voice that no one was working and to keep your eyes open.

The man in the doorway has a grey beard with chalk in it and forearms as thick as cart-shafts. He lets you come. When you stop a few paces short and leave the doorway clear, he notices, and something in his shoulders lets go a quarter-inch.

"Hale," he says. "Osric Hale. Warden." He looks at you, then at Pell's raised hand, then at Sefa. "Thorn's lot. Thought so."

He turns his eyes to Pell. "Crew walked. Yesterday. Noon bell." His jaw works as if he were chewing something. "Three weeks. Not a copper come down from the Gate."

To your question he gives a short breath through his nose. "All right. Nobody's hurt, if that's what you're asking. Nobody's paid either."

Then he turns to Sefa, since she asked for the warden by name.

"Your case is in there. It's ready. Been ready a week." He unfolds his arms and hooks a thumb in the key ring, not taking it off. "Thorn paid for it. She'll have paid somebody. It wasn't me, and it wasn't my lads. Before that box leaves this house I want to know who she paid, and how much." He stops, then adds, "That's all."

Past his shoulder you can see a low room with a hearth, a kettle, and a table stacked with papers and a slate. The smoke from the chimney keeps rising, thin and straight. The yard is so quiet you can hear the kettle ticking as it cools.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: quarry yard, a few paces from the warden's doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

You said you had stood waiting for wages yourself, and that you wouldn't call it a small matter. Then you told Hale that Thorn had hired the three of you to carry the case and not to handle her accounts. She hadn't said whom she paid or how much, only that you would share ninety gold on delivery before sunset. You asked whether he had an order or a receipt naming who took her money.

Sefa then stepped forward, stopping short of the doorway so as not to crowd him. She said you hadn't been sent with an answer, that Maela had hired you off the Trade Way yesterday to fetch the case, and asked what Thorn had told him: a name, a day, a sum. She said the box had to be on the road soon or no one would be paid, and asked to come in and look at the table. Pell stepped up level with you and said the three of you were hired legs and had never seen Thorn's ledger. He said somebody up in the Gate seemed to be keeping the coin meant for the quarry. He asked whether the hammers left upside down on the block in the lower cut were a strike mark or a message, and who the owner was, who sent the pay and who carried it. He offered to carry a note from Hale to Thorn alongside the case, today.

Hale heard you out without moving. At your mention of waiting for wages his eyes went to the old company mark painted over on his shield, then came back up.

"Receipt," he says. "No. Order. That I've got."

He looked at Sefa a long moment, then stepped aside, just far enough. You followed her in. The room smells of cold ash and wet slate. On the table are a slate covered in chalk tallies, two sheets of cheap paper written in a heavy hand, and a folded letter with a broken wax seal, a black tower on grey. He pushes the letter across the boards to Sefa with one finger.

It is a short letter in a clerk's neat hand:

*To the warden at Whitestone. Release to M. Thorn, apothecary, of Beregost, one case of salt of the low seam, twelve pounds, sealed. Paid in full at the Gate. Release on her messenger's word. For House Vandarren, by the hand of Jeren Vossick, factor.*

It gives no sum. Under it, the two cheap sheets are letters Hale wrote to Vossick, dated nine days apart. The second is shorter, and its last line is pressed so hard the pen tore the paper: *The men will not wait past the feast of the month.*

"Paid in full," Hale says to you. "At the Gate. So Vossick's had her money. A week, at least. Ten days." He doesn't look at the shelf. "Wages come down with the same man who carries Vossick's letters. Every month. Not this month."

He answers Pell one question at a time. "Owner's House Vandarren. Patriars. Never seen one up here. Vossick sends the pay." He jerks his head at the yard. "Hammers. That's a strike. The tools are the House's. Lads left them where the House can find them, set out proper. Nobody's hurt. Nobody stole."

He takes the chalk and writes on the slate under the tallies, slowly: *14 men. 3 wks. 56 gp. Carter 8.*

"Sixty-four gold," he says. "That's what's owed."

He puts the chalk down and thinks about the offer. He isn't a man who does that quickly.

"Your note. All right. Names and days, so Thorn sees it's not a number I made up. Names and days are in the tally-book." He pauses. "Book's in the cutting-shed. Down by the low cut. I don't keep it here."

Then he looks at each of you in turn and stops at you, because you were the one who spoke about waiting for wages.

"Box goes with the note. One of you puts a name to it. Somebody brings me back what Thorn says. Who took it, how much." He pauses. "Not a promise from her. From you."

Behind him the kettle ticks once more and goes quiet. Through the open door, down the slope, you can see the roof of the cutting-shed at the lip of the lower cut, a low stone hut with a plank door. Beyond it the white terraces step down into a cutting where the stone turns grey and wet.

Where you are: inside Hale's hut at the Whitestone quarry · Time: Day 1 · morning

Hale takes the letter back from under Sefa's finger and folds it along its old creases. The order says to release on her messenger's word, he says, but not what day. He means to keep holding the box.

Sefa leaves for the cutting-shed. Pell gives his name and Hale chalks *Dunmore* under the sixty-four, the letters as heavy as his tallies. You give yours with its limits stated, and Hale listens to all of it, including that you will come back and say so if Thorn won't answer. He chews on that, then chalks *Halloway* beside the first name. "Two," he says. "Good." He tells you the book is on the shelf left of the door, in oilcloth, and the box stays on its shelf here till he is back.

Then Pell asks quietly about the cut, and for the first time Hale doesn't answer straight away. He puts the chalk down and wipes his fingers on his apron, one at a time. "Low seam. Yes. Salt grows on the wall down there. Pinkish." He stops. "Air's bad. Wet, close. Men get slow in it. I don't keep a man on that face more than an hour." He looks at Pell, and this time he means it. "Stay off the grey. Nothing down there but water."

He unhooks a single long iron key from his ring and goes out, Pell a half-step at his side. You are left in the room with the slate and the box on its shelf.

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Thorn's Answer for Osric

Where you are: in the warden's room up the slope, with the slate and the box · Time: Day 1 · morning

You leave the box where it sits, and the order and the torn letters stay on the table. You step out into the glare.

From the doorstep the slope runs down white and bare to the cutting-shed, a hundred-odd feet below. The plank door stands open, and Hale's broad, aproned back fills the threshold. You cup a hand and call the warning down: bad air at the low face, and the grey stone is to be avoided. In that dead quiet your voice carries the whole way, off the stone and back again. Whether it reaches the shed in time to matter is down there with them.

Then you do what you did for ten years at the edge of every camp. You pick a spot where the doorframe is at your shoulder and the room behind you has only the one way in, and you let your eyes work the ground in a slow circle.

You know this kind of ground without needing to think about it. The terraces above are bare white steps with no lip deep enough to hide a man. Anyone coming in has three ways to do it. There's the cart track, which drops in two long bends toward the Way and is empty for a mile, its dust lying undisturbed. There's a goat-path along the spoil heaps on the north side, gone soft and crumbly, with nothing on it fresher than the rain. And there's the lip of the lower cut, which nobody would walk unless he had to. Nobody is on any of them. A jackdaw sits on the crossbeam of the idle lifting frame, cocks its head at you and goes back to picking at something in the joint.

Far off to the west, where the hill falls away to the plain, the Trade Way shows as a thin pale line through green. One ox-wagon crawls along it northward, so slow it hardly seems to move, the only thing out there and well past caring about Whitestone.

Behind you in the house the kettle has gone completely quiet. The case sits on its shelf with the red wax towards the room. On the table the slate holds two names in chalk, and one of them is yours.

Nothing comes up the track while you stand there.

Where you are: doorstep of the hut, above the cutting-shed · Time: Day 1 · morning

You set the rim of your shield against your boot and lean its weight on your leg. It's a sentry's stance, and your body settles into it without being told.

The sun has climbed while you've stood there. The shadow of the doorframe has shrunk to a hand's width on the step, and the white terraces throw the glare back so hard you have to squint at the far side of the yard. The jackdaw has given up on the lifting frame and moved to the edge of the half-loaded cart. It walks up and down the stones as if it were counting them.

Every so often you look down the slope. The shed door is still open, and Hale's broad back still fills it. Voices drift up the hundred feet of chalk, low and steady. One is a woman's, reading something in an even run, a name and then a pause, then another name. The other voice is short and heavy, a word or two at a time. You can't make out the words, only the rhythm. Nobody calls out, and nobody's voice rises.

Out on the plain the ox-wagon has crawled maybe a quarter-mile further north. Nothing moves on the cart track. Behind you in the house a log settles in the cold hearth with a soft tick, and the case sits on its shelf with the wax toward the room.

You keep your ears on the shed and go on watching.

Where you are: in the house doorway at the top of the slope, above the yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

You call down the slope that all is quiet up here and ask how the note is coming, adding that the walk back is still half a day. Then you stay by the doorway, watching the yard while they finish.

Your voice carries off the white stone as cleanly as your first warning did. What comes back isn't an answer about the note.

You catch the end of a sound first, a soft heavy rush, like a sack of meal emptied onto a floor. Under it comes a deep knock of stone on stone, muffled as if it came from under the ground. The steady rhythm of the reading has stopped. A plume of white dust rolls out of the shed doorway and hangs in the still air, glowing in the sun.

Then a voice rises up the hillside, louder than anything the man has said all morning: "Halloway!"

Through the settling dust you can see the warden flat on his belly across where the threshold used to be, his head and one arm reaching down into the ground in front of the door. The doorway itself has changed shape. The bottom of it is a broken lip of chalk, and nobody is standing in it. You can't see the others anywhere on the slope or by the shed. Faint and flattened by the distance, a second shout comes up, aimed down into the ground rather than up the hill: something about *thrash*.

The jackdaw bursts off the cart in a clatter of wings and heads for the terraces.

Behind you the house is silent. The case is on its shelf with the wax facing the room, the slate holds its two names, and your hempen rope hangs coiled at your belt. Down the slope the dust drifts slowly toward the lower cut.

Where you are: in the doorway of the house, up the slope from the shed · Time: Day 1 · morning

You shout and run down the slope, shaking the rope loose from your belt as you go. The chalk is hard and white, and you know where it's firm, so you take the straight line. Your mail rings with every stride. Near the shed you slow and keep off the broken chalk, as you meant to. Thirty feet out, you see a broad dark patch of damp running from the lip of the cut toward the doorway. The chalk over it looks dull and swollen, like bread dough. You swing uphill around it and come in along the shed's side wall on dry, bright ground that rings under your boots.

You call ahead to Hale, asking who is down and whether they can hear him, and you call into the hole for Pell and Sefa, telling them the rope is coming and asking if they are hurt. You look around for a stout post or solid beam to tie off to.

The doorway is gone. Where the threshold was there is a ragged hole about four feet across, its edges still crumbling. Cold air comes up out of it, smelling of wet stone with something sweet underneath. Hale lies flat across the outer lip with his arms spread, his beard and apron white with fresh dust. Past the hole, inside the shed, Sefa is on the far side, close against the wall left of the door.

Hale turns his head at the sound of your mail.

"Dunmore," he says. "Down there. Eight foot. Water to his chest. Leg's under a stone. Not drowned." His jaw works. "He hears. He's talking."

Your eyes go to the doorframe out of habit, and Hale sees you look.

"Not the frame. Same rot as this." He jerks his chin into the shed. "Back. Under the boards. New plank, pale one. Joist under it's sound. Tie there. Rope goes down through the boards, not through here."

Then he looks you over, mail and shield and all, and takes a short breath through his nose.

"Flag left of the hole holds her. Holds you in that iron, I don't know." He lifts one hand off the chalk and points across the hole at Sefa. "Coil goes across. Or you go round to the back wall and think of something. That's all."

You stand at the side of the doorway with the rope over your arm. The hole lies between you and the inside of the shed, and your call down into the dark is still sounding off the water.

Where you are: in the doorway of the house, up the slope from the shed · Time: Day 1 · morning

You don't wind up. You swing the coil once at your hip, the way you'd throw a line to a man on a wagon roof, and let it go underhand. Inside the shed the lid of boards at the back is open now. A pale plank is propped up on iron wedges, and Sefa kneels on the last flag beside the gap. The coil sails over the ragged hole and across the floor, paying out as it goes, and drops in a loose heap on the flags at her knee. You keep the other end wrapped twice round your fist. The slack lies across the hole, a hand above the broken lip.

You bend over the hole and send your question down into the dark. It goes down past Hale's shoulder and comes back off the water flattened.

Then you slip the shield off your arm and lay it face-down on dry chalk a long stride back from the wall, where nothing is going to give under it. The arm feels light without it. The mail doesn't. You feel every pound of it as you look along the side of the shed.

There isn't much to see. The wall is dry-laid white block, shoulder-high to the eaves, with no window and no gap bigger than a mortar joint. Round the back corner the ground doesn't go on. The rear wall stands right at the lip of the lower cut, and below it the white falls away into wet grey. The dark seep-stain runs along its foot like a tide line. Nobody walks round that way unless they mean to swim.

Hale hears your question and answers without lifting his eyes from the hole.

"No. One door. This one." His jaw works. He takes one hand off the chalk and lays it flat on the broken lip, then moves it left, onto the flag Sefa knelt on before. "Long step. There. Then the wall, all the way back. Don't stop on the dull ones."

He puts the hand back down and spreads his weight again. Nothing else from him. In the shed the coil lies where it fell. The water down in the hole slaps once against stone, and you are on the outside of the doorway with your end of the rope in your fist.

Where you are: outside the shed doorway on dry chalk, holding the rope end · Time: Day 1 · morning

You unwind the two turns of hemp from your fist and let the end drop. Across the hole the line goes slack, sags until it nearly touches the broken lip, then lies still. Nothing pulls it toward the edge now. At the far end, in the dim back of the shed, you can see it go down through a gap under the pale plank, which is propped on its iron wedges. It is already tied off to something below. Sefa's end was made fast before you called.

Then the long step.

You judge it the way you'd judge a wagon-bed from the ground: four feet of ragged hole, and on the far side a flag with a darker seam along its edge. You set your rear foot on the bright chalk by the doorpost and keep one hand flat on the wall stones. You don't jump. You reach, the way you step over a ditch with a pack on, and bring your weight down onto the flag all at once.

The flag grates. It is a short, gritty sound, stone settling on stone, and it drops perhaps the thickness of a fingernail under your boot. A trickle of chalk runs off the hole's edge beside it and patters into the water. Then the flag stops moving. It holds you, mail and all.

Hale is still flat on the outer lip and watches it the whole way. He lets his breath out through his teeth.

"Holds," he says. "Don't stand there admiring it."

For the moment you're over the hole, you can see down into it. It is eight feet of green-white light coming up off the silt, with ripples crawling over a hewn ceiling. A man's head and shoulders stand up out of the water, and beside them a squared block lies tilted with its top face out. A black beam rises from under its far corner at a slant toward you, like a pump-handle waiting for a hand. The smell coming up is sweet and thick, like a cold bakehouse.

Then you're past it. You put your shoulder to the wall and follow it toward the back, testing each flag with your heel before you trust it. Every one along the wall rings clean and hard, the way the ground did all morning. The brazier goes by on your right with its crust of rose-coloured ash. Ahead, the flags stop in a straight edge and the dark sweating boards begin. Beside the edge, Sefa's pack leans against the wall and the pale plank sits up on its wedges. A cold breath comes out of the gap and smells of wet stone and something sweeter.

Your question goes down ahead of you, through the hole behind and the gap in front: one loose stone, or part of the roof?

Hale answers first. That one he can answer from what he's seen.

"Block. One. Size of a meal-chest." He jerks his chin at the ceiling of the shed and the dark boards. "Roof's sound. That's the old floor come down. Doorstep with it." His jaw works once. "He'll tell you the rest."

You are at the back of the shed now, at the edge of the boards. The rope runs down through the gap at your feet into the dark.

Where you are: back of the shed, at the edge of the boards by the gap where the rope goes down · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa takes in the slack hand over hand and coils it on the flag beside her, keeping well back from the broken lip. When the line lies clean she slips the broad chisel through her belt and lays out the plan to you: you go down first because you carry the weight on the lever, she tails the rope from up top and follows. Keep near the wall where the mud is soft, wade to Pell, tip the beam up under the block, and lift. She asks Hale to sing out if the light below goes out, and he says the light is steady and he'll say. She braces her heels against the last sound flag with the line running through her hands.

You kneel at the edge of the boards with your knees on two flags and one hand flat on a third to spread your weight. The flags take it without a sound. You put your face to the gap under the pale plank.

The first thing you see is how narrow it is. Sefa eased the plank down onto its wedges, and the opening at its end is about as wide as your forearm. A rope and an arm fit through it. A man in chain mail won't fit until that plank comes off, and maybe the one next to it as well. The planks are wide and not nailed. They're only heavy.

You look down past the black joist with Sefa's two turns of hemp on it. Eight feet below is water, dark at first and then paler where the light comes through. Pell had it at his chest, so on you it should come about to the waist. The working runs forward from under your knees, hewn square with a low roof, for a dozen feet to where the green glow lies on the silt under the hole at the door. Pell is in that glow with his head and shoulders out of the water. A rope comes down over the lip of the hole to his chest, the same line Sefa is holding up here.

The beam is to the left of Pell as you look at it. The black joist comes up out of the water at a slant, its top end a little above the surface and leaning toward the hole. You used to lever loaded wagons out of the ruts below Nashkel, and you read the rig without trying. The low end is pushed into a dark gap a hand high under the block's far corner. That corner sits on the edge of the fallen threshold flag, and the flag is the only thing for the beam to pivot on. The bite is shallow. A straight push down on the top end will lift that corner. A push off to one side could twist the beam out of the gap. When the weight comes off the beam, the block will come down exactly where it is now.

You send your question down the gap to Pell, then tell Sefa that Pell pulls clear before anything is lowered, to keep the rope steady, and not to haul him against the stone.

Hale answers from the front, since he's had it from Pell twice already.

"Set. Far corner. Lean on the top end. Slow." He looks down at the rope crossing the lip by his elbow. "She's not hauling. I'm watching it."

You kneel where you are, with the sweet cold breath of the working coming up into your face. For a moment your eyelids feel heavy, as they do on the last hour of a night watch. It passes. Nobody has come down into the water yet.

*(Out of game: Hale dropped the rope's end to Pell in Pell's own scene and Pell tied it round his chest, so it can't be fed down through the gap. You can still hang from the joist and drop into the water.)*

Where you are: kneeling at the edge of the gap in the boards at the back of the shed · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa's player has left the table. Sefa leaves the scene and is not played again.

You look at the gap and then at the man beside you, and say it once: the bad air is reaching up this far, so Sefa stays above with the line, and one of you down there is enough.

You don't wait for anyone to agree. You get your fingers under the end of the pale plank, and the wedges drop out and ring on the joist below. The plank is waterlogged and heavy, about what a wet door weighs. You walk it back hand over hand and lay it flat across the solid flags. The board beside it is darker and older. It comes up with a wet sucking noise, slime trailing from its underside, and you lay it on top of the first. The gap is as wide as a man's shoulders now. The cold, sweet breath of the working comes straight up into your face.

When you look round, Sefa has already turned away. She lays the broad chisel down flat on the last flag and picks her pack up off the wall. Along the left wall the flags ring under her steps, past the brazier and the bench, where the tally-book still lies open beside the fallen pencil. She takes the long step over the corner of the hole onto the flag that holds and goes out through the broken doorway into the glare. The light swallows her and she's gone. Hale, flat on the outer lip, turns his head to watch her go by. Then he looks back down into the hole and says nothing.

The rope stays where she left it: two turns round the black joist and the knot, tied off and snug. Nobody has to hold it.

You sit on the edge of the flags with your legs down in the gap, take hold of the joist with both hands and lower yourself. The mail drags at your shoulders the whole way and your arms take every pound of it. You hang at full stretch with your boots about two feet above the black water, then let go and bend your knees as you land.

The cold hits you harder than the drop does. The water closes round your waist and comes straight in through the rings and the padding underneath, spring-cold and sharp enough to stop your breath. Your boots sink into the silt up to the ankle. Something hard lies under it, a fallen flag or a loose stone, and you find it with your heel before you trust your weight to it.

The working is low enough that you have to stoop. Bands of daylight fall through the planks overhead. Ahead, a dozen feet off, the green glow comes up from the silt under the front hole. You can see a head and shoulders above the water there, the tilted block, and the black beam slanting up past the block's far side toward the square of white sky.

You go along the wall the way you'd go along a riverbank with a horse, slowly, testing every step, your left hand flat on the wet stone. Pink crystal crusts every seam under your palm and crunches as you go. The sweet smell is thick enough down here to taste. Halfway along, your eyelids get heavy the way they do in the last hour before dawn on a night watch. You know that feeling and how to deal with it. You breathe through your teeth and keep moving.

You come in on the beam from the side away from its bite, keeping your hip and your mail clear of it. The top end is right under the hole, and Hale's dust-white face is a yard above it.

"Straight down," the warden says. "Not toward me. It twists, it's out."

You tell Pell to get ready to pull clear, say you'll lift slowly, and ask him to tell you when the leg is free. Then you set both hands on the slimed black wood, one above the other like a man on a pump-handle, plant your heels in the silt and lean.

You don't heave. You put your shoulders over your hands and let your weight go down into the beam a little at a time, and the mail adds its own weight. For a moment nothing happens except the wood creaking and the water slapping against your ribs. Then the beam goes down a finger's width under your hands, and then a hand's width. On the far side of the block the corner riding on the fallen flag comes up out of its bed with a gritty grind of stone, and a cloud of silt rolls up through the green light. The whole block tilts back off whatever it was lying on. It rises the height of a fist and stops there, held up by the lever and the man on the end of it.

You hold it there with your arms locked and the beam steady and straight. Every muscle in your back is talking to you. Above you Hale has his arm all the way down into the hole beside the rope, his fingers spread a foot above the water.

"Holding," Hale says, down to the water. "Now."

Your records, changed:
Conditions: Waist-deep in cold water, Holding the lever

Where you are: In the flooded working under the floor, waist-deep, holding the beam that lifts the block, beside Pell and below Hale · Time: Day 1 · morning

You hold the stone up, weight straight over the lever, arms locked on the slimed black beam. The block hangs a fist's height off its bed, and you watch Pell through the silt-clouded water. You tell him that it's steady and the stone is up, and that you won't lower it until he says. You tell Hale to help him up as soon as he's clear.

Pell, one hand flat on the wet wall and the swollen leg held just off the bottom, calls to you to ease it down slow and straight, the way Hale said, let it settle where it was, and not to drop it. His voice crossed yours on the water. He waits, as he said he would, and uses the time for the rope.

He calls up that he is slipping it. Hale, still flat across the outer lip, hooks two fingers under the hemp where it crosses the edge and lifts it clear of the rotten chalk, letting slack slide down to the water. Pell works the bowline loose with numb fingers. The wet knot fights him, then gives, and the end lies in a slow coil on the water beside him. He glances round once for his pack. It is still on his shoulders under the satchel, soaked and heavy.

Hale looks down at the two of you for a long moment and takes a short breath through his nose.

"Not through here," he says.

He draws his arm out of the hole for the first time since Pell went in, gets his knees under him, then his feet, testing the chalk before he stands. He steps over the corner of the hole onto the flag that holds, which grates under him the way it did under you, and puts his shoulder to the wall. He goes along it toward the back, heel first on each flag, eyes on the boards and not on the brazier. At the edge of the boards he goes down on one knee beside the lifted planks and the gap you opened, spreads one big hand on the flag and reaches the other down past the black joist toward the water.

"Here," he says, down into the working. "I'll take him here."

The silt is starting to settle in the green light. The block hangs where you hold it, its carved face tilted toward the hole above, the sunburst and its ring of notches just under the surface. Behind it the plaster patch stays dry and pale. The seep goes on trickling in from the cut side.

Where you are: on the black beam in the flooded working, holding the lever with the block raised · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell called out that he was clear and told you to ease the block down slow and straight. He watched it go back onto its bed and waited for the silt to stop rolling. Then he told you to leave the beam where it lay and get out with him.

You let the beam rise under your hands the way you leaned it down, a little at a time, keeping it straight. The block comes down off its fist of air. Its far corner finds the edge of the fallen flag with a soft grinding of stone and sinks back into its bed. Another cloud of silt rolls up brown through the green light and starts to drift. You hold the beam until it carries nothing, then take your hands off. The black wood stays where it is, slanting up toward the square of sky. Pell's word to ease it down reaches you just as the stone settles, so the two of you were already doing the same thing.

The carved face ends up where it was before, tilted toward the hole and just under the surface. The plaster behind it is still dry.

"Leave anything heavy if you need to," you say. "Let's get out of this air."

You come round onto Pell's bad side with your shoulder down and ready. He is already moving along the right-hand wall, one hand flat on the wet stone and the good leg leading, keeping off the pink crust where he can. He counts aloud and tells you to push him along if he stops. You keep a half-step behind and just to his left, close enough to catch a sleeve. The silt sucks at your boots. Pink crust crunches wherever a palm touches the wall. Nobody stops counting.

The bars of daylight between the planks get wider overhead. Then the gap is above you, a man's width of white, with the black joist across it, your hemp in two turns round the joist, and Hale's big hand reaching down past it.

"Coming to you, Master Hale," Pell says.

He takes Hale's wrist rather than his fingers, and Hale's hand shuts on his wrist like a vice. You plant yourself in the silt, get a shoulder under Pell's good thigh and lift. With the warden pulling from above and you pushing from below, Pell goes up the way he'd climb a drainpipe, arms doing the work, quick and light, the swollen shin held off the edge of the boards. He rolls clear onto the sound flags by the wall and out of your sight.

He thanks Hale. Then, quietly, he says that's twice today Hale has been where he needed a hand.

"Once," Hale says. "First time I missed."

Pell calls toward the door for Sefa: prop it wide, get your arm when you come up, and look at his eyes. Nobody answers from the yard. A jackdaw calls somewhere up on the terraces, and that's all.

"She's gone," Hale says. "Took her pack. Walked out while Halloway was going down. Didn't say."

He turns Pell's face to the light from the door, looks into one eye and then the other, and lets go. "Seen men come up off that face. You're slow. Not gone. Clean air does it. An hour." He leans back over the gap, and the same hand goes down past the joist toward the water again. "Halloway."

You stand waist-deep under the gap, your breath smoking a little in the cold and water running off your rings. The rope is tied off and taut, the joist is sound, and the warden's hand waits a yard over your head. Behind you the green light still lies on the silt. The seep keeps trickling in from the cut side.

Your records, changed:
Conditions: Waist-deep in cold water

Where you are: waist-deep in the flooded cellar, at the foot of the gap · Time: Day 1 · morning

You take the rope in both hands above Sefa's two turns. The wet hemp creaks against the joist but doesn't creep. You walk your boots up the wall below the gap. The first place you try is soft, a slab of grey crusted with pink that crunches and slides under your toe. A hand's width higher you find bare hewn stone that holds. You go up hand over hand with the mail dragging at your shoulders and water pouring off the rings and back into the dark.

You tell Hale to mind his footing, since you're heavier than Pell.

"I know what you weigh," Hale says. "Watched you step."

The warden is already braced for it. He has dropped from one knee onto both, spread them wide on the sound flags and set his free hand flat on the floor behind him. When your wrist comes up level with the boards, Hale's hand closes on it the way it closed on Pell's. He doesn't pull at once. He waits until your other hand is over the joist, then leans back, and his shoulders take the weight. For a moment the two of you hold there with the joist between you. Then you get an elbow onto the flags, then a knee. You come up out of the cold in a long scrape of iron on stone, crawl clear of the gap and sit back against the wall. The working's cold has gone right through the padding, and water pools round you on the flags.

The shed air smells of tallow, ash and chalk dust after the working. It's still faintly sweet, but it's nothing to what's down there. The heaviness behind your eyes thins in a few breaths, the same as when you walk away from a fire on the last hour of a night watch.

You thank Hale.

Hale doesn't answer it. He gets up off his knees, one at a time, and wipes his palms down his apron. He looks down the gap once more, at the green glow on the silt and the slack end of rope lying on the water, and then he doesn't look at it again.

You ask Pell across the floor about the leg and whether he can put weight on it.

Hale has turned to the room. He looks at the hole where the doorstep was, the brazier, the open tally-book on the bench and the pencil on the flags, and his jaw works once.

"Not here," he says. "House. There's a fire laid. You're both wet through." He nods at the broken doorway. "Same step out. Left flag. Wall."

He doesn't go yet. He stands by the back wall, between the two of you and the gap, with his arms hanging at his sides and chalk and water to the elbows. He waits for you to be ready.

Your records, changed:
Conditions: Soaked through, cold to the padding

Where you are: in the shed, sitting against the wall by the gap, with Hale nearby · Time: Day 1 · morning

You get to your feet against the wall. The wet padding drags at your shoulders, and water runs out of the rings and pools on the flags. You turn with your arm out for Pell.

Nobody is there to take it. The shed emptied while you caught your breath. The bench is bare, and the tally-book is gone from where it lay. Only the pencil is left, down on the flags where it rolled. From outside, up the slope, comes the sound of the warden's boots on chalk, fading.

You pick up the pencil and put it in your belt pouch. Behind you the gap at the back of the boards still breathes up cold and sweet. Your hempen rope is tied off round the joist in Sefa's two turns, and its end lies somewhere down on the water. The green light still sits on the silt. You leave the rope where it is.

You go along the wall the way Hale showed you, heel first. Every flag rings clean. You pass the brazier with its crust of rose-coloured ash, then the bench. At the hole you put one hand flat on the doorpost and take the long step onto the left flag. It grates under your weight, the same short gritty settling as before, and then holds. One more stride puts you out onto bright, hard chalk.

Your shield is where you left it, face-down a stride from the wall. You pick it up and the strap goes back over your forearm, and the arm stops feeling light.

The climb back is the same hundred feet of white you ran down an hour ago, and it's slower now, in soaked mail, with the cold still deep in you. The sun on your back helps a little. The jackdaw has gone back to the lifting frame. Thin grey smoke is rising from the house chimney again, thicker now, with the smell of fresh kindling in it.

The door stands open. Inside, Hale is on his knees at the hearth, feeding split wood to a small fire that has just caught. He looks round at the ring of mail on the step, takes you in from boots to collar, and has another short breath through his nose.

"Mail off," he says. "Hang it by the fire. Rings'll rust by noon." He turns back to the flames. "Stool by the wall."

The case is on its shelf above him, red wax toward the room, and the slate on the table still has its two names.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Pencil; − Hempen Rope (50 feet)

Where you are: the house on the chalk slope, by the hearth with Hale · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.

How was the table?
Was there something you wanted to do and didn't?
Who did you take the other two players to be?

messages.text:
“Quiet for a working quarry,” I murmur to Pell and Sefa.

I walk into the yard toward the house, sword sheathed and shield low, looking over the abandoned tools and terraces for signs of trouble. I stop a few paces short of the man, leaving his doorway clear.

“Morning. Bram Halloway. Maela Thorn sent us for a sealed case of dye-salts. Are you the warden?” I glance back across the silent yard. “Everyone all right here?”

“I’ve stood waiting for wages myself. Won’t tell you it’s a small matter.”

I keep my voice level. “But Thorn hired us to carry the case, not handle her accounts. She didn’t say who she paid or how much. Promised the three of us ninety gold on delivery before sunset.”

I nod toward the papers inside. “Have you got an order or a receipt naming who took her money? We can look at that together. Might give us something better than guesses.”

“I’ll put my name to that. Bram Halloway. I’ll ask Thorn who she paid and how much, and bring you her answer myself. If she won’t answer, I’ll come back and tell you that plainly. I can’t promise her honesty or the House’s wages.”

I glance at Pell and Sefa. “That’s my promise. Doesn’t bind either of you.”

Then I turn back to Hale. “Let’s get your tally-book and put the names and days in writing. Where in the shed do you keep it?”

I leave the case and papers untouched and step to the doorway.

“Sefa—Hale says there’s bad air at the low face. Stay clear of the grey stone.”

I stay by the hut, keeping the case behind me and watching the path down to the cutting-shed. While they fetch the book, I look over the yard and quarry approaches for anyone coming our way.
I settle my shield against my leg and keep watch from the doorway, giving the others time to fetch the tally-book. Every so often I look down toward the shed, listening for voices or a call for help.

With the yard still clear, I call down toward the shed, “All quiet up here. How’s the note coming? We’ve still half a day’s walk back.”

I stay by the doorway, watching while they finish.

“Coming!”

I run down the slope, pulling the rope free as I go. Near the shed I slow, keeping off the broken chalk and approaching on intact ground.

“Hale, who’s down? Can they hear you?”

I look for a sound anchor—a stout post or solid beam—to secure the rope, and call toward the hole, “Pell! Sefa! Rope’s coming. Are you hurt?”

“Sefa, catch the coil. Hale says there’s a sound joist beneath the pale plank at the back. Secure it there and lower the rope through the boards—not over this lip.”

Keeping on the dry ground, I hold one end and toss her the coil across the gap.

“Pell, we’re getting a line to you. Don’t pull against the trapped leg. Can you keep your mouth above water without struggling?”

I take off my shield and set it clear of the broken ground, then look along the shed’s side for a safe way round to the back. “Hale, is there a rear door?”

“Sefa, secure your end first. I’m coming across to help.”

I unwrap the rope from my fist so it can’t drag me onto the broken lip, leaving slack for her to work. Once she has it anchored, I take the long step onto the sound flag Hale indicated, then follow the wall toward her, avoiding the dull stones.

“Pell, what’s pinning you—one loose stone, or part of the roof?”

I kneel on the sound flags beside the gap, spreading my weight, and look down to see where the rope reaches Pell and whether I can reach the raised end of the black beam.

“Pell, I saw a beam under that block. Is it set to lever the stone off your leg?”

To Sefa I say, “If we can lift it, he’ll need to pull clear before we lower it. Keep the rope steady—don’t haul him against the stone.”

I check what the beam rests on and where it would move before putting any force on it.

“Bad air’s reaching up here. Sefa, stay above with the line. One of us down there is enough.”

I help lift the loose plank clear, and the next if needed, keeping my weight on the sound flags. Then I lower myself from the sound joist and drop the remaining distance into the water, bending my knees.

I wade toward Pell along the wall, careful not to knock the lever sideways.

“Ready to pull clear, Pell. I’ll lift slowly. Tell me when your leg’s free.”

Once he’s ready, I press straight down on the beam’s raised end, steadily, keeping its shallow bite aligned beneath the block. I hold the pressure while he works his leg out.

“Steady, Pell. Stone’s up.”

I keep my weight straight over the lever, holding it down without shifting sideways. I watch Pell through the silt-clouded water.

“Hale, help him up as soon as he’s clear. Pell—tell me when you’re out from under it. I won’t lower till you say.”

“Lowering.”

With Pell clear, I ease the beam upward slowly, keeping it aligned until the block settles fully onto its bed. Only then do I let go.

“Leave anything heavy if you need to. Let’s get out of this air.”

I offer Pell my shoulder on his injured side and help him along the wall toward the rear gap, testing my footing as we go. Beneath Hale’s hand, I brace myself to help Pell up onto the sound floor.

I take hold of the secured rope and use it to climb within reach of Hale’s wrist, bracing a boot against the wall where I can find sound purchase.

“Mind your footing. I’m heavier than he is.”

With Hale’s help, I haul myself over the joist onto the sound flags and crawl clear of the opening. I sit back against the wall for a few breaths.

“Thank you.” I look toward Pell. “How’s the leg? Can you put any weight on it?”

“Aye. House.”

I get to my feet and offer Pell an arm. “Lean on me along the wall. At the gap we’ll go one at a time—don’t want both our weight on that flag.”

I take the tally-book and pencil from the bench as we pass, then follow Hale’s safe route out. Once we’re on firm ground, I retrieve my shield and help Pell up toward the house.

Strong atmosphere, and Hale felt like a believable man with a genuine grievance rather than an obstacle to the job. The rescue was especially good: clear physical stakes, useful environmental details, and room for Bram’s practical experience to matter.

The main frustration was continuity between player scenes. Pell sometimes appeared to have already acted beyond what Bram could see, and the final turn had everyone leave while Bram was offering to help them. That made coordinating feel unreliable. Brief updates about companions’ movements before asking for my next action would help.

The repeated watchkeeping turns also dragged a little; those could have been compressed until something changed.

Overall, an engaging opening. Bram’s promise to Hale gave him a personal stake without forcing one onto the whole party.

Yes—coordinate the rescue more directly with Pell, then check his injured leg and help him back to the house. A few times my actions arrived after he’d already moved on in his own scene, so that cooperation never quite landed.

I also wanted to finish the note with Hale, collect the case, and get moving before the deadline. The rescue was worth the detour; I just wanted a little aftermath together before the session ended.

I took them to be the players controlling Pell Dunmore and Sefa Marrin, each acting independently in parallel with me. I assumed the GM relayed their dialogue and actions into Bram’s view, just as it relayed mine to them.

I didn’t know anything about who was behind those characters—human or AI. When Sefa’s player left, I understood that as an actual table departure, not an in-character decision I could negotiate with.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Sefa Marrin — Human, warlock 5 (The Celestial — the Lantern; Pact of the Tome), former hospice novice, level 5
HP 38/38 · AC 14 · Speed 30 feet
STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 10 · CHA 18
Skills: Persuasion +7; Arcana +4; Religion +4; Insight +3
Saves: Wisdom saving throw +3 (proficient); Charisma saving throw +7 (proficient); Strength saving throw −1; Dexterity saving throw +2; Constitution saving throw +2; Intelligence saving throw +1
Attacks: Eldritch Blast +7 to hit, two beams, 1d10+4 force each, range 120 feet; Dagger +5 to hit, 1d4+2 piercing, thrown 20/60
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Spell attack +7; spell save DC 15; Pact Magic: two 3rd-level pact slots, recovered only on a short or long rest; Healing Light: a pool of six d6 per long rest; a bonus action spends up to four dice to heal a creature within 60 feet; Pact of the Tome: the Book of Shadows holds three extra cantrips (Guidance, Spare the Dying, Thaumaturgy); Agonizing Blast: +4 to each Eldritch Blast beam's damage; Repelling Blast: a beam that hits pushes the target up to 10 feet away; Eyes of the Rune Keeper: reads all writing
Spells: Eldritch Blast (cantrip); Light (cantrip); Sacred Flame (cantrip); Mage Hand (cantrip); Minor Illusion (cantrip); Guidance (cantrip); Spare the Dying (cantrip); Thaumaturgy (cantrip); Cure Wounds (1); Guiding Bolt (1); Misty Step (2); Lesser Restoration (2); Hold Person (2); Daylight (3)
Limits: Two pact slots only, back only after a rest; Light armour; Strength 8 — weak up close; One concentration spell at a time
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Pact slots 2/2; Healing light 6/6; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 1 pp; 8 gp; 41 sp; 12 cp
Worn: Amulet: Prayer Beads; Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Book of Shadows; Main hand: Dagger
Pack: Bedroll and Rations; Candle ×2; Tinderbox

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

Beside you, Pell murmured to you and Bram that a quarry this size should not be silent at mid-morning, and that the warden is either waiting for you or for someone else. He stayed a pace back, off to Bram's side, hands well away from his shortsword, and called a friendly greeting, saying Maela Thorn of Beregost had sent you for her case and asking where the crew had got to. Bram walked on into the yard with his sword sheathed and shield low, and stopped a few paces short of the man in the doorway, leaving it clear. He gave his name, said you had come for a sealed case of dye-salts, and asked whether the man was the warden and whether everyone was all right.

The man has a grey beard with chalk in it and forearms as thick as cart-shafts. He lets you come. When Bram stops short and leaves the doorway clear, something in his shoulders lets go a quarter-inch.

"Hale," he says. "Osric Hale. Warden." He looks at Bram, then at Pell's raised hand, then at you. "Thorn's lot. Thought so."

He turns his eyes to Pell. "Crew walked. Yesterday. Noon bell." His jaw works as if he were chewing something. "Three weeks. Not a copper come down from the Gate."

To Bram's question he gives a short breath through his nose. "All right. Nobody's hurt, if that's what you're asking. Nobody's paid either."

Then he turns to you, since you asked for the warden by name.

"Your case is in there. It's ready. Been ready a week." He unfolds his arms and hooks a thumb in the key ring, not taking it off. "Thorn paid for it. She'll have paid somebody. It wasn't me, and it wasn't my lads. Before that box leaves this house I want to know who she paid, and how much." He stops, then adds, "That's all."

Past his shoulder you can see a low room with a hearth, a kettle, and a table stacked with papers and a slate. On a shelf above the fire sits a squat box bound with iron straps, a blob of red wax on its lid. The smoke from the chimney keeps rising, thin and straight. The yard is so quiet you can hear the kettle ticking as it cools.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: quarry yard, near its edge, facing the warden's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

You stopped just short of the doorway so as not to crowd Hale, and asked to come in and look at what was on his table. Before that, Bram had said he had stood waiting for wages himself. He told Hale that Thorn had hired the three of you only to carry the case, that she hadn't said whom she paid or how much, and that she had promised ninety gold between you on delivery before sunset. He asked whether Hale had an order or receipt naming who took her money. After you spoke, Pell stepped up level with Bram and said you were hired legs who had never seen Thorn's ledger. He said somebody up in the Gate seemed to be keeping the coin meant for the quarry. He asked about the three hammers set upside down on the block in the lower cut, and who the owner was, who sent the pay and who carried it. He offered to carry a note from Hale to Thorn alongside the case, today.

Hale heard Bram out without moving. At the mention of waiting for wages his eyes went to the old company mark painted over on his shield, then came back up.

"Receipt," he says. "No. Order. That I've got."

He looks at you a long moment, then steps aside, just far enough. The room smells of cold ash and wet slate. On the table are a slate covered in chalk tallies, two sheets of cheap paper written in a heavy hand, and a folded letter with a broken wax seal, a black tower on grey. He pushes the letter across the boards to you with one finger.

It is a short letter in a clerk's neat hand:

*To the warden at Whitestone. Release to M. Thorn, apothecary, of Beregost, one case of salt of the low seam, twelve pounds, sealed. Paid in full at the Gate. Release on her messenger's word. For House Vandarren, by the hand of Jeren Vossick, factor.*

It gives no sum. Under it, the two cheap sheets are letters Hale wrote to Vossick, dated nine days apart. The second is shorter, and its last line is pressed so hard the pen tore the paper: *The men will not wait past the feast of the month.*

Bram has come in behind you. "Paid in full," Hale says to him. "At the Gate. So Vossick's had her money. A week, at least. Ten days." He doesn't look at the shelf. "Wages come down with the same man who carries Vossick's letters. Every month. Not this month."

He answers Pell one question at a time. "Owner's House Vandarren. Patriars. Never seen one up here. Vossick sends the pay." He jerks his head at the yard. "Hammers. That's a strike. The tools are the House's. Lads left them where the House can find them, set out proper. Nobody's hurt. Nobody stole."

He takes the chalk and writes on the slate under the tallies, slowly: *14 men. 3 wks. 56 gp. Carter 8.*

"Sixty-four gold," he says. "That's what's owed."

He puts the chalk down and thinks about Pell's offer. He isn't a man who does that quickly.

"Your note. All right. Names and days, so Thorn sees it's not a number I made up. Names and days are in the tally-book." He pauses. "Book's in the cutting-shed. Down by the low cut. I don't keep it here."

Then he looks at each of you in turn and stops at Bram.

"Box goes with the note. One of you puts a name to it. Somebody brings me back what Thorn says. Who took it, how much." He pauses. "Not a promise from her. From you."

Behind him the kettle ticks once more and goes quiet. Through the open door, down the slope, you can see the roof of the cutting-shed at the lip of the lower cut, a low stone hut with a plank door. Beyond it the white terraces step down into a cutting where the stone turns grey and wet.

Where you are: inside Hale's hut at the Whitestone quarry · Time: Day 1 · morning

Hale lets you finish, then takes the letter back from under your finger and folds it along its old creases. The order says to release on her messenger's word, he says, but not what day. He means to keep holding the box, and he says nothing more about it.

You are already at the door when Pell gives his name and Hale chalks *Dunmore* on the slate under the sixty-four. Bram gives his as well, with its limits stated, and Hale chalks *Halloway* beside it. You are away down the slope before you hear more.

The cutting-shed is older close up than it looked from the house. The walls are dry-laid white blocks, with moss crept green into the joints on the downhill side. The plank door is shut with an iron hasp and a padlock the size of a fist. Beyond the shed the ground falls away into the lower cutting, where the white turns grey and slick. A cold breath of air comes up out of it, smelling of wet stone.

Pell and Hale reach you there. Hale opens the lock and swings the door in, but he stays on the threshold with one hand on the frame.

Inside, the shed is dim and smells of tallow, and under that something faint and sweet, like a bakehouse with the oven gone cold. A bench runs along one wall with a box of wedges and feathers and a row of chisels on pegs. On the shelf left of the door lies a fat book wrapped in oilcloth and tied with twine. You take it down. It is heavier than it looks, and swollen with damp at the corners.

In the middle of the floor stands a cold iron brazier on three short legs. The ash crusting its bowl is a faded pink, like old roses. The back third of the shed is boarded rather than flagged, with wide planks laid over something, dark with damp and sweating at the seams.

Without looking at the brazier, Hale says from the doorway that the names are near the back, the last three weeks. You are to read them out, and he will know if you skip one.

Where you are: in the cutting-shed doorway, with the tally-book, Hale at the threshold · Time: Day 1 · morning

You untie the book and open it with care, angling it to the light from the doorway, and read out the last three weeks of names with their days, as written. Your eyes slide over the smeared marks and the words straighten for you.

Pell stays on the threshold with his boots on the white chalk, breathing shallow through his nose, and goes over the room with his eyes the way he would a strongroom: the brazier, the flags round it, the boarded back third. As you read, the faint sweet smell of bread left too long in a cold oven sits under the tallow.

You give each name with its days: Aldo Pike, Gerrit Pike and Wynn Carrow, eighteen days each, then Dace Tolliver, Ned Furrow, Ansel Brooke, Jory Venn, Cobb Sallow, Ulf Dray, Perrin Lusk, Tam Greave, Ivo Rendle, Sim Barrow and Hew Madden, eighteen days each. On a line to itself comes Hobb Marl, carting, twenty-one days, and the mule.

Hale nods a little at each name, like a man counting stones into a cart. He doesn't check you once. "Fourteen," he says when you're done. "And Hobb. Right."

Pell speaks low to Hale: someone has been burning his salt in that brazier, he says, since pink ash doesn't come from charcoal, and the back is a lid, not a floor. Then, level and straight in the warden's face, he asks whether one of the men got slow in here, with sweet smoke and a hole under the boards, and whether that is why they really walked. He tells you quietly to read quick and keep away from the brazier, and to come out if your head swims. You ask your own question from inside, about what burned there. Hale stands with his hand on the doorframe and hears you both out.

He takes a short breath through his nose.

"Me," he says. "I burn it." He nods at the bowl without looking at it. "Comes off the wall wet. Won't keep wet. Rots the case. So you dry it. Low fire, the coals under, salt on a tray over." His hand moves flat in the air, showing the tray. "Door open. Man outside. Stir it with a long rake. That's how it's done. That's how it was done before me."

That would account for the band of clean iron inside the bowl, where the tray was lifted off and the grit that spat through it was left behind.

"Thorn's twelve pound. Dried here. Eight days back."

To the question about the lid he answers more slowly. "Old working. Under there. Wet. Goes down to the low seam the back way. Boarded before my time." He stops. "One board's mine. Last spring. Old one went soft."

Then he comes to Pell's last question, whether one of them got slow in here, and for a moment he doesn't answer at all. He looks at Pell's face, then past him at the white glare outside.

"Not in here," he says. "Down there. Three years back. Tobin Reed." His jaw works. "Drowned. Drink."

He says *drink* as flatly as he said *eighteen days*. But his free hand wipes itself on his apron once, slowly, as if there's chalk on it that won't come off.

"Lads walked for wages," Hale goes on, steadier now that he's back on ground he's sure of. "Nothing else. Ask any of them. They're in Beregost drinking what they haven't got." He looks at you and the open book. "Copy it, then. The three weeks. Bench is dry."

He stays on the threshold, half a step to Pell's left, and his boots don't move. The cold breath from the corner of the boards keeps coming, steady as breathing.

Where you are: inside the salt-drying room, near the door and the brazier · Time: Day 1 · morning

You cross to the bench while Hale stays where he is. The bench is dry, as he said. The book lies flat under your hands and breathes out chalk and old tallow. A stub of pencil sits in a tin cup at the back. You find the last three weeks, a column of names down the left-hand page with Hale's slow sums beside them, and begin to copy by the light from the door. (The facing page has no entry for a Vossick advance. That line was in your own words only, and the book does not show it.)

At the doorway, Pell taps the hollow flag once more with his heel. It gives the same dull note, and he steps back onto the white chalk at Hale's elbow. He remarks that it is hollow under the doorstep too, so old workings must run everywhere under here. Hale doesn't answer. Pell then says the name Tobin Reed and nothing more, and adds that he has himself put things on paper because that was easier than carrying the truth. He tells Hale that if the book and his own mind differ, and it ties to that seam and Thorn's salt, he should say so before they hand her the case. There are two names on his slate now, and two people will come back up the hill. Hale's hand has stopped on his apron.

Hale speaks of four foot of water, where they found Reed, not deep enough to stand in to your chin. His jaw works once. He says Fist wanted a word for the book, and he gave them one. He looks at the open door and says he'll write the note at the house, where the paper is. To your back he says to copy clean.

Pell tells you to copy as fast as you can keep it clean, since the sun is climbing and it is half a day back. He tells Hale to write the note while you copy: the sum of sixty-four owed, the House's order, and Vossick's name, plus his two letters, the dates, all short enough for Thorn to read through.

Then the ground goes without warning. There is no crack and no creak first, only a soft rush of white, and the threshold flag tips up on its edge and falls away. Hale's hand snatches at air a foot from Pell's collar. Pell is gone into dark and the noise of falling stone.

You are at the bench with the pencil in your hand. The doorway you were copying by is a broken lip of chalk and a hole full of noise, and Pell isn't in it any more. Hale is down on his belly at the edge, his beard white with dust. He shouts for Pell not to thrash, then, with his head turned up the slope, bellows for Halloway. The shout goes up the white hillside and comes back off the terraces.

Your copy is started but not finished.

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: The Sunburst Under the Shed

Where you are: in the salt-drying room at the copy-bench, by the broken doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

You let the pencil fall and it clicks on the flags as you move off the bench, low, testing each flag with the ball of your foot before you trust it. The ones nearest the bench are solid and ring like stone on stone. Two strides from the door the note goes dull, the same dull sound Pell's heel found. You edge sideways along the wall with the door frame at your shoulder.

What's left of the threshold is a ragged lip of chalk, and bits of it keep breaking off and pattering into the dark. Hale lies spread flat across the outside edge with his arms reaching in, his weight laid out the way a man lies on bad ice.

"Not there," he says, without looking round. "Lip's going. Left of you. That flag holds."

You call down. Your voice goes into the hole and comes back off the water. Then you turn your head and send a second shout up the hill, toward the house, calling for Bram to bring rope because the yard is undermined.

You scoop up a chip of chalk the size of a thumbnail and murmur the cantrip. The chip lights in your palm, clean and white. You open your fingers over the hole and let it fall.

The chip drops eight feet in a quick bright streak, hits the water with a small sound and keeps shining as it sinks. It comes to rest on the silt, and for a moment the whole flooded working lights up from below, green-white through the water, throwing ripples onto the walls.

Pell is down there, chest-deep and upright, his face turned up into the light. He's alive and moving, his arms up, holding himself above the water. His left leg goes down into the silt below the knee and doesn't come back up. A block of squared white stone, about the size of a small chest, lies tilted across that leg with its top face out of the water. A blackened beam as long as a man floats against the wall beside him, one end sunk in the mud. Up close the walls are crusted pink in every seam, like hoarfrost on a cellar step, and the sweet bakehouse smell comes up through the hole thick enough to taste.

The underwater light catches the block's upper face. There's a carving on it, a wide sunburst with a round face at its centre, worn soft but cut on purpose, and a ring of small even marks running round it. Behind the block, low on the wall, one patch of the hewn grey stone isn't hewn. It's smooth and pale, about the width of two hands, and it shines back at you a little more evenly than raw rock does.

Somewhere out of sight, on the side toward the cut, you can hear water trickling in, thin and steady.

Hale has watched the light go down. He takes a short breath through his nose.

"Leg's held. Not drowned." He pulls one arm back out of the hole and points behind you, into the shed, at the boarded back third. "Joist under them boards. Sound one, under the new plank. Tie off there, not this side. This side's rotten to the yard." His jaw works. "Rope goes down through the boards. Not through here."

He doesn't move to do it himself. He stays flat on the lip, with his eyes on the man in the water.

*(Out of game: freeing Pell takes two people working the rope and that beam as a lever, it takes a few minutes, and it costs nothing else. You didn't need Spare the Dying: Pell is conscious.)*

Where you are: in the shed beside the broken threshold, above the flooded working where Pell is trapped · Time: Day 1 · morning

You go down on one knee on the flag left of the hole, the one Hale said would hold you, and brace a hand against the doorpost. You don't lean over. Bits of the lip still break off now and then and patter into the water below.

You keep your voice low and level and send it down to Pell: he's been seen, he shouldn't wrench the leg, they're rigging a lift, he should keep his arms free and his head up. From the dark comes the steady trickle off the cut side, and the slap of water against stone as the man down there shifts his weight.

As you turn, your eyes pass over the block once more. The sunburst lies just under the green-lit water, and around it runs the ring of small, even marks. You only glance at it, but in that glance your eyes do what they always do with writing. They don't slide off the marks the way they would off a mason's idle scratches. They catch on them, the way they catch on a line of letters in a language you haven't looked at properly yet. These are groups, spaced like words. It would take a proper look to read them, and you don't stop for one now.

You call across the hole to Bram, telling him to bring the rope up along the wall beside the new plank, mind the floor near the doorway, and follow your voice. Then you go to the bench. The box of wedges and feathers is heavy for its size. You take two iron wedges and a broad chisel off the pegs and carry them low against your hip, your shoulder brushing the wall all the way to the back of the shed. The flags ring true under your feet the whole way.

The flags stop where the boards begin, in a straight line like the edge of a step. The planks run side by side toward the back wall, dark and sweating at the seams. The new one is easy to find. It's the pale one, third from the left wall, with its sawn end still crisp. You don't need the chisel. The plank isn't nailed. When you kneel on the last flag and get your fingers under its end, it lifts in your hands, heavy with damp. You lift it a hand's breadth, then more, and kick a wedge into the gap to hold it up.

Under it, a foot below the boards, lies the joist. It's as black as the one in the water, but this one doesn't give when you press the heel of your hand along it, and the wood feels hard and cold, not soft. Beyond it there's nothing but dark and a cold breath coming up, with the sweet bakehouse smell riding on it, thicker here than anywhere else in the shed. A long way down and off toward the front, the water shows a faint green glow where your first chip lies on the silt, and the light moves over the hewn ceiling. Somewhere under that glow is Pell. The drop through here is about eight feet, and it ends in water. From where the rope would go in, it's a wade of a dozen feet forward to the block.

You breathe the sweet air for a moment while you work the second wedge in. Behind your eyes there's a slight heaviness, like the end of a long night shift, and it passes when you turn your face back toward the door and the daylight.

At the hole, Hale doesn't look round when you ask him to watch Pell. He's been watching him all along.

"Aye," he says, eyes down in the hole. Then, louder, so it carries to you: "Feel that joist with your hand before anybody hangs on it. Lift the board. Don't stand on it."

He stays where he is, stretched flat across the lip.

*(Out of game: Light only holds one object at a time, so lighting a second chip puts out the one on the silt down by Pell. Do you still cast it? I haven't played it yet.)*

Carried: + Broad Chisel

Where you are: at the back of the shed, kneeling by the lifted plank over the joist · Time: Day 1 · morning

You leave the light where it is. Down through the gap the chip still glows on the silt, and green-white ripples run across the hewn ceiling over the trapped man's head.

You lay the broad chisel flat on the last flag and get your fingers back under the pale plank. The second wedge has worked loose a little, so you tap it home with the heel of your hand. You shrug your pack straps off, set the pack against the wall where it won't catch, and let the plank settle slowly until both wedges take its weight. The gap between its end and the next board is about as wide as your forearm, room for a rope and an arm. It breathes cold up into your face.

The sweet smell comes up with it, heavier here than at the door, and for a moment your eyelids feel thick. Then it passes, as it did before.

You say, mostly to the room, that there's air enough here to stand and breathe, sweet but passing.

You call to Bram in the doorway: rope to you, end first, along the left wall, and keep to the flags that ring true. Then, more quietly, you speak to Hale, the broad back stretched across the lip: the first light stays with the man below, and if he goes under Hale should shout and you'll bring something brighter.

Hale doesn't turn his head. He lifts one hand a finger's width off the chalk to show he heard, then puts it back down.

The coil Bram threw already lies in a loose heap at your knee, and its free end is right there. The rest of the line runs off across the flags and over the hole to the doorway, where Bram still holds the other end wrapped round his fist. You take the free end, reach down through the gap, pass it under the black joist and bring it up the other side. When you draw it along the beam the hemp slides over hard, cold wood. Nothing gives, nothing crumbles, and the joist doesn't so much as creak. You pull gently on both strands, and it's the pull of something anchored in stone.

You tie it off with the knot you learned at the hospice, the one that takes a man's arm in a sling and comes undone with one tug on the tail. It's snug and neat, and it holds when you lean your weight back on it.

At the hole, Hale has turned his head after all. He looks at the knot across the length of the shed for a long moment.

"Two turns round," he says. "Not one. Wet rope walks."

He looks back down into the hole.

The line now runs from the joist at the back of the shed, across the flags and over the broken lip, to the doorway. It's slack, a hand above the chalk where it crosses the hole. Below, the green light lies steady on the water, and the thin sound of the seep comes in from the cut side.

(Out of game: Bram threw the coil across in his own scene and is still outside the doorway holding the other end, so the anchoring and the lever wait for his move.)

Where you are: in the shed by the opened plank gap, near the black joist, with Hale at the hole's lip · Time: Day 1 · morning

You don't argue. The knot comes open in your hand, as the hospice taught it should. You take the wet hemp round the black joist a second time and lay the two turns side by side against the old wood, then tie off again. When you sit back on the line with your full weight it doesn't creep or shift. It holds as if the joist were part of the hill.

"Two turns. Done."

Hale lies flat on his belly at the lip and turns his head to watch. He looks at the knot for about as long as he did the first time. "Aye," he says. "That's a lift." Then he looks back into the hole.

You pick the broad chisel up off the flag. When you tell him to say so if the rope walks, he lifts two fingers off the chalk without looking round. You lean over the gap and send your voice down to Pell: the line is anchored, keep your arms clear of the stone, don't try to move it alone, you're coming in by the back boards. The cold air from below takes your words and throws them back off the water. Past the joist the green light lies steady on the silt, and the seep keeps trickling in from the cut side, thin and patient. For a breath your eyelids feel heavy again. You lift your face out of the draught and it passes.

You turn toward the door to call about two ropes and the lip, and Hale answers before anyone else can.

"One rope. That one." He jerks his chin at your line without lifting his chest off the chalk. "Beam's set already. He said. Lean on the top end. No sling wanted." He works his jaw once. "Not from this lip. Lip won't take a woman kneeling, never mind working a beam. Both of you go down by the boards, or it doesn't shift."

He points at the long slack of hemp lying across the hole, its loose end trailing over the broken edge toward the yard. "And haul that in. It's lying on rot. Somebody'll put a foot on it."

The rope runs from your two turns on the joist, across the flags and over the hole, and lies loose on the far lip. The gap under the pale plank breathes up cold and sweet at your knees.

Bram has already crossed the shed and stands at the back edge of the boards beside you, so your call reached him there. What he does about it comes next.

Where you are: by the black joist in the shed, beside the hole · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram kneels at the edge of the boards, spreading his weight over two flags with a hand on a third, and looks down through the gap. He calls down to Pell, asking whether the beam is set to lever the stone off his leg. Then he tells you that Pell must pull clear before anything is lowered, that you should keep the rope steady, and that you must not haul Pell against the stone. He says he is checking what the beam rests on and where it would move before he puts any force on it.

You take the slack in hand over hand and lay the coils on the sound flag beside you, keeping your feet back from the broken lip. The first arm-lengths come in light and wet, dragging a little chalk across the floor. Then the rope stops coming. Something heavy is holding it down in the hole, though it isn't fighting you. You keep a gentle pull on it and the line lies snug along the flags, rises over the inner edge of the hole and goes straight down into the green light.

Hale is still flat on the outer lip and doesn't look round.

"That's on him now," he says. "Round his chest. He tied it." His jaw works once. "Keep it like that. Snug, not hauled."

So the coil beside you is short. Most of Bram's fifty feet runs from the joist under your knee, across the shed and down to Pell, and none of it hangs through the gap at the back.

You slip the broad chisel through your belt and talk Bram through the plan: he goes first because he's the weight, you follow, they keep to the wall where the mud is soft, then the beam and the lift. You turn your head toward the door to ask Hale to sing out if the light below goes out.

"Light's steady," Hale says. "I'll say."

You set your heels against the last sound flag with the line running through your hands. The draught from the gap brushes your face, and the heaviness behind your eyes comes and goes with it.

Hale also answers Bram from the front: the beam is set at the far corner, lean on the top end, slow. He says you're not hauling, he's watching the rope.

Where you are: on the sound flags at the back of the shed, holding the rope above the gap · Time: Day 1 · morning
