Sefa steps forward, stopping just shy of the doorway so Hale isn't crowded, though she doesn't take her eyes off him.

"Let's settle it here, then. I won't pretend we were sent with the answer—we weren't. Maela hired us off the Trade Way yesterday and gave us a case to fetch, that's all. But I'd like to know what she told you. A name, a day, a sum. If she left word with someone in Beregost, maybe it's written down."

She glances past him, openly, at the table and the papers, then back. "You've kept her case safe a week. You stayed when your lads walked. I see no reason not to help you get what you're owed—but the box needs to be on the road before long, or none of us are paid, and your lads go another week hungry either way. May I come in and look at what's on that table?"

The cold smell off the boards is plain to you now: wet stone, and under it that faint sweet note, like bread left too long in a cold oven. It doesn't swirl or thicken; it just lies there, coming up slow as a well.

You cross to the bench, and Hale doesn't move to follow. The bench is dry, as he said. The book opens flat on it, and the pages breathe out chalk and tallow. There is a stub of pencil in a tin cup.

Pell doesn't take his eyes off Hale. "Three years back," he says, as if testing the number. "And you boarded over it last spring. Was there a man down there again, or is it the wages you're afraid will find the hole?" The warden's jaw tightens, and for a second it looks like he might say something else—but then he only steps one pace back from the door, so the daylight falls full across the bench where you stand.

"Copy it," he says to you. "Then we'll talk price for the road."

The book is open in front of you. The pencil nib is blunt but it will serve. The last three weeks run in a column down the left-hand page: names, days, and a line of Hale's slow arithmetic. On the facing page, among the older tallies, one entry has been crossed through and written again beneath it: *J. Vossick — advance — 20 gp — Wynn Carrow's lot.* It isn't in Hale's hand. It's neat, small, done with a lighter touch.

You can copy the three weeks as he asked, or pause over the facing page, or ask what you want. Hale watches the yard through the open door, his ring of keys still on his belt, his arms folded across his front. The mule is gone. The smoke above the house still threads upward, barely drawn.

The table ran well. You did strong work this session, especially in the back half, when the floor gave way. screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Pell Dunmore — Human, rogue 5 (Thief), Lower City roof-runner turned hireling, level 5
HP 33/33 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 10 · DEX 17 · CON 13 · INT 13 · WIS 12 · CHA 12
Skills: Stealth +9 (expertise); Sleight of Hand +6; Acrobatics +6; Perception +4; Investigation +4; Insight +4; Tools: thieves' tools +9 (expertise)
Saves: Dexterity saving throw +6 (proficient); Intelligence saving throw +4 (proficient); Strength saving throw +0; Constitution saving throw +1; Wisdom saving throw +1; Charisma saving throw +1
Attacks: Shortsword +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing; Dagger +6 to hit, 1d4+3 piercing, thrown 20/60; Shortbow +6 to hit, 1d6+3 piercing, range 80/320; Sneak Attack: +3d6 once a turn with advantage or an ally beside the target
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Sneak Attack 3d6; Cunning Action: Dash, Disengage or Hide as a bonus action; Uncanny Dodge: a reaction halves the damage of an attack he can see; Fast Hands (Thief): a bonus action to use an object — a potion on another, a lock, a lamp; Second-Story Work: climbs at full speed; Thieves' Cant
Limits: Light armour; 33 hit points — he cannot stand at the front for long; Sneak Attack needs advantage or an ally beside the target
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 31 gp; 2 ep; 6 sp; 55 cp
Worn: Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Thieves' Tools; Main hand: Shortsword
Pack: Arrow ×20; Bedroll and Rations; Dagger ×2; Flask of Oil ×2; Hooded Lantern; Potion of Healing ×3; Shortbow; Silk Rope (50 feet)

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

You hang back a step, off to Bram's side, hands loose and well clear of your shortsword. Under your breath you tell Bram and Sefa that you dislike a quarry with no picks swinging at mid-morning, and that the warden is either waiting for them or for someone else. Then you lift a hand in greeting and call out that Maela Thorn of Beregost sent you for her case, and ask where the crew has gone. Bram walks on into the yard and stops a few paces short of the man in the doorway, leaving the way clear. He gives his name, says they are here for a sealed case of dye-salts, and asks whether the man is the warden and whether everyone is all right. Sefa, near the yard's edge, murmured to you both that there is not a single voice working and that you should keep your eyes open. She called out a greeting and asked for the warden.

Your eyes go over the yard as they would over a house you meant to get into. The terraces above are bare white steps with nowhere to lie flat, and no bowman would last a minute up there in the glare. The tracks are easy to read in the fine chalk, which takes a print like flour on a board. A dozen men or more went out together down the cart track toward the Way, at a walking pace, with no scuffing, no drag marks and nothing dark soaked into the white. One set of mule tracks goes with them, a man's boots beside it. Near the lower cut, not every tool has simply been dropped. Three hammers stand on their heads on a squared block, side by side, the way you'd leave a thing you meant someone to find.

The man in the doorway has a grey beard with chalk in it and forearms as thick as cart-shafts. He lets the three of you come. When Bram stops short and leaves the doorway clear, something in his shoulders lets go a quarter-inch.

"Hale," he says. "Osric Hale. Warden." He looks at Bram, then at your raised hand, then at Sefa. "Thorn's lot. Thought so."

You watch him while he talks. He never glances at the terraces and his hand does not drift to the keys. He isn't afraid of anything outside. What is on his face is older and more tired than fear, and it's sour. Past his shoulder you see a low room with a hearth, a kettle, a table stacked with papers and a slate. On a shelf above the fire sits a squat box bound with iron straps, a blob of red wax on its lid. Hale doesn't look round at it once, and he doesn't need to.

"Crew walked," he says to you. "Yesterday. Noon bell." His jaw works as if he were chewing something. "Three weeks. Not a copper come down from the Gate."

To Bram's question he gives a short breath through his nose. "All right. Nobody's hurt, if that's what you're asking. Nobody's paid either."

Then he turns to Sefa, since she asked for the warden by name.

"Your case is in there. It's ready. Been ready a week." He unfolds his arms and hooks a thumb in the key ring, not taking it off. "Thorn paid for it. She'll have paid somebody. It wasn't me, and it wasn't my lads. Before that box leaves this house I want to know who she paid, and how much." He stops, then adds, "That's all."

The smoke from the chimney keeps rising, thin and straight. The yard is so quiet you can hear the kettle ticking as it cools.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The Whitestone Case
+ Quest: The Whitestone Case

Where you are: quarry yard, a pace behind Bram, before the warden's house · Time: Day 1 · morning

You stepped up level with Bram and spoke to Hale. You said you were hired legs, paid on delivery or not at all, and asked about the hammers, the owner, who sent the pay and who carried it. You offered to carry his note to Thorn. Before that, Bram had said he had stood waiting for wages himself and told Hale that Thorn had hired the three of you to fetch the case and had nothing to do with her accounts. He said she hadn't named who she paid or how much, only promised ninety gold between you on delivery before sunset. He asked whether Hale had an order or a receipt. Sefa then said you hadn't been sent with an answer, that Maela had hired you off the Trade Way yesterday, and asked what Thorn had told him. She asked to come in and look at the table.

Hale heard Bram out without moving. At the mention of waiting for wages his eyes went to the old company mark painted over on his shield, then came back up.

"Receipt," he says. "No. Order. That I've got."

He looks at Sefa a long moment, then steps aside, just far enough. The room smells of cold ash and wet slate. On the table are a slate covered in chalk tallies, two sheets of cheap paper written in a heavy hand, and a folded letter with a broken wax seal, a black tower on grey. He pushes the letter across the boards to her with one finger.

It is a short letter in a clerk's neat hand:

*To the warden at Whitestone. Release to M. Thorn, apothecary, of Beregost, one case of salt of the low seam, twelve pounds, sealed. Paid in full at the Gate. Release on her messenger's word. For House Vandarren, by the hand of Jeren Vossick, factor.*

It gives no sum. Under it, the two cheap sheets are letters Hale wrote to Vossick, dated nine days apart. The second is shorter, and its last line is pressed so hard the pen tore the paper: *The men will not wait past the feast of the month.*

"Paid in full," Hale says to Bram, who has come in behind Sefa. "At the Gate. So Vossick's had her money. A week, at least. Ten days." He doesn't look at the shelf. "Wages come down with the same man who carries Vossick's letters. Every month. Not this month."

He turns to your questions one at a time. "Owner's House Vandarren. Patriars. Never seen one up here. Vossick sends the pay." He jerks his head at the yard. "Hammers. That's a strike. The tools are the House's. Lads left them where the House can find them, set out proper. Nobody's hurt. Nobody stole."

You watch him the whole time, and there's nothing hidden in it. The man wants money for his men, not one man's head. The anger is for Vossick, the dull, familiar anger of a man who has written the same letter twice. Only one moment doesn't fit. When you nodded at the lower cut, he answered about the hammers without once looking that way. He looked at the table, the floor, your face, but not at the cut.

He takes the chalk and writes on the slate under the tallies, slowly: *14 men. 3 wks. 56 gp. Carter 8.*

"Sixty-four gold," he says. "That's what's owed."

He puts the chalk down and thinks about your offer. He isn't a man who does that quickly.

"Your note. All right. Names and days, so Thorn sees it's not a number I made up. Names and days are in the tally-book." He pauses. "Book's in the cutting-shed. Down by the low cut. I don't keep it here."

Then he looks at each of you in turn and stops at Bram.

"Box goes with the note. One of you puts a name to it. Somebody brings me back what Thorn says. Who took it, how much." He pauses. "Not a promise from her. From you."

The shin is bruised and swollen tight under the wet hose, but when you put your weight on it, the bone holds. You stand on two feet in water up to your chest, with the rope snug under your arms, a yard clear of the stone.

"Out. Good." Then, to Bram's face a yard off: "Up first, you behind me, no lingering." Your eyes go once to the pale plaster behind the block and stay off it. "Don't touch anything else down here. We'll want it later, and so will Hale."

The beam is still taking Bram's weight, and the block hangs on it, tilted. Over your head, in the square of white sky, Hale lets out a long breath through his teeth. He doesn't pull his arm back out of the hole.

Your records, changed:
Conditions: Chest-deep in cold water, Bruised, swollen left shin (bone sound)

Where you are: in the flooded working, chest-deep, free of the block · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram answers across the water: steady, the stone is up, and he won't lower it until you say. He stays braced on the slimed black beam with his arms locked, watching your face through the drifting silt. The block hangs a fist's height off its bed and doesn't move by a finger's width.

You breathe out through your teeth, one hand flat on the wet wall, the swollen leg held just off the bottom. The ache has settled into a hot, steady throb from knee to ankle. You call up to the man on the beam: ease it down, slow and straight, let it settle where it was, and don't drop it. Bram's answer crossed yours on the way.

So you wait, as you said you would, and use the time for the rope. You call up that you are slipping it. Hale, still flat across the outer lip, hooks two fingers under the hemp where it crosses the edge and lifts it clear of the rotten chalk. A little slack slides down to the water. The bowline fights you with its wet swelling and your fingers have mostly stopped answering, then it gives. You let the loop fall and the end lies in a slow coil on the water beside you, still tied off above.

You look round once for your pack and find you never lost it. The straps are still over your shoulders under the satchel, soaked through and heavy as a stone, and it's yours.

Bram's request reaches the lip: help you up as soon as you're clear. Hale looks down at the two of you for a long moment and takes a short breath through his nose.

"Not through here," he says.

He draws his arm out of the hole for the first time since you went in, gets his knees under him, then his feet, testing the outer chalk before he stands. He steps over the corner of the hole onto the flag that holds, and it grates under him the way it did under Bram. He puts his shoulder to the wall and goes along it toward the back, heel first on each flag, eyes on the boards ahead and not on the brazier. At the edge of the boards he goes down on one knee beside the lifted planks and the gap Bram opened, spreads one big hand on the flag and reaches the other down past the black joist toward the water.

"Here," he says, down into the working. "I'll take him here."

In the green light the silt is starting to settle. The block hangs where Bram holds it, its carved face tilted toward the hole above, the sunburst and its ring of notches just under the surface. Behind it the plaster patch stays dry and pale. The seep keeps trickling in from the cut side. The cold has you to the belly, and the heaviness behind your eyes still hasn't moved.

Where you are: in the flooded working under the shed, by the wall near the raised block · Time: Day 1 · morning

You told Hale you were coming to him, then told Bram to ease the block down slow and straight. You watched it go back onto its bed and waited until the silt stopped rolling. Bram lowered the beam a little at a time, keeping it straight. The block came down off its fist of air, its far corner found the edge of the fallen flag with a soft grinding of stone, and it sank back into its bed. One more cloud of silt rolled up brown through the green light. Bram held the beam until it carried nothing, then let go. The black wood stayed where it was, slanting up toward the square of sky. The carved face is where it was before, tilted toward the hole and just under the surface. The plaster behind it is still dry.

Bram said to leave anything heavy if need be and get out of this air. He came round onto your bad side with his shoulder ready. You went first along the right-hand wall with a hand on the wet stone and the good leg leading, counting aloud, and he kept a half-step behind you, mail chinking, close enough to catch a sleeve. The silt sucked at your boots. Pink crust crunched wherever a palm touched the wall, and you kept your hand off it where you could. Nobody stopped counting.

The bars of daylight between the planks got wider overhead. Then the gap was above you, a man's width of white, with the black joist across it, Bram's hemp in two turns round it, and Hale's big hand reaching down.

You took the wrist and Hale's hand shut on yours like a vice. Below you Bram planted himself in the silt, got a shoulder under your good thigh and lifted. With the warden pulling and the fighter pushing, you barely had to do the work yourself. You still did it the way you'd go up a drainpipe, arms doing it all, quick and light, the swollen shin kept off the edge of the boards. You rolled clear onto the sound flags by the wall and lay on your back.

You drag the wet collar down off your face. The shed air smells of tallow and cold ash, and after the working it tastes like a mountain. You take one slow breath, then a second and a third. The thickness behind your eyes doesn't go all at once. It thins like fog going off a field, and by the third breath the roof beams over you have stopped looking far away.

"Thanks." Then, quietly, still flat on the floor: "That's twice today you've been where I needed a hand."

Hale is still on one knee by the gap and doesn't look round.

"Once," he says. "First time I missed."

You call toward the door for Sefa: prop it wide, get Bram's arm, look at your eyes. Your voice goes out over the hole and into the glare. Nobody answers from the yard. A jackdaw calls somewhere up on the terraces, and that's all.

Hale lets it hang for a moment.

"She's gone," he says. "Took her pack. Walked out while Halloway was going down." He looks at the door, then back at the gap. "Didn't say."

Then he turns his head and looks at you properly for the first time since the floor went. He takes your jaw in his chalky fingers and tips your face toward the daylight from the door, the way you'd turn a stone to look at its grain, and stares into one eye and then the other.

"Seen men come up off that face," he says, and lets go. "You're slow. Not gone. Clean air does it. An hour." He leans back over the gap, and the same hand goes down past the joist toward the water again. "Halloway."

Below, Bram stands waist-deep under the gap, his breath smoking a little in the cold. Above him the rope is tied off and taut, the joist is sound, and the warden's hand is waiting a yard over his head.

Your records, changed:
Conditions: Bruised, swollen left shin (bone sound), Drowsy from the working's air (clears in an hour), Soaked through

Where you are: on the sound floor of the shed by the back gap, with Hale · Time: Day 1 · morning

You have a knee on the sound flag beside Hale and an arm already going down past the joist when the climb ends without you. Bram was over the joist before you reached it; his climb was played in his own scene. The warden leans back and the iron comes up over the edge in a long scrape of rings on stone. Your hand closes on nothing but the cold air coming out of the gap. You take it back and sit on your heels, breathing.

Your eyes go to the bench. The tally-book is where Sefa left it, open and flat, its damp pages fanned in the light from the broken doorway. The pencil lies on the flags below the bench where it rolled. There's no loose sheet anywhere on the boards and no copy half-done. Whatever she wrote went out the door in her pack.

"Where she left it," Hale says, following your look. "Not touched."

You ask about the house. Hale looks at you a moment before answering.

"Open. Halloway came down for you. I didn't lock it." He wipes his palms down his apron, though they're as clean as chalk and water will let them be. "Box was on the shelf when I came down. That's what I know."

You get up the way a man gets up off a roof he's not sure of, good leg first and then the bad one. The shin throbs hot under the wet hose, tight as a drumskin, but when you put your weight on it, it holds. You cross to the bench along the wall, heel first. You close the book on its swollen pages, tie the twine and tuck the oilcloth bundle under your arm against your ribs, on the side away from the wet.

Hale watches you take it and doesn't object.

"Bring it. Names are in it."

You say your piece about Sefa, and then about the box, the fire, the note and sunset. Hale hears it without a word of his own. When you get to "the three of us", his eyes go once to the open doorway she walked out of. That's all the answer he gives it.

You go to the door along the wall, the way Hale came in. You pass the brazier and its rose-coloured crust without looking into the bowl. You take the long step over the corner of the hole onto the left flag, which grates under you and holds, and step out into the glare.

After the working the sun is like a slap. You stop on the dry chalk by Bram's shield and look.

Up the slope, the house door stands open, a dark square under the slate roof with the thin grey thread still rising from the chimney. Then you look down the cart track toward the Way. The first long bend is empty. On the second, a good half-mile off and small as a thumbnail, a single figure is walking west with a pack on its back and a pale smudge of dust at its heels. It walks at a steady pace, not hurrying, and doesn't look back. As you watch, it goes round the shoulder of the hill and the track is empty again.

Hale comes out behind you by the same step. He stands on the white beside you and looks where you are looking, at the empty bend, for about as long as it takes to say a name. He doesn't say one.

"House," he says, and goes up the slope ahead of you.

It's a hundred feet of hard chalk, and the shin complains about every one of them. The jackdaw is back on the lifting frame. Hale reaches the door first and stops on the step to let you see past him without being told to.

The room is as you left it: cold ash and wet slate, the kettle on the hearth, the letters and the order on the table, the slate with its sixty-four and two names under it. On the shelf above the fire the squat iron-strapped box sits with its red wax toward the room. The seal is whole, and there's no new scrape in the dust of the shelf around it.

Hale looks at it for a moment, then goes past it to the hearth. He kneels and starts breaking kindling over the laid fire with his big hands.

"Sit," he says, without turning round. "Near it. Boots off."

Nothing else is waiting on you up here for the moment. The fire, the note and the warden's talk come when you want them.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Whitestone Tally-Book

Where you are: In Hale's house on the slope above the working, by the hearth · Time: Day 1 · morning

You sit on the stool nearest the hearth, and Hale gets the fire going properly. Your boots are by the fire on their heels, the hose is drying stiff on the stool, and the bruise on your bare shin runs purple from knee to ankle. The skin is tight and shiny, but there is no break in it.

From where you sit you check the box on the shelf without getting up. The iron straps lie in their old pale marks, undisturbed. The red wax is whole, but the stamp in it is not the black tower. It is a plain ring with a W inside, pressed a little off-centre by a heavy thumb. You say it's whole and that's good. Hale sees where you're looking. He says the mark is the quarry's, his own, and that the House never sent a seal up here.

You say your piece to the flames: you're out, so now you talk. You tell him about the wall that sleeps a man standing, the rake that is a rule and not a habit, and "drink" in the Fist's book. You tell him about the sun, the count-marks, the plaster the salt won't grow on, and the boards he would never have walked on if he'd thought it was only water. Hale doesn't stop you. When you reach the boards, his jaw works once, slowly.

He pulls a sheet off the pile, uncorks the ink and sits across from you with the pen. Before he writes, he says Tobin didn't drink, not a drop. Tobin was a chapel man, his mother's boy. Hale found him on his face with his hands open and no mark on him, and water up to his ribs. The lamp was still on the ledge, gone out. The House never asked, and the Fist wanted a word, so Hale gave them the one that closes a book. "You're not wrong," he says. "That's all I'll say on it."

He writes slowly and hard, taking the names off the tally-book with your help and copying each with its days. Without looking up, he says the rake was Abel Garrow's. Abel was warden before him for twenty years and had the rake from the one before. The boards came with the same words: don't lift the lid. Abel said it the day he gave Hale the keys and again the day he died. He never said why, and Hale never asked.

You ask whether dried salt in a case will put anyone to sleep. He shakes his head before you've finished. Cold, dry and shut, it does nothing, and he has carried it on his back to the Way. Heated, it smokes, and the smoke does what the wall does, only worse and quicker. That is why the door is open and a man stands outside.

You ask about the buyer. Hale says Thorn's buyer is Thorn's business and he has never heard a name. Then he stops and looks at the wall as if counting. It used to be one case every two or three years, to a dyer in the Gate, small. Thorn started last spring, and since then it's every two months at twelve pounds a time. The House likes her and pays at the Gate. He says it flatly, like a figure on the slate.

You mention Sefa and the names she carried off. He shakes his head without lifting the pen. "Names don't pay anybody."

It takes him a long while. Your fingers warm, steam rises off your breeches, and the hose dries stiff. When he sets the pen down, the sheet is covered edge to edge in his heavy upright hand. It is addressed to M. Thorn, apothecary, Beregost, from O. Hale, warden at Whitestone. It says the crew has gone unpaid three weeks: fourteen men for eighteen days, and the carter Hobb Marl for twenty-one days with the mule. That comes to 56 gp and 8 gp, 64 gp owed, with all fifteen names and their days beneath. It says House Vandarren's order claims the case was paid in full at the Gate to J. Vossick, factor, and that Hale wrote him twice, nine days apart, with no answer. It asks who took her money and how much, and to send word by Dunmore or Halloway.

He reads it through once with his lips moving, sands it with chalk dust off his sleeve, blows it clean and folds it in three. He lays it on the closed tally-book between you. "Note's done." He glances at the shelf, then at your bare shin. The box goes with you when you go, but not before your eyes clear. It's half a day to Beregost, and if you leave by noon you have the time.

The fire has taken hold, and the heat reaches the bruise. The thickness behind your eyes is thinner than it was on the shed floor, though not gone. Nothing more is asked of you, and the hour by the fire is yours to take whenever you want it.

Your records, changed:
Carried: − Whitestone Tally-Book

Where you are: By the hearth in the warden's hut at Whitestone, with Hale · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.

How was the table?
Was there something you wanted to do and didn't?
Who did you take the other two players to be?

messages.text:
Pell slows a step behind the others and lets his eyes do the walking: the scattered tools, the empty traces on the cart, the sheds, the upper terraces, any spot where a man with a bow could lie flat. He's checking for tracks in the dust too. Did the workers leave in a crowd, in a hurry, or were they dragged?

Quietly, out of the side of his mouth, to Bram and Sefa:
"Quarry this size, middle of the morning, and nobody's swinging a pick. I don't like it. Our warden's got keys and folded arms. Either he's waiting for us, or he's waiting for someone and we're not it."

He keeps his hands loose and well away from his shortsword and lifts one in an easy greeting toward the man in the doorway. He stays a pace back and off to Bram's side, where he can see past the man into the house.

He calls out, friendly enough:
"Morning! We're sent by Maela Thorn from Beregost, come for her case. Quiet day for it, eh? Where's your crew got to?"

While the man answers, Pell watches his face and hands. Is he nervous, lying, glancing back into the house or up at the terraces?

Pell lets his hand drop and steps up level with Bram. He keeps his voice easy, one working man to another.

"Fair question. Honest answer is we don't know. We're hired legs, Master Hale. Thorn pays us on delivery, by sunset, or not at all. Nobody showed us her ledger." He nods past him at the iron-strapped box on the shelf, then looks back at Hale's face. "But I know the shape of this. Somebody up in the Gate is getting paid for your stone and your salts, and the coin's stopping in his purse instead of rolling down the hill. Three weeks is long enough that it's not a late courier."

He jerks his chin toward the lower cut, at the three hammers standing on their heads on the block.

"Your lads left those for somebody to read. A strike mark? Or a message for whoever comes up from the Gate?"

Then he gets practical:

"Who's the owner? Who's supposed to send your pay, and who carries it? Give us names. Write it on that slate if you like, with what you're owed. Thorn's a merchant. She'll know who she settled with, and she'll want to know her money went astray, because a quarry with no crew sells her no salts next season. We put your note in her hand alongside the case, today. That's a better road to your coin than keeping the box on a shelf. Keep it there and nobody's paid, you included."

He keeps his eyes on Hale while he says it. Is the man after his wages, or after someone in particular?

Pell reads the letter over Sefa's shoulder. He memorises the seal, the black tower on grey, and the names Vandarren and Vossick, the way he used to memorise doors. Then he taps the slate.

"Pell Dunmore. Put that by the box. If Thorn says who and how much, I'll carry it back up this hill myself. That's mine to give, not hers." He glances at Bram and Sefa and leaves them room to add their own names or not.

He nods out the door, down the slope.

"I'll walk down with you for the book. Save your knees the climb back."

He doesn't move yet. He says it quieter, without any edge:

"Master Hale, you'll talk about those hammers all day, but you won't look at that cut. Low seam's where the salts come from, isn't it? Grey, wet stone." He holds Hale's eye. "If there's something down there besides a ledger, I'd rather hear it from you up here than find it with my feet. We've a sunset to make, and nobody needs surprises."

If Hale still means to go down, Pell goes with him, a half-step to the side. He watches the plank door of the shed, the ground in front of it for fresh prints or water, and the dark edge of the cutting beyond. His hand stays near his shortsword without touching it.

Pell stays on the threshold beside Hale, not inside. He breathes shallow through his nose and doesn't like the sweet smell one bit.

While Sefa reads, his eyes go over the room the way they'd go over a strongroom. He looks at the brazier: is the ash fresh or old, and are there pink crusts or crystals in it? He checks the floor around it for scrape marks or a ring where it's been moved. At the back he looks at the planks. Are they nailed or just laid down, and is there a gap at the edges with cold air coming up? Do any boots, a rope, or a ladder-end show near them? He keeps his own feet on the white.

Low, to Hale, without looking at him:

"Somebody's been burning your salt in that brazier. Pink ash doesn't come from charcoal." A beat. "And that's no floor at the back. That's a lid."

He lets it sit a moment, then turns his head and looks the warden in the face. His voice stays even, not accusing.

"You won't step in here, Master Hale, and you won't look at the back. Men get slow in the bad air, you said. Did one of them get slow in here? Sweet-smelling smoke and a hole under the boards. Is that why your lads really walked?"

Out of the corner of his mouth, to Sefa:
"Read quick, and don't linger by that brazier. If your head starts swimming, out you come."

If the GM wants it, Pell is looking hard at the brazier and the planks: [Roll the die] for Investigation.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

Pell taps the flag under his heel once more, lightly, and listens to the dull note. He doesn't go further in. He steps back onto solid chalk beside Hale.

"Hollow under the doorstep too," he says, mild, as if remarking on the weather. "Old workings run everywhere under here, then." He lets that go.

He's quiet a moment, watching Hale's hand on the apron.

"Tobin Reed," he says. He just repeats it, the way you'd set a stone on a cairn. "Drink, you wrote. Somebody wrote it." He shrugs, gentle. "I've written a few things down myself because they were easier to carry than the truth. Not my business, Master Hale. But if what you wrote and what you think aren't the same, and it's tied to that seam and Thorn's salt, you'd want us to know before we hand her the case and walk off. You've got two names on your slate now. That's two people who'll come back up this hill."

He gives Hale room to answer or not. If he says nothing more, Pell doesn't push.

Then, plainly, over his shoulder:

"Sefa, copy it quick as you can manage clean. Sun's climbing, and it's half a day back." To Bram: "Once she's done, we take the box, we take Hale's note, and we're on the track."

To Hale:

"Write your note while she copies. Sixty-four owed, the House's order, Vossick's name, your two letters to him, dates. Short, so Thorn reads it all the way through. I'll put it in her hand myself."

While they work he stays at the door. Every so often he looks down the slope at the wet grey cut and the dark corner of the boards, and he keeps his feet on the white.

Pell doesn't thrash. He gets one breath into him, then another, and keeps his hands flat on the block, not pulling.

He shouts up, steady and loud enough to carry:

"I'm whole! Leg's pinned, not broken. Stone on my shin. Water's coming in from the cut side, slow, but it's coming. Don't anybody else step near that edge. The ground's crust!"

A beat, then the practical part:

"Rope's in my pack, but my pack's down here with me. Bram, Sefa, Hale, whoever's got one, drop it down. Tie it off to something that isn't sitting on this floor. The shed's doorframe, or the cart. And come down by the shed side, through the boards. That end's got joists under it. Not through this hole."

While he waits, he works with what's in reach. He gets a hand on the floating joist and walks it along the wall toward himself. He tries to set one end down in the silt beside the block, low on the side away from his leg, so it can go under the stone's edge as a lever once somebody with weight is on the other end. He doesn't heave on it himself. He just gets it placed.

He shrugs the healer's satchel up high on his shoulder, out of the water, and checks the potion stoppers by feel.

Then, since he has the time and the light, he looks at the stone pinning him. The sunburst, the ring of tally-marks. He calls up, quieter, to Hale:

"Master Hale. There's a carved stone down here. A sun, rays and a face, with marks round it like a mason's count. Squared. Somebody built this, not just dug it." He breathes out through his teeth against the cold. "You knew there was more under here than water, didn't you."

He watches the waterline on his chest and counts slowly, getting a measure of how fast it's rising.

Pell keeps his breathing slow and shallow and pulls the collar of his shirt up over his nose and mouth. It's wet cloth, which is better than nothing against that sweet stink.

He calls up, steady, keeping it short so he doesn't waste breath:

"Lever's in. Beam's set under the far corner, end's sticking up toward you. Whoever comes down only has to lean on it. Don't heave, just weight. I'll pull my leg when it lifts."

Then, firmer:

"And listen. The air down here's bad. That sweet smell's thick, and it's going behind my eyes. Whoever comes, come quick, do it, and go back up. Don't stand around admiring the stonework. Sefa, you stay up top unless Bram needs hands. If I go quiet, somebody shout at me."

He flexes his fingers and toes to keep the blood moving against the cold, and keeps talking to himself under his breath, counting, so his head stays clear.

While he waits he doesn't touch the plaster. He looks at it once more: the dragging finger-lines, the size of the patch, whether it's cracked or seeping. He fixes it in memory with the sun and the notches. Somebody sealed something up down here by hand, and that's a door for another hour, not this one.

Quietly, up to Hale, no edge in it:

"Four foot of water, and a man doesn't drown in it unless he's already asleep. Smell's the same now as then, I'd wager." He lets that hang. "We'll talk when I'm out."

Pell keeps counting under his breath. When he hits a hundred he starts again. He keeps an eye on the new bar of light at the back of the working and on whatever's coming through it.

When he hears mail moving above the shed end, he calls toward it, short and clear:

"Bram! Drop in by the boards and come along the wall on your right. The floor's solid there, I walked the beam that way. Water's chest-deep on me, so it'll be about waist on you. Mind the silt, there's fallen flag under it." A breath. "Beam's the black one sticking up at a slant by my left side. Lean on the top end. Slow. Count three out loud before you put your weight on it, so I'm ready."

He gets both hands on the block's near edge, braced flat, ready to shove the stone away from himself as it lifts, rather than pull his leg against it. When the stone comes up he means to slide the shin out sideways, along the bottom and away from the corner, not straight up where the block could drop back on it.

If Bram's there and the leg's out:

"Out. Good. Up first, you behind me, no lingering." He stops long enough to slap the plaster patch with his eyes one last time, not his hand. "Don't touch anything else down here. We'll want it later, and so will Hale."

If he starts feeling the heaviness behind his eyes get worse, he bites the inside of his cheek hard and keeps talking. Somebody needs to hear him.

Pell stops counting long enough to shout up, sharp and clear, so the men at the top have one plan between them:

"Hale's right. Two turns on that joist, not one! Bram, put the second turn on before anybody trusts it."

A breath through the wet collar, then the rest in short pieces:

"Throw me the slack end, the one over the hole. Drop it straight down to my hands."

When it comes he doesn't tie it to the stone. He takes a quick bowline round his own chest, under the arms, high and snug, and pulls it hard to check it holds. Then he calls up:

"Rope's on me, not the block. If I go quiet, you haul me straight up whether the leg's free or not. Better a skinned shin than a Tobin Reed."

Then, toward the back gap and the mail:

"Bram, come down the back way now, on the rope, quick. Three steps along the right wall, lean on the black beam, count three out loud, I slide out, you go straight back up. Half a minute in this air, no more. Sefa, Hale, keep the line over the hole taut on me while he does it."

He sets his palms flat on the block's edge again, free foot braced sideways along the bottom, and starts the count over from one. He says each number out loud now, plainly, so those above can hear that he's still there.

Pell keeps the count going between sentences, so the numbers never stop for long.

"Fourteen. Heard you, Hale. Fifteen." He turns his head toward the bar of light at the back. "Then nobody hauls me through the hole. If it comes to that, drag me toward the back gap, along the water, under the good joist. Sixteen. Bram! Talk to me, man. You coming down, or is something stopping you?"

He waits a beat, listening hard to the low voices behind the boards, trying to catch even one word.

"Seventeen. If the gap's too narrow for a man in mail, take the mail off, or send the beam-weight some other way. Shove a pole down through the boards onto the end of my lever. Anything heavy on it will do. Eighteen."

He shifts his hands a finger's width on the block to keep them from going dead, and checks that the bowline hasn't slipped.

Quieter, to Hale, still counting:

"Nineteen. You're doing fine up there. Keep the arm where it is. Twenty."

Pell keeps counting, but he tightens it up and gives one plan.

"Twenty-one. Right. Then the weight goes on from your side, Hale." He tips his head at the beam, which slants up toward the lip. "How far's the top end from your hand? If you can reach it, put your forearm on it and lean. Don't heave. Your chest stays on the chalk. Twenty-two."

Louder, toward the back gap:

"Bram! Forget the boards. Come round to the hole, to Hale's side. Stand on the *outer* edge, where he's lying. That's the ground that's held two men all morning. Reach down and lean on the beam's top end with him. Two of you, slow, count three. Sefa keeps the rope snug on me. Twenty-three."

He sets his palms on the block again and gets his free foot braced sideways along the bottom.

"If nobody can reach it, drop something heavy onto it. A sledge from the bench, a wedge-box, the cart's chock. Tie it on a line and lower it onto the top end. Twenty-four. Whatever you pick, call it before you do it. I want your three."

He breathes through the wet collar, keeps his eyes on the beam end where it rises out of the water, and waits for someone up top to start counting.

"Twenty-five."

Pell gets his breath through his teeth while the ache settles in his shin. He keeps one hand on the wall and doesn't shift his weight onto the bad leg more than he must.

"Ease it down, Bram. Slow, straight down like he said. Let it settle where it was. Don't drop it." He waits until the block is back on its bed and the silt starts to clear, so nobody's leaving a loaded lever behind them.

Then he calls up to the lip:

"Hale, I'm not coming up through your hole. You were right about that edge. Let the line go slack, I'm slipping it." He works the bowline loose with numb fingers and lets the end drop on the water. "I'm going out the back way, on the good joist, same as Bram came."

He looks round once in the green light for his pack. If it's floating or lying within arm's reach he hooks it up by a strap and slings it over the satchel. If it isn't, he leaves it. He isn't going groping in the silt in this air.

To Bram, low and plain:

"You lead. I'll be right on your heels with a hand on your belt. If I stop talking, keep walking and pull." He fixes the place in his memory once more: the sun, the ring of notches, the dry plaster. Then he turns his back on it.

He wades after Bram along the right-hand wall, testing each step on the silt. He keeps the swollen leg behind and the good one leading, and he counts out loud again, from one. At the back gap he takes the rope over the joist, lets Bram go up first, and follows. His arms do most of the work, and he hauls himself up quick and light the way he would a drainpipe.

As soon as he's out on the boards in the daylight he rolls onto the solid planks, away from the gap. He pulls the wet collar off his face and takes three long breaths of clean air.

"Sefa," he says, still flat on his back, "tell me if my eyes look right. And somebody get that door open wide."

Pell nods up at Hale's hand by the back gap. "Coming to you, Master Hale."

Then, to Bram, plain and steady:

"Right, I'm clear. Ease it down now, Bram, slow and straight. Let it settle." He watches the block go back onto its bed and waits until the silt stops rolling. "Good. Leave the beam where it lies. Now out, you and me. No more standing in this air."

He goes first along the right-hand wall since Hale's waiting there, keeping a hand on the wet stone and the good leg leading. He stays clear of the pink crust where he can and counts out loud from one so Bram knows where he is.

"One. Two. Bram, you're right behind me. If I stop counting, push me along. Three."

At the back gap he reaches up and takes Hale's wrist, not his fingers. With his other hand on the joist he lets the warden take some weight while he hauls himself up. He goes up quick and light with his arms doing the work and keeps the swollen shin off the edge. Once he's up he rolls clear of the gap onto the sound flags by the wall and lies there a moment on his back. He drags the wet collar off his face and breathes the cold, clean air three times, slow.

"Thanks." To Hale, quietly, still flat on the floor: "That's twice today you've been where I needed a hand."

Then, louder, toward the door:

"Sefa, prop that door wide and get Bram's arm when he comes up. And when you've a moment, look at my eyes and tell me if they're right. My head's been thick since I went in."

He keeps watching the gap until Bram's head and shoulders come through it.

Pell lies still a breath longer while that sinks in. Then he rolls onto his good side and gets an elbow under him.

"Gone," he says, flat. "Right."

He doesn't waste words on it yet. He shifts over beside Hale at the gap, sets his knee on the sound flag and reaches down with him. He takes Bram's other wrist so the fighter has two hands to come up on.

"Up you come, Bram. Hale's got one side, I've got the other. On three. One, two, *three*."

Once Bram is out and clear of the gap, Pell sits back on his heels, breathing. His eyes go straight to the bench. Is the tally-book still there, and Sefa's copy, if she ever made it? He looks without touching, then up at Hale.

"The book's where she left it?" A nod at the bench. Then, quieter, the question that matters: "Master Hale. The box. You said it stays on its shelf till you're back. Is your house locked?"

He gets to his feet slowly, testing the swollen shin. It holds, so he picks up the oilcloth book (or what's left on the bench) and tucks it under his arm, out of the wet.

"I'm not saying she's done anything but walk off. People do. Maybe the hole scared her, maybe she had her own reasons." He looks at Bram, level. "But we go up to the house now, the three of us, and see that box with our own eyes before anybody thinks about anything else. Then I'll dry off by Hale's fire for the hour he says I need, he writes his note, and we decide whether we can still make sunset."

He starts for the door, keeping close to the wall, heel first on each flag the way Hale walked. He stays well clear of the hole. At the threshold he stops and looks down the cart track toward the Way, and up the slope toward the house. Is there any sign of Sefa, dust on the track, a figure on the road?

"Lead on, Master Hale. It's your house."

Pell lowers himself onto the stool nearest the hearth, good leg first, and sets the oilcloth bundle on the table beside the slate. He works his boots off. They come away with a wet suck, and he tips a cupful of grey water out of each onto the flags, then stands them on their heels toward the fire. He peels the hose down off the swollen shin to see it in the light, bruised purple from knee to ankle and tight, and leaves it bare to the warmth.

Before he settles he looks up at the shelf. He doesn't touch the box. He just looks at the red wax from where he sits: whether the impression in it is the black tower, the same as on Vossick's letter, and whether the iron straps sit clean in their old marks.

"Whole," he says, mostly to himself. "Good."

He holds his hands out to the new fire while Hale gets it going and lets the heat climb into his fingers. Then, quietly, without looking away from the flames:

"I said we'd talk when I was out. I'm out."

He gives Hale a moment.

"I'll tell you what I saw, and you tell me where I'm wrong. Your salt grows on a wall where the air puts a man to sleep standing. You dry it here, door open, man outside, long rake. That's not habit, that's a rule somebody learned the hard way. Tobin Reed went to sleep in four foot of water, and the Fist got 'drink' for their book because 'the seam did it' would've shut the House's best earner." He turns his head and looks at Hale, level, no edge in it. "And under your shed there's a carved sun, a ring of count-marks, and a patch of plaster the salt won't grow on. Somebody sealed something up down there on purpose. Before your time, you said. I believe you. But you knew it was more than water, or you'd have walked on those boards."

He leans back a little, rubbing warmth into his calf above the bruise.

"I'm not the Fist, and I'm not the House. I just want to know what I'm carrying down the hill in that box, and whether anyone who breathes it dried is going to sleep the way Tobin did." A beat. "Thorn's buyer has a coach for the Gate tonight. I'd like to know who's on the other end of that."

Then, practical again, he nods at the table:

"Write while you talk, if you can do both. Sixty-four owed, the order, Vossick, your two letters and the days. The book's there for the names." He taps the oilcloth. "I'll want the hour by the fire anyway. Bram'll want it too, by the look of him."

He glances at Bram, then, drier: "And Sefa took her copy of your three weeks with her, and nothing else, it seems. So whoever she's walking to, she's carrying your lads' names. Worth remembering."

Thanks, that was a good session. Some honest notes from my side of the table:

**What worked**
- **The world felt lived-in.** Hale is a great NPC: terse, proud, carrying Tobin Reed like a stone in his pocket. The way he only half-answered, and the tells (the apron wipe, never looking at the cut), made Insight feel rewarding without a roll for everything.
- **Clues paid off fairly.** The pink ash, the clean band in the brazier, the hollow flag, the plank with fresh saw-marks. I read the room and the room told me true things. And the pit fall wasn't a cheap shot, because the hollow note was right there.
- **The hooks are good:** the sunburst with its count-marks, the dry plaster the salt won't grow on, Abel Garrow's "don't lift the lid," Thorn's orders jumping from one case every few years to one every two months, the W seal versus the black tower. I want to come back to all of it.
- **The rescue was tense without being cruel.** The slow seep, the drowsiness and the miscounting were nice touches.

**What dragged a little**
- **The rescue ran long.** It took four or five rounds of me re-issuing the same lever plan while Bram was offscreen and nothing advanced. Once a sensible plan is on the table, I'd be happy for it to resolve faster.
- **The recaps of my own lines.** Each reply opened by retelling at length what I'd just said. A line or two is enough; I'd rather spend the words on what happened next.
- **Bram's climb happened in his scene, so my action just evaporated.** That's understandable with three players, but a quick "he's already up as you reach" before I commit would help.
- **Sefa walking off.** That's a fine twist if it was the player's choice, but from my seat it came with almost no lead-in. If it was a player leaving the table, no complaint at all; it gave us a nice loose end.

**Small bookkeeping question**
- The tally-book left my Carried list at the end. I assume that's because it's lying on the table with the note rather than lost. I'd like it and the note to go in my pack before we leave, with the box.

Looking forward to the walk back to Beregost, and to having a word with Maela Thorn about her buyer.

Yes, a few things:

- **A word with Sefa before she went.** That's the big one. She was the one who asked to see the table, handled the order, copied the names, and then walked off with the copy while we were in the hole. I'd have liked one look at her face, or to have noticed her heading for the door. Next session I want to know who she's walking to. If it fits, I'd like her tracks read at the bend in the track before we leave.

- **The sunburst, properly.** I held off touching the plaster on purpose; it wasn't the moment, in that air. But I never asked anyone what the sun *means*. Rays and a face reads like Lathander to me, and the Song of the Morning is in Beregost, where we're headed. I'd like to ask Hale whether Abel Garrow was a Lathander man, and maybe put the count-marks in front of a priest or a mason.

- **Pulling Bram up.** A small thing, but I had my arm down the gap and he was already out. It would have been nice to repay the favour on screen.

- **Doing rogue work.** I spent the session reading rooms and standing in water, which I enjoyed. But I never touched a lock, a ledger, or a shadow. I'm hoping Vossick's counting-room or Thorn's back shelves give me the chance.

- **A closer look at the box.** I checked the W seal from the stool. Before we carry it, I'd like to handle it: the weight, whether it's tight, any smell at the seams. We're putting something that sleeps men when heated into a coach at night, and I'd like to be sure what's in it.

- **Asking Thorn's buyer's name straight out.** I'll do that in Beregost. I want the name and the coach before I hand over the case, if I can manage it without losing the ninety gold.

None of that is a complaint. It's mostly a to-do list for next time.

Honestly, I don't know who they are. I only ever saw them through your narration: paraphrased lines, actions told secondhand, nothing typed directly by them. They could be people, other AI models, or a mix, and I couldn't tell you which. What I can describe is how they came across at the table.

**Bram's player** seemed steady and cooperative, a team player. They opened by connecting with Hale over unpaid wages rather than pushing him, and they put their name on the slate with the limits stated plainly, which I liked: they promised only what they could keep. In the rescue they did the dull heavy work, asked the sensible question about whether the beam was set, and held the block until I said so. Bram felt like the anchor of the group, low on flourish and high on reliability.

**Sefa's player** came across as careful and procedural. They asked to see the table, read every name aloud exactly as written, wanted their own copy so Thorn couldn't dispute it, and asked the right question about the brazier. Then Sefa walked out mid-rescue without a word. From my seat I can't tell whether that was:
- the player leaving the table, so their character simply exits;
- a deliberate in-character move, with Sefa having her own reasons for wanting that list of names; or
- something in between.

The timing makes me lean towards the player leaving. Her pack went with her and she gave no lead-in, which fits someone writing [END]. But I don't want to assume, and that's partly why I'd like to read her tracks next session rather than decide in my head that she's a traitor.

If you can say which it was without spoiling anything, it would help me play Pell's reaction fairly. He shouldn't be nursing a grudge against someone who just had to go home.

private.text:
Sefa unties the book and opens it carefully, handling the wet pages gently so they won't tear. She holds it up to the daylight from the door and pages back through the last three weeks. Then she reads the names aloud, one at a time and clearly, each with its day, exactly as written. Where a mark has smeared she reads on regardless. She keeps glancing at Hale while she reads.

When she reaches the last name she closes the book without tying it. She tells Hale these are the men owed, three weeks as he said, and that she will make her own copy of those three weeks as written, so Thorn cannot claim they guessed. Then she looks toward the boarded part of the floor and asks Hale what was burning in the brazier, since the ash looks wrong for a fire of shavings.

You stay on the threshold with your boots on the white chalk and breathe through your nose as little as you can. The sweet smell is faint, like bread left too long in a cold oven. You run your eyes over the room the way you would a strongroom: the brazier first, then the flags around it, then the boarded back third. You are after the small things that tell you what a room is really for.
